Audit fees for organizations stuck at the 40 percent major-program coverage threshold typically run $8,000 to $20,000 higher per cycle than for comparable low-risk auditees.

The five low-risk criteria under 2 CFR 200.520 are mostly inside management's control: a clean Single Audit two years running, no material weaknesses in internal controls over major programs, no GAGAS qualified opinion, no fraud findings affecting major programs, and timely Federal Audit Clearinghouse submission.

The catch is that you cannot reverse-engineer eligibility at audit time. The two prior fiscal years either qualify or they do not.

The shops that consistently keep low-risk status track the criteria themselves quarter by quarter, the same way they track cash. The shops that lose it find out from the auditor in March.

Per the AICPA Government Audit Quality Center benchmarking work, the additional testing required for non-low-risk auditees is the single largest avoidable line item in most Single Audit engagements.

GrantPipe surfaces low-risk status indicators alongside grant compliance so the criteria do not get rediscovered at fieldwork.

#singleaudit #grantcompliance #nonprofitfinance #lowriskauditee

Myth: interest earned on a federal advance drawdown counts as program income.

Reality: it does not. Program income is governed by 2 CFR 200.307 and means revenue earned by the recipient that is directly generated by activities supported by the federal award. Interest on cash advances is a separate animal handled under 2 CFR 200.305(b)(9), which requires recipients to remit interest above $500 per year to the HHS Program Support Center.

The two get conflated because both involve money sitting in the recipient's bank account that was not in the original budget. They are not the same thing and they get reported on different schedules.

The other place this matters: the additive-versus-deductive treatment election under 2 CFR 200.307. Once made at award time, that election is binding for the life of the award. Most program officers never ask about it until the auditor does, and by then changing it requires retroactive correction.

If your sub-award says nothing about program income treatment, that is itself a finding waiting to happen.

#programincome #grantcompliance #2cfr200 #federalgrants

Steps 5 and 6 of the in-kind contribution valuation workflow are where most organizations create their next audit finding.

Step 5 is the journal entry. Under ASU 2020-07, debit the asset account (food inventory, supplies, property) or the relevant expense account if the goods are consumed in program delivery, and credit contribution revenue with or without donor restrictions depending on intent. Do not net in-kind gifts against expenses. Netting is the most common error and it understates both revenue and program expense on the 990.

Step 6 is the donor acknowledgment letter. IRS rules require written acknowledgment for any contribution of $250 or more. For in-kind gifts, the letter describes the goods or services in enough detail to support the donor's deduction but does not state a value — that is the donor's responsibility to substantiate.

The standard took effect for fiscal years beginning after June 15, 2021. Most organizations updated their journal entries and forgot to update their footnote disclosures. Audit firms catch this in year three.

#nonprofitaccounting #inkindcontributions #asu202007 #fasb

Pass-through entity, defined at 2 CFR 200.1: a non-federal entity that receives a federal award and provides a sub-award to a subrecipient that carries out part of the federal program.

Pass-through status is functional, not optional. The moment a recipient issues a sub-award, it becomes a pass-through entity for that portion of the award and inherits the responsibilities under 2 CFR 200.332.

Two examples that show how broad the definition is. A state department of health receives a $5M HHS grant and sub-awards $3M to 12 county health agencies — the state is the pass-through. A nonprofit receives a $1.2M DOL workforce grant and sub-awards $400,000 to a training partner for one program track — the nonprofit is a pass-through for that $400,000.

The 2 CFR 200.332 obligations include classifying every downstream relationship as subrecipient or contractor, performing risk assessments before issuing sub-awards, and monitoring throughout the period of performance. Pass-through amounts also flow onto the SEFA filed with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse.

If your organization writes checks to a partner under a federal grant, you are probably a pass-through entity. The right time to find out is before the agreement is signed.

#passthroughentity #2cfr200332 #subrecipientmonitoring #grantcompliance

Neon One is not a single product. It is a portfolio assembled through acquisition: Neon CRM at the center, Arts People for arts organizations, Rallybound for peer-to-peer, and a few others stacked around them.

The pitch is vendor consolidation. The reality for buyers is uneven module quality and a UX that varies depending on which acquired team built the surface you are looking at. Cross-module reporting is the place this shows up first — pulling a clean view across donor activity, event registrations, and grant tracking usually requires either a custom report build or an export-to-Excel step.

For organizations that mostly need donor management, Neon CRM on its own is a reasonable choice. For organizations that need donor CRM plus active grant management in one system, the bundle approach asks the buyer to integrate modules that were not designed together.

The tradeoff to know going in: you trade a single login for a sprawl that grows as Neon One acquires more products. Mid-sized nonprofits that already feel stretched thin tend to feel that sprawl most.

#nonprofittech #donorcrm #neonone #grantmanagement

Church donor management runs on a weekly cadence — tithes, offerings, designated gifts — not the quarterly cycle most nonprofit CRMs assume.

A typical secular nonprofit drops appeal letters in Q4, runs an end-of-year campaign, and cultivates major donors across a 12-month plan. A church processes giving every Sunday and every online gift in between, with designated funds for building campaigns, missions, benevolence, and youth programs running in parallel year-round.

When the same church also receives grants for secular programs — early childhood, food pantry, after-school — the data model gets more complicated. Restricted grant funds cannot be commingled with the General Fund or the Building Fund in the books, even if one bank account holds all of it.

Most church-specific tools handle the giving side well and ignore grants entirely. Most nonprofit CRMs handle grants and treat weekly tithing as an afterthought. The shops that get this right pick a system that separates donor giving records from restricted grant funds at the data layer, then maps both up to the appropriate fund balance under FASB ASC 958.

If your accounting system and your donor system disagree about which fund a check belongs to, you have a reconciliation problem waiting to happen.

#churchaccounting #fundaccounting #restrictedfunds #nonprofitfinance

A sub-award that is missing a required provision is a compliance finding even when the program runs perfectly.

2 CFR 200.332(a) lists the data elements that every sub-award document must contain before execution: federal award identification number, federal award date, sub-award amount, federal award project description, name of the federal awarding agency, CFDA/Assistance Listing number and title, indirect cost rate, and a statement of applicable requirements. Missing any one of them is a citable finding regardless of how well the subrecipient performs.

The most common gap on the audited list is the indirect cost rate — pass-through entities often leave it blank or use language that does not reference the negotiated rate or the de minimis 15 percent rate at 2 CFR 200.414(f).

The Subrecipient Agreement Checklist walks through every required provision under 2 CFR 200.332(a), the additional provisions that reduce monitoring risk, and program-specific additions that some federal programs require on top of the baseline. Use it before the agreement is signed, not after.

Free download in the resources section of the GrantPipe site.

Little Green Light at $45 to $200 per month versus GrantPipe at $329 to $1,079. The right answer depends on one variable: do you actively manage federal or foundation grants, or just donors.

Little Green Light is a strong tool for organizations under $500K in budget that are donor-funded and need clean gift entry, acknowledgments, and basic reporting. Any staff member can learn it without training. The ceiling shows up around $500K to $1M in budget when reporting needs go beyond what an Excel export can handle and when grant management enters the picture.

The wrong reason to pick either tool is current pricing. Replatforming in 18 months costs more than the price difference in any direction.

If your organization is past $500K in budget and your grant load is growing, the cheap tool stops being cheap when you outgrow it.

# What 5,000+ Nonprofit CRM Reviews Actually Tell Buyers in 2026

Across Capterra, G2, and Software Advice, more than 5,000 nonprofit CRM users have left ratings on the platforms they use every day. The aggregate picture as of early 2026 is striking: Little Green Light sits at 4.75/5, Bonterra/Network for Good at 4.72/5, Bloomerang at 4.66/5, and DonorPerfect at 4.55/5. Blackbaud Raiser's Edge NXT trails at 4.0 to 4.2/5 and Salesforce Nonprofit at 3.8 to 4.1/5. The gap between the top and bottom of the list — nearly a full point on a 5-point scale — is unusually large for a mature software category.

The 2025 Fifty & Fifty Nonprofit Peer Report adds the category-level frame: only 33.3 percent of nonprofits rate their CRM as effective, 46.5 percent are neutral, and 20.1 percent rate it outright ineffective. ITQlick's separate sentiment analysis confirms the pattern from a different methodology: DonorPerfect 85/100, Bloomerang 82/100, Neon CRM 80/100.

Aggregated reviews are not perfect, but the consistency across three independent review platforms and two independent sentiment data sources is hard to dismiss. The pattern is real. The question is what to do with it.

## The Tier Structure Vendor Marketing Hides

The data sorts cleanly into two tiers.

The purpose-built tier — Little Green Light, Bonterra, Bloomerang, DonorPerfect — sits above 4.5/5. These tools were built for nonprofit fundraising teams that do not have dedicated technical staff. They make a deliberate tradeoff: less customization in exchange for a working product on day one.

The mid-tier and enterprise tier — Neon CRM, Blackbaud Raiser's Edge NXT, Salesforce Nonprofit — sits between 3.8 and 4.3/5. These platforms offer more depth, more customization, and in Salesforce's case more integration surface than any other product in the market. The cost is implementation complexity that most mid-sized nonprofits cannot absorb without consultant support.

This tier structure is not a moral judgment. It is a fit signal. A platform that requires three months and $40,000 of consultant time to configure will deliver high satisfaction at a $50M-budget healthcare nonprofit and low satisfaction at a $2M community arts org. The review averages reflect the audience that actually buys each tool, weighted by how well that audience can support the tool after purchase.

## Why Ease of Use Wins

The single strongest predictor of overall rating across all 5,000+ reviews is one sub-score: ease of use. Platforms scoring above 4.5/5 on ease of use score above 4.5/5 overall. Platforms below 4.0/5 on ease of use — Blackbaud and Salesforce — pull their overall ratings down regardless of feature depth.

The staffing data explains why. Most mid-sized nonprofits do not employ a CRM administrator. The development director, the office manager, or the executive director themselves are the primary users. A platform that requires a trained admin to maintain will be used poorly by this group, regardless of what is theoretically possible inside it.

The NTEN Benchmarks Study found that 60 percent of fundraisers say better training would improve their technology use. Yet only 1 percent of nonprofit technology budgets goes to training. The result: tools that need training to deliver value are used at a fraction of their capability, and the satisfaction scores reflect that gap.

For software buyers, the practical implication is clear. The platform's feature ceiling matters less than its floor. The right question is not "what can this tool do?" but "what can this tool do without a consultant?"

## Enterprise Platforms Are Not Bad — They Are Mismatched

Salesforce Nonprofit and Blackbaud Raiser's Edge NXT score lower not because the products are weak. They score lower because most reviewers are not the audience the platforms were designed for.

Salesforce Nonprofit (formerly NPSP, now branded Agentforce Nonprofit) is the most customizable platform in the category. With consultant time and a clear data model, it can do almost anything. The 3.8 to 4.1/5 rating reflects organizations that adopted it under the free 10-license program, did not budget for implementation, and got stuck with a half-configured system. Salesforce retired NPSP development in March 2023 and is pushing customers toward Agentforce Nonprofit, which is a re-implementation rather than an upgrade. Only 25 percent of Salesforce nonprofit consultants have completed Nonprofit Cloud implementations as of early 2026, so the implementation supply is tight.

Blackbaud Raiser's Edge NXT carries different weight. Its depth in major-gift fundraising and wealth screening is unmatched in the category. The 4.0 to 4.2/5 rating reflects the learning curve, which steepens quickly for organizations without fundraising operations staff. For a $20M-budget university foundation, Blackbaud is often the right tool. For a $2M community nonprofit, it is overkill that becomes underused.

The pattern holds: enterprise tools deliver high value to organizations that can support them and low value to everyone else.

## Acquisitions Distort the Trailing Numbers

A static review average can hide a trajectory. Three acquisitions in the past three years are reshaping the data.

Bonterra emerged from the 2022 merger of EveryAction, Social Solutions, CyberGrants, and Network for Good. The Network for Good product still posts strong ratings (4.72/5), but reviews from the past 18 months increasingly cite declining customer service and integration confusion across the merged entity. The product is still well-regarded; the support experience is in transition. A 2026 buyer reading 2023 reviews is reading old information.

Bloomerang acquired Qgiv in 2023. Early signals suggest stable satisfaction, but pricing implications for existing customers are not yet fully clear and the integration is ongoing.

Salesforce's NPSP-to-Agentforce migration is the largest forced re-implementation the category has seen in a decade. Customers are not upgrading — they are rebuilding. Satisfaction data on the new platform is too sparse to draw conclusions.

When evaluating any nonprofit CRM, check the date range on the reviews you are reading. Filter to the last 12 months. A platform's 2023 rating may not reflect its 2026 reality, especially post-acquisition.

## A Practical Evaluation Framework

The review data supports a five-step approach for buyers who want to avoid the most common mistakes.

**Step 1: Define the actual user.** Who logs in every day? If the answer is "the development director and one part-time bookkeeper," the implementation profile is very different from "the development ops team and a Salesforce admin." Pick from the tier that matches the user, not the tier that matches the wishlist.

**Step 2: Filter reviews to the last 12 months.** Three of the major platforms have been in transition since 2023. Older reviews encode an experience that may no longer exist.

**Step 3: Read the ease-of-use sub-score before the overall rating.** This sub-score predicts post-implementation satisfaction better than any other data point in the public review corpus.

**Step 4: Price the implementation, not the subscription.** A $99/month tool that needs a $25,000 consultant to configure is a $25,099 first-year decision. A $499/month tool that works on day one is a $5,988 first-year decision. The subscription line is rarely the dominant cost.

**Step 5: Map grant management onto the same evaluation.** Most pure donor CRMs treat grants as an add-on or skip them entirely. If the organization manages active federal or foundation grants, the right system tracks restricted-fund balances, reporting deadlines, and budget-versus-actual against grant budgets in the same place donor records live. Splitting that across two systems creates a reconciliation problem that grows with the grant portfolio.

## The Single Most Common Mistake

The dominant failure mode in nonprofit CRM selection is buying for the demo, not for the staff.

Demos showcase the platform's ceiling. Daily use happens at the platform's floor. The 20.1 percent of nonprofits that rate their CRM ineffective did not buy a bad product — they bought a product that required staffing, training, or implementation budget the organization did not have. The product never reached the level shown in the sales call.

The countermeasure is to treat the user, not the feature list, as the binding constraint. If the development director cannot configure a new segment, build a saved view, or pull a board-ready report without help, the tool is the wrong fit, regardless of what the demo showed.

## What to Do This Week

For organizations currently evaluating a platform, pull the last 12 months of reviews on Capterra and G2 for every shortlisted product. Sort by the ease-of-use sub-score, not the overall rating. Verify the implementation timeline and cost in writing before committing.

For organizations already on a platform that scores below 4/5, the right move is rarely an immediate switch. The right move is identifying which specific workflows are broken — segment building, gift entry, grant tracking, board reporting — and quantifying the time cost. A platform decision should rest on hours saved per month, not vendor preference.

For organizations weighing donor management and grant compliance separately, GrantPipe is built for the case where both belong in one system: donor CRM, restricted-fund tracking, and grant reporting in a single platform, priced for mid-sized nonprofits that need real depth on both sides without an enterprise implementation.

A grant writer starts the year with 30 to 50 prospects on a spreadsheet. By Q2 the deadlines have shifted, two program officers have changed jobs, the organization has pivoted one program, and the spreadsheet has not kept up.

The writing itself is maybe 70 percent of the role. The other 30 is pipeline hygiene — tracking deadlines, reusing narrative content across submissions, and handing off won awards to the grants manager with the budget intact.

The handoff is where most awarded grants quietly start losing money. The proposal said one thing, the grants manager inherits another, and by the second drawdown the budget categories no longer line up with what the funder approved.

Question for the grant writers and development directors here: when you win a grant, what does your handoff to compliance actually look like? Is it a meeting, a folder, an email thread, or a system that carries the budget and narrative forward without retyping?

The answer says a lot about how your post-award reporting will go six months from now.

The average mid-sized nonprofit uses three donor segments — everyone, major donors, and lapsed donors. Organizations with strong retention programs use fifteen or more.

The difference is not the technology. It is whether the segmentation tool stays current as donor records change, or whether it requires a manual Excel export every time someone wants a list.

Donor segmentation in GrantPipe is a saved-filter system. Build a segment once using any combination of giving history, recency, source, fund, custom fields, and demographics. The segment stays current automatically as gifts post and contact records update. A segment named "Major Gift Prospects — Not Yet Asked" might filter on lifetime giving between $5,000 and $24,999, last gift within 18 months, no open ask in the pipeline, and a custom field flagging board referral.

The segments drive everything downstream — appeal lists, stewardship workflows, board reports, and renewal campaigns — without re-exporting. When a donor's giving crosses a threshold, they move into the new segment automatically the next time the filter runs.

If your org is operating on three segments because building more is too much work, the tool is the bottleneck.

The nonprofit CRM market reached $846 million in 2025, and 48% of nonprofits are actively considering switching platforms in the next 12 months — up from 10% the year before.

For mid-sized nonprofits running both, that gap is operational drag, not a feature checklist. The vendor you sign with today may be a different company in two years. Prioritize data portability and contract flexibility over brand loyalty.

Myth: software marketed as "grant tracking" handles post-award compliance.

Reality: most of it covers the pre-award pipeline only. Pre-award is grant discovery, application stages, deadline reminders, award decisions. Post-award is restricted fund balances by budget category, expenditures linked to grant lines, and SF-425-ready compliance reports pulled from real posted transactions.

The two are different problems with different data models. A tool that tracks "applied → awarded → reporting" without ever touching the GL is a calendar with a logo. It cannot answer the only question that matters at audit: did the dollars spent against this grant match the approved budget categories.

Three capabilities separate compliance tools from pipeline trackers — restricted fund balance tracking by budget category, expenditure documentation linked to individual grant budget lines, and compliance report generation from actual expenditure data. If a tool cannot do those three, it tracks grants informally.

Foundant GrantHub Pro was sunset January 31, 2026, and never covered restricted fund tracking in the first place. Buyers searching for a GrantHub replacement should be very clear about which problem they are actually solving.

The mistake most buyers make is searching for "grant tracking software" when what they actually need is post-award compliance.

Step 4 of responding to a Single Audit finding: draft the Corrective Action Plan with all five required elements under 2 CFR 200.511(c).

The five elements are the finding reference number, the auditee's position (agree or disagree), the specific corrective action, the named responsible party with title, and the target completion date. Vague language like "management will strengthen controls" is not acceptable and produces a follow-up letter from the awarding agency.

Step 5 is committing realistic timelines. Aggressive but achievable — typically 30 to 180 days depending on complexity. A policy update closes in 30. A system implementation may need 180. Missed CAP deadlines become a finding in the next year's audit, which is how organizations end up in repeat-finding territory.

The package is due the earlier of 30 days after the auditor's report or nine months after fiscal year-end, per 2 CFR 200.512(a)(1). The CAP is part of that package and travels with the report to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse at harvester.census.gov.

A strong CAP reads like a project plan, not a compliance document. "The CFO will update the procurement policy by May 31, circulate it with attestations, and present completed attestations to the audit committee at the June meeting" is what auditors and program officers want to see.

#singleaudit #2cfr200 #correctiveactionplan #grantcompliance

The Unique Entity Identifier is a 12-character alphanumeric code assigned by SAM.gov. It replaced DUNS effective April 4, 2022.

Without an active UEI and current SAM.gov registration, a federal grant recipient cannot draw funds — even on an award already in flight. SAM.gov registration is valid for 12 months. There is no grace period. A registration that lapses on Tuesday halts payments on Wednesday.

The UEI is not the EIN. The EIN is the IRS tax identifier. The UEI is the SAM.gov procurement and grants identifier. Both are required, both go on federal applications, and they are different numbers stored in different systems.

Domestic activation runs 7 to 14 business days, with IRS verification typically the bottleneck. Renewal reminders go out 60 days before expiration. The recommended practice is to start renewal on the first reminder, not the last one.

Pass-through entities have a separate obligation under 2 CFR 200.332: collect the subrecipient's UEI before executing any sub-award and check the SAM.gov exclusions list. If the subrecipient is not registered, the pass-through cannot legally execute the agreement.

Registration lapses are among the top five administrative reasons OMB cites for delayed grant drawdowns. The fix is calendar discipline, not a software purchase.

#uei #samgov #federalgrants #grantcompliance

Bloomerang Standard runs $125 per month for up to 1,000 records and Pro runs $249 per month for up to 5,000. Capterra puts it at 4.66 out of 5 across more than 1,286 reviews — second highest in the nonprofit CRM category.

The product earns those numbers honestly on the donor side. The retention dashboard, lapse-risk indicators, and donor timeline are the most developed in the under-$300 tier. Development staff coming off spreadsheets find it intuitive on day one.

The gap is grants. Bloomerang has no grant lifecycle module — not a thin one, a complete absence. No restricted fund tracking, no budget-versus-actual against grant line items, no compliance report generation. An organization that wins a $500,000 federal grant cannot model where the restricted dollars go inside Bloomerang.

The result for grant-receiving nonprofits is a parallel system: Bloomerang for donors, a spreadsheet or standalone tracker for grants. Duplicate entry, manual reconciliation, and compliance records that drift away from CRM records by month six.

The honest evaluation question is whether the organization is donor-funded or grant-funded. Donor-funded under $5M with no restricted grant exposure — Bloomerang is a strong choice. Grant-receiving with three or more active awards — the parallel-system tax becomes the actual cost.

Per-record pricing also keeps climbing as the database grows.

#bloomerang #nonprofitcrm #grantmanagement #donormanagement

A church that receives a USDA Community Food Projects grant cannot spend a single grant dollar on worship services, religious instruction, or staff time supporting religious activities — even if the food pantry runs out of the same building.

Federal funding requires documented separation between grant-funded secular programs and religious activity. That means tracking personnel time by grant-funded versus religious duties, allocating facility costs proportionally, and documenting that grant participants were not required to participate in religious activities. Reconstructed records at audit time do not satisfy the standard.

The data structure most congregations already use makes this harder than it looks. Building Fund, Missions Fund, General Fund, and youth program designations are restricted in the church's internal sense. They are not the same as grant restriction. Commingling a federal award into the General Fund creates Form 990 reporting errors and audit exposure.

There are roughly 380,000 religious congregations in the U.S. with combined annual revenue of $100-$120 billion (Duke National Congregations Study). Faith-based organizations account for about 32% of all U.S. charitable giving (Giving USA 2023). FEMA Public Assistance, USDA Community Food Projects, and historic preservation grants are the most common federal entry points.

The compliance fix is fund separation enforced at the transaction level — not a tag retroactively applied to a journal entry someone already posted to the wrong account.

#churchaccounting #fundaccounting #faithbasednonprofits #federalgrants

Federal grant closeout is not a single event. It starts 90 days before the period of performance ends and continues for 3 to 7 years after the grant formally closes.

The 90-day mark is for budget-versus-actual review, no-cost extension decisions, and subrecipient closeout planning. The 30-day mark is for equipment review (capitalization threshold $10,000 under 2 CFR 200.313), unspent funds calculation, and the final obligation lock. The final week is for expenditure lock and reconciliation to the dollar against the accounting system.

Post-period, the final SF-425 is due within 120 calendar days for most agencies, 90 days for some HUD programs. The cumulative federal expenditures on that report must match the GL exactly. A discrepancy is an audit finding.

Record retention under 2 CFR 200.334 is 3 years from the date of final expenditure report submission — not from the period end date. USDA and HUD programs commonly require 7 years. Records involved in pending audits, litigation, or claims must be retained until the matter resolves.

Bloomerang wins on donor retention analytics — the lapse-risk dashboard and donor timeline are the most developed in this tier. Keela wins narrowly on grant tracking because Bloomerang has none and Keela has a basic module covering funder records, grant amounts, status, and deadline reminders. Basic, not compliance-grade.

For an Executive Director who signs a federal grant agreement, that distinction is the whole game. The ED takes on personal accountability for fund separation and compliance reporting under the agreement. Neither platform tracks restricted fund balances by budget category. Neither produces budget-versus-actual against approved grant line items. Neither generates compliance documentation that survives a Single Audit.

Three-year cost on 2,500 contacts is roughly $6,120 for Bloomerang and $5,400 for Keela, both scaling with contact volume. Add a separate grant tool for compliance and the gap closes against any unified option.

If donors are the entire universe — Bloomerang. If grants are part of it — neither, by themselves.

# Time and Effort Certification: The Federal Grant Compliance Step Most Nonprofits Get Wrong

A nonprofit that charges $400,000 of staff salary to a federal award over twelve months and cannot produce after-the-fact time records owes the federal awarding agency $400,000. Not a portion. The full amount. Personnel costs without supporting time and effort documentation are disallowed in full under 2 CFR 200.430, and the repayment obligation does not scale down for partial documentation.

This is the compliance area that creates more dollar-for-dollar exposure than any other in federal grant management. Personnel costs are 65 to 75 percent of total expenditures on most human services, health, and victim services awards. The HHS Office of Inspector General lists inadequate time and effort documentation as a top-three cause of disallowed costs across federal grant single audits.

The rule is short. The execution is where organizations get into trouble.

## What 2 CFR 200.430 Actually Requires

The Uniform Guidance section governing personnel cost documentation says that records must "accurately reflect the work performed" and be "supported by a system of internal controls which provides reasonable assurance that the charges are accurate, allowable, and properly allocated."

Three principles flow out of that language.

First, the after-the-fact rule. The record must be created based on what happened, not what was planned. The certification covers a period that has already ended. The certified allocation may differ from the budget — and that is acceptable, even required, when actual time differed from budget.

Second, the certifier qualification. The employee can certify their own record. A supervisor with first-hand knowledge of the work performed can certify on behalf of the employee. A finance officer signing timesheets for program staff she does not directly oversee does not have first-hand knowledge.

Third, the documentation must be retained. Under 2 CFR 200.334, time records are kept for 3 years from the date of the final expenditure report for the award. Lost or disorganized records are treated the same as missing records.

The 2024 Uniform Guidance revision confirmed that electronic time records are fully acceptable. A paper timesheet, a spreadsheet, a project tracking tool, or a payroll system with project coding are all acceptable formats — provided the after-the-fact rule and the certifier qualification are satisfied.

## The Most Common Failure Pattern

The most common compliance failure is signing a timesheet that simply copies the budget percentages.

If an employee was budgeted 60 percent to one grant and 40 percent to another, and the timesheet shows exactly 60/40 every month for three years without variation, auditors treat this as presumptive evidence of a budget-based allocation rather than an after-the-fact record. Real work does not produce flat percentages over multiple years. Programs ramp, staff cover for absences, priorities shift across reporting periods. A record that never moves is a record that was never actually filled out from observation.

The second pattern is the payroll system that auto-allocates without employee confirmation. ADP, Paychex, and QuickBooks Payroll can be configured to automatically code an employee's pay to a specific grant each period. The configuration is convenient. It is also a budget-based allocation unless the employee or supervisor confirms the allocation at period end. Auto-allocation without confirmation fails the after-the-fact rule.

The third pattern is the inappropriate certifier. The CFO or finance director signs the timesheet because she controls payroll. She does not have first-hand knowledge of what the program staff actually did. A program director who works alongside or directly oversees the staff member is the right certifier. A supervisor two levels removed who only sees the budget is not.

## The Five-Step Certification Workflow

Organizations that get this right run a standard cycle. The cycle is not complicated. It is the discipline of running it consistently that separates clean audits from disallowed costs.

**Step 1 — Identify all employees with grant-funded time.** Build the list at the start of each project year. Include executives if any portion of their time is budgeted to an award. Update when staff change or budget allocations shift. Missing one employee on this list is the easiest way to end up with no documentation for that employee at audit.

**Step 2 — Choose a record format and stick with it.** Paper timesheets, a spreadsheet template, a time-tracking tool like Harvest or Toggl, or a payroll system with project coding plus end-of-period confirmation. The format matters less than the consistency. Over-engineered systems generate poor compliance because staff avoid them. Under-engineered systems lose data.

**Step 3 — Establish a certification cycle.** Semi-monthly or monthly is the practical standard. The regulation does not specify a frequency, but records certified less frequently than monthly create gaps between actual work and certification. Memory degrades. Contemporaneous records are the goal.

**Step 4 — Separate federal award time from non-award time, and split between awards.** Employees splitting time across awards must show how each period was distributed. When an employee splits between federal awards and non-federal activities, both sides must be documented. Organizations sometimes certify the federal portion and leave the non-federal portion blank — that gap fails the standard.

**Step 5 — Store certified records with audit access.** Three years from final expenditure report submission, organized by award and period, in a location the audit team can pull on request. The grant might have closed in 2025. The records still need to be findable in 2028.

## The Special Rule for 100-Percent Time Employees

Under 2 CFR 200.430(i)(1), employees who work solely on a single federal award may use semi-annual certifications rather than detailed period-by-period timesheets. The conditions are specific.

The employee's effort must be confirmed as 100 percent to a single award for the entire semi-annual period. The certification must be signed by the employee or a supervisor with direct knowledge. The organization must maintain supporting documentation that the employee's duties during the period were consistent with the award's scope.

This exception applies only when there is genuinely no split. If the employee did any work on other awards or non-award activities during the period, even briefly, semi-annual certification fails and period-level records are required. Auditors test this. The exception is narrower than it looks.

## Cost Transfers and Time Records

Time and effort documentation interacts directly with cost transfers — moving previously posted salary from one award to another.

A cost transfer that moves a salary charge from Grant A to Grant B must be supported by time records showing the employee actually worked on Grant B during the period being adjusted. Without those records, the transfer fails the benefit test regardless of whether the timing was within the allowed window.

The right workflow checks time records before initiating personnel cost transfers, not after. Organizations that discover at the point of the transfer that records do not support the reallocation have two options — abandon the transfer or reconstruct records. Retroactive reconstruction is not acceptable. The first option is the only legitimate one.

This is a frequent finding pattern in fiscal years that include grant restructuring. Cost transfers proliferate during budget changes, and time records do not always keep up.

## The Three Findings Auditors Find Most Often

Single audit findings on time and effort cluster into three categories.

Budget-based certifications — timesheets that mirror budget percentages without variation — are the most frequent. The fix is reviewing certified percentages period-over-period before submission and asking the employee or supervisor whether they actually reflect what happened.

Missing records — time records not collected for all covered periods or all covered employees — are second. The fix is the master list at the start of the project year, plus a tracking mechanism for late or missing certifications. Letting a single period slide creates a gap that does not fill itself in.

Inappropriate certifier — certifications signed by finance staff without direct knowledge of the employee's work — are third. The fix is identifying the right certifier when the employee is added to the master list, not when the timesheet is being signed.

A pattern of any of these across the audit sample produces a significant audit finding. In major programs, this can escalate to a material weakness, which carries different consequences for the organization's audit risk rating in subsequent years.

## What This Costs When It Goes Wrong

The dollar exposure is direct. A salary charge without supporting time records is an unallowable cost. Unallowable costs are repaid to the awarding agency in full, not at a partial rate. A single year of a $50,000 program staffer charged to a federal award without proper records is a $50,000 repayment obligation, plus any associated fringe.

The indirect exposure is the audit rating downgrade. Repeat findings under 2 CFR 200.208 can trigger specific conditions — prior approval requirements, enhanced reporting, high-risk auditee designation. These conditions persist until the underlying issue is resolved, and they affect every federal award the organization holds.

The opportunity cost is staff time spent on remediation. Reconstructing missing records, responding to questioned costs, and revising the corrective action plan often consume more staff hours than running the certification cycle correctly would have required in the first place.

## What to Do This Week

Pull the list of employees whose pay is charged to any federal award. For each one, identify who has first-hand knowledge of their work and who currently signs the certification. Where those names do not match, fix it.

Pull the last twelve months of certifications for any employee splitting time across awards. Look at the percentages. If they are flat — exactly 60/40 every month, or exactly 50/50 every month — the next certification needs to reflect actual variation. Continued flat percentages will read as budget-based.

Set the certification cadence at monthly if it is not already there, and put the due date on a calendar with reminders. Late certifications signed more than 30 days after period end are a deficiency, and the calendar discipline is the cheapest insurance available.

# Form 990 Filing: What Mid-Sized Nonprofits Get Wrong, and How to Fix It Before May 15

A $4M nonprofit with a December 31 fiscal year owes the IRS a Form 990 by May 15. Miss the deadline three years running and tax-exempt status is automatically revoked under IRC Section 6033(j). Reinstatement is a separate application, and the lapse covers the period of non-filing — meaning donations received during the gap may not have been deductible.

That is the headline risk. The day-to-day risk is more mundane and more common: the wrong form filed, the wrong schedules attached, the public copy of Schedule B mishandled, or executive compensation reported in a way that pulls an audit trigger that should never have been pulled.

This guide walks the filing decisions that mid-sized nonprofits get wrong most often — and the practitioner answers for each.

## Which version of the 990

The form an organization files is a function of two numbers: gross receipts and total assets.

Form 990 (full): required if gross receipts are $200,000 or more, or total assets are $500,000 or more. Either threshold triggers the full return.

Form 990-EZ: available only if gross receipts are less than $200,000 and total assets are less than $500,000. Both thresholds must be under.

Form 990-N (e-Postcard): available if gross receipts are normally $50,000 or less. Eight pieces of identifying information, filed online, no financial detail.

Form 990-PF: required for all private foundations regardless of size.

Two practitioner notes. First, gross receipts is not net revenue. A $190,000 gross-receipts nonprofit that processes $400,000 through a fiscal sponsor relationship may need a closer look — gross receipts in some scenarios includes amounts received before netting. Second, total assets is the year-end number from the balance sheet, not an average. A one-time gift that lands on December 30 can push an organization across the $500,000 threshold for that year only.

## Due date and the automatic extension

The return is due on the 15th day of the 5th month after fiscal year end. For calendar-year filers, that is May 15.

The automatic 6-month extension is granted by filing Form 8868 by the original due date. It is not discretionary. No reason is required. The extension is the default move for any organization that does not have a clean reason to file early — audited financial statements are usually not finalized in time for the original deadline anyway, and filing a 990 that conflicts with the audited statements is one of the most cited inconsistency triggers.

For December 31 fiscal year filers, the extended deadline is November 15. That is enough time to align the 990 with audited statements, finalize Schedule J compensation analysis, and reconcile restricted net asset categories — three places where rushed returns produce inconsistent figures.

## Schedules: which ones and why

The full 990 is a 12-page form. The schedules are where most of the actual work and most of the audit exposure lives.

Schedule A (Public Charity Status and Public Support): required for all 501(c)(3) public charities. The public support test is a five-year calculation. Get it wrong and the organization can be reclassified as a private foundation, which carries excise taxes and stricter rules on grants.

Schedule B (Schedule of Contributors): required when contributions meet specific thresholds. The big change is on the public copy, covered below.

Schedule C (Political Campaign and Lobbying Activities): required if any lobbying or political activity occurred. The 501(h) election changes the calculation, and organizations that filed Form 5768 should know which method applies.

Schedule D (Supplemental Financial Statements): required for restricted endowments, conservation easements, art and museum collections, escrow arrangements, and other items. Restricted-fund nonprofits almost always file Schedule D.

Schedule G (Fundraising Activities): required if gross fundraising receipts exceed $15,000. Special events are reported here in a way that ties back to Part VIII of the core form.

Schedule J (Compensation Information): required when any officer, director, or key employee earns more than $150,000, or when other thresholds are met. This is where executive compensation gets scrutinized.

Schedule L (Transactions with Interested Persons): required for certain related-party transactions. Loans to officers, business dealings with board members, grants to related organizations.

There are more — Schedules F, H, I, K, M, N, O, R each apply in specific scenarios. The point for finance teams: confirm the schedule list before fieldwork starts, not in mid-April.

## The Schedule B donor disclosure change

Revenue Procedure 2018-38 and subsequent litigation reshaped the public-disclosure rules for Schedule B.

The current state: most tax-exempt organizations other than 501(c)(3) public charities are exempt from including donor names and addresses on the publicly-disclosed copy of Schedule B. Public charities still report contributor names and addresses on the IRS copy, but the publicly available version may omit donor identifying information.

Two failure modes show up in practice. First, tax software that has not been updated correctly produces a public copy that still includes donor names — this is the more common error and it has resulted in inadvertent donor disclosure that violated state-law expectations. Second, organizations that wrongly believe they are fully exempt from Schedule B and do not file it with the IRS at all.

The fix is procedural. Before the return is filed, someone other than the preparer reviews both the IRS copy and the public-inspection copy of Schedule B. The two copies should be different documents in the workpapers. If they look identical, the public copy was probably never redacted.

## The Form 990 to audited financials reconciliation

The single most common audit trigger for mid-sized nonprofits is not high executive compensation. It is inconsistency between the Form 990 and the audited financial statements.

The IRS knows the audited statements exist. State charity regulators ask for both. Watchdog sites pull both. Discrepancies between the two are the cheapest red flag a reviewer can find.

Common discrepancies. Net asset categories that do not match — temporarily restricted on one document, with donor restrictions on the other, with no reconciliation. Special event revenue reported gross on the 990 but net on the audit. Functional expense allocations that differ because they were prepared by different people from different worksheets. Restricted contribution revenue recognized on different bases.

The fix is sequencing. Audit first. 990 second. Reconciliation memo in the workpapers explaining any presentation differences and why each is appropriate. The audited financials are the primary source. The 990 follows.

## The most-cited audit triggers

Six patterns get cited most often in IRS Form 990 examination summaries.

High executive compensation relative to organization size, especially when comparable-data documentation is missing. Significant related-party transactions on Schedule L. Large unexplained changes in program service descriptions year over year. Discrepancies between Part VII compensation and Schedule J detail. Failure to consistently report restricted and temporarily restricted net assets — often a leftover from the FASB ASC 958-205 transition that some organizations never fully completed. Inconsistent figures between the 990 and audited financial statements.

None of these are aggressive positions. All of them are documentation gaps. The trigger is not the underlying activity — it is the lack of supporting workpapers when the IRS asks.

## The state extension question

The federal Form 8868 extension does not automatically extend every state charitable-registration renewal.

California's RRF-1 follows the federal extension automatically when properly documented. Many other states do not. New York's CHAR500 has its own extension form. Pennsylvania's BCO-10 is independent. Several states do not recognize the federal extension at all.

Multi-state filers should keep a one-page matrix: state, registration form, extension policy, due date with extension. Update it annually. The matrix takes 30 minutes to build the first time and prevents the late filing that triggers state penalties.

## The single most common failure

The most common failure mode is filing the 990 before the audit is complete and assuming the figures will match.

They do not match. The audit adjusts net asset categories, reclassifies restricted contributions, finalizes functional expense allocations, and trues up accruals. The 990 filed in April with preliminary numbers does not survive the audit unchanged. The result is either an amended return — which itself flags the file — or two public documents that disagree.

The fix is to use Form 8868. The automatic 6-month extension exists for exactly this reason.

## What to do this week

For a calendar-year organization with May 15 approaching:

File Form 8868 before May 15 if the audit is not finalized. The extension is automatic and costs nothing.

Confirm the filing version. Recompute gross receipts and total assets at year-end values. If either crosses the threshold, the full 990 applies regardless of last year's filing.

Build the schedule list before the preparer does. Schedule A, B, D, G, J, L are the high-frequency ones for mid-sized nonprofits. Confirm whether each applies.

Pull the 2024 audited financials and the prior-year 990. The current-year 990 needs to reconcile to both — to the audit for current numbers, to the prior 990 for trend comparability.

Have someone other than the preparer review the public copy of Schedule B against the IRS copy. They should not be identical.

# SEFA Preparation Checklist: Where 80% of Single Audit Findings Originate

The Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards is the foundation of every single audit. Auditors use it to determine which programs are "major programs" requiring opinions on compliance. When the SEFA is wrong, audit scope expands, fieldwork compresses, and findings multiply. The OMB Single Audit Quality Study has cited SEFA cluster-identification errors as one of the top five recurring findings, appearing in roughly 30% of audited entities with multiple federal programs.

Most SEFA errors are not accounting mistakes. They are classification errors: programs that should be in a cluster get listed separately, pass-through subrecipient data is missing, indirect costs are omitted from program expenditures, or pass-through awards are filed under the state agency that disbursed the cash rather than the prime federal agency. Each of these has a specific fix.

## What the SEFA Has to Show

Per 2 CFR 200.510(b), each line of the SEFA must include the federal agency name, pass-through entity name when applicable, the Assistance Listing Number (ALN, formerly the CFDA number), federal program name, program cluster name when applicable, total expenditures, and amounts passed to subrecipients. The SEFA is a supplemental schedule — not part of the basic financial statements, but presented with them — and it is management's representation of every federal program the organization administered during the fiscal year.

The single audit threshold is $1,000,000 in federal expenditures during the fiscal year per 2 CFR 200.501(a). This figure has been in place since the 2014 Uniform Guidance and was retained in the 2024 revision. Organizations crossing the threshold must file a single audit; organizations operating just below it should track aggregate federal expenditures month-by-month so the trigger does not arrive as a surprise.

The Federal Audit Clearinghouse receives roughly 30,000 single audit submissions annually. The volume is large; the rules are specific. Knowing what each column requires is the difference between a clean opinion and a finding.

## The Five-Part Preparation Framework

A reliable SEFA preparation process has five named components. Each addresses a specific failure mode auditors have flagged repeatedly across federal awarding agencies.

### Part 1: The Federal Award Inventory

Pull a complete list of all federal awards active during the fiscal year, including awards that started or ended mid-year. Three categories must appear: direct federal awards (received from a federal agency), pass-through federal awards (received from a state agency, local government, or another nonprofit acting as pass-through entity), and federal cost-reimbursement contracts.

The most common omission is pass-through funding from state agencies that administer federal programs. A state Department of Health receiving HHS dollars and disbursing them to nonprofits is a pass-through entity. The award is federal, not state, on the SEFA. State workforce boards distributing Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act dollars are passing federal funds. The same is true for state arts agencies disbursing NEA grants-to-states.

Capturing pass-through status at award acceptance — when the grant agreement is signed — is far more reliable than reconstructing it during SEFA prep. The grant agreement should disclose the federal source. If it does not, the pass-through entity is required to provide that information under 2 CFR 200.332.

### Part 2: ALN Lookup and Verification

Look up each program's ALN at SAM.gov. The format is XX.XXX (for example, 93.914 for HIV Emergency Relief, 10.561 for SNAP, 84.063 for Federal Pell Grants). Every SEFA row requires an ALN.

For pass-through awards, the pass-through entity is required to provide the ALN in the award agreement. If it is missing, contact the pass-through entity and request it before SEFA finalization. Awards without an ALN cannot be correctly reported on the SEFA.

ALNs change over time as programs are reorganized at the federal level. Using a stale ALN from a prior-year grant agreement is a finding when the auditor cross-references against the current SAM.gov listing. The verification step is brief; the cost of skipping it is not.

### Part 3: Cluster Identification

This is where 80% of cluster-related findings originate. OMB defines program clusters in Appendix VI to 2 CFR Part 200 and updates the cluster list annually in the OMB Compliance Supplement. A cluster groups related programs — Research and Development cluster, Student Financial Aid cluster, SNAP cluster, Aging cluster — and treats them as one program for major-program selection.

When an organization receives funding under multiple ALNs that belong to a defined cluster, those ALNs must be grouped on the SEFA and labeled with the cluster name. An organization receiving funds under ALN 93.914 (HIV Emergency Relief) and ALN 93.917 (Ryan White Part B), both in the same cluster, must list them together as a cluster — not as two standalone programs.

Listing them separately understates cluster expenditures. The auditor uses cluster totals in major-program determination under 2 CFR 200.518. Misclassifying a cluster shifts which programs get tested, which can either expand scope (additional programs become major) or undertest (a program that should have been major is treated as non-major).

The OMB Compliance Supplement is updated each year. The current year's supplement controls. Cluster membership shifts year to year, particularly as new programs are added or older programs are reorganized. Use the current supplement, not a prior year's reference document.

### Part 4: Pass-Through Subrecipient Reporting

For each program where the organization passes federal funds to a subrecipient, the SEFA must identify the total amount passed through and the names of the subrecipient organizations. 2 CFR 200.510(b)(4) requires this disclosure regardless of dollar amount. A $5,000 subaward from a $500,000 federal grant must be disclosed.

This is one of the most common findings in HHS-funded single audits. The omission usually traces to subawards that were administered outside the grants management process — small community-partner grants treated as program expenses rather than as pass-through activity.

Document the subrecipient's UEI number, prior DUNS if available, and the federal program ALN under which the funds passed. Subrecipient monitoring documentation is a separate requirement under 2 CFR 200.332; the SEFA disclosure is only the dollar amount and the subrecipient identification.

### Part 5: Reconciliation to the General Ledger

Every dollar on the SEFA must trace to a general ledger transaction. Auditors reconcile SEFA to GL detail. Unexplained differences become findings.

Common reconciling items that must be explained in the notes to the SEFA: accrued expenditures recognized in one period and paid in another, indirect cost allocations posted at year-end versus grants-paid basis, deferred revenue for federal advances not yet earned, and cost-sharing contributions if separately tracked.

Indirect costs deserve special attention. Indirect costs charged to a federal award are federal expenditures and belong on the SEFA. Organizations that omit indirect cost recovery understate program activity and may misidentify which programs cross the major-program threshold. For organizations using a negotiated indirect cost rate (NICRA), include the indirect costs recovered during the year. For organizations using the de minimis rate (now 15% of modified total direct costs under the 2024 revision), include indirect costs at that rate. The SEFA notes must disclose which rate was used.

## Step-by-Step Preparation Sequence

The five-part framework translates into a numbered preparation sequence:

1. Compile the federal award inventory from grant agreements and subaward notifications. Capture pass-through entity information at award acceptance, not at year-end.

2. Verify ALN for every program against the current SAM.gov Assistance Listings.

3. Reference Appendix VI to 2 CFR Part 200 and the current OMB Compliance Supplement to identify clusters. Group ALNs that belong together.

4. Calculate expenditures per program — direct costs, allocated indirect costs, and subaward amounts — using the accrual basis unless the award requires cash basis.

5. Document each pass-through subrecipient with name, UEI, and amount passed through under each ALN.

6. Address loan and loan guarantee programs separately under 2 CFR 200.502. Outstanding balances plus current-year disbursements are typically reportable.

7. Reconcile SEFA totals to federal revenue per the Statement of Activities. Document every reconciling item.

8. Prepare SEFA notes disclosing basis of accounting, indirect cost rate (NICRA or de minimis), and significant accounting policies.

9. Deliver the SEFA to the auditor at least 30 days before fieldwork begins.

For a well-maintained ledger with grant coding throughout the year, this sequence takes 8 to 16 hours. Organizations reconstructing grant detail from function-level coding can spend 40+ hours, with material risk of error.

## The Single Most Common Failure

The single most common SEFA failure is not a math error. It is reporting pass-through awards under the pass-through entity instead of under the prime federal agency.

A nonprofit receiving CDBG dollars from a state Housing Finance Agency is receiving HUD funds. The SEFA must list the program under HUD with the HFA disclosed as the pass-through entity. Filing it under "State Housing Finance Agency" as a state grant fails the classification test entirely.

This error appears every audit cycle because the cash receipt looks like state revenue in the bank — the wire is from the state agency, the contract is signed with the state, the reporting flows back to the state. The federal source is upstream, not visible in day-to-day operations. The fix is capturing federal-source status at the moment the grant agreement is reviewed, not trying to reverse-engineer it from a state-issued check.

GAO has identified incomplete SEFA as a material weakness classification risk. $1.17 trillion of federal award spending from 2017-2021 was linked to severe and persistent single audit findings according to GAO April 2024 analysis. The classification problem is at the core of those numbers.

## What to Do This Week

If your organization is approaching fiscal year-end with federal awards, run three checks now rather than at SEFA prep time. First, list every active federal award and confirm the pass-through entity for each — identify the prime federal agency, not just the entity that issued the contract. Second, pull the current OMB Compliance Supplement Appendix VI and verify cluster membership for each ALN. Third, run a query of subaward payments and confirm every subrecipient is captured with name and amount, regardless of dollar size.

These three checks take a few hours. They prevent the most common findings on a document that drives audit scope.

GrantPipe tracks expenditures by award and ALN as costs are incurred, captures pass-through entity status at award acceptance, and flags subrecipient relationships at grant setup — making SEFA preparation a report run rather than an annual reconstruction exercise. The grant inventory, ALN, pass-through chain, and subrecipient data are captured at the source, not rebuilt from email and contract files in the days before fieldwork.

# How to Calculate Donor Retention Rate (With Formula and Example)

A nonprofit closes the fiscal year with 150 donors. Twelve months later, 65 of those original 150 give again. That is a 43.3% retention rate, sitting almost exactly on the sector average — and it means 85 donors from the prior year are gone, taking their fundraising investment, relationship-building time, and future revenue with them.

Most organizations do not calculate this number. They look at total dollars raised, total donor count, and major gift activity, but the retention rate itself rarely appears on the development director's dashboard. The first step in fixing donor retention is knowing the number, and a surprising share of nonprofits cannot pull it from their current system without a manual VLOOKUP across two year-end exports.

## The Formula

The donor retention rate formula is straightforward:

**(Donors who gave in the current year who also gave in the prior year) / (Total donors who gave in the prior year) x 100**

The denominator is always the prior year's donor count, not the current year. The denominator represents the population the organization is trying to retain.

If 150 donors gave in 2024 and 65 of them also gave in 2025, the retention rate is 65 / 150 x 100 = 43.3%. The 85 who lapsed are the gap. To maintain 2024 revenue without growing it, the organization had to acquire at least 85 new donors in 2025 just to replace the lapsed ones.

That replacement math is why retention matters more than acquisition. Acquisition costs five to ten times more per dollar raised than retention. An organization losing 57% of its donors annually is running on a treadmill that gets faster every year.

## A Worked Example

Consider an organization with three years of donor counts:

- 2023: 120 donors gave at least one gift

- 2024: 150 donors gave at least one gift

- 2025: 135 donors gave at least one gift

To calculate 2025 retention rate, the relevant comparison is 2024 to 2025. Pull the list of 150 donors from 2024 and check which of them also appear in the 2025 donor list. Suppose 65 do.

65 / 150 x 100 = 43.3% retention rate for 2025.

Note what this number does and does not tell you. It tells you how well the organization held onto its existing base. It does not tell you whether the organization grew, because the 135 total in 2025 includes 70 new donors who were not in the 2024 group. Total donor count and retention rate are independent metrics, and both matter.

## The Three-Part Retention Framework

A single retention rate is a starting point, not an answer. The number breaks down into three sub-calculations that determine where to focus retention investment.

### New Donor Retention Rate

First-time donors retain at much lower rates than multi-year donors. Calculating new donor retention separately reveals whether onboarding and second-gift strategies are working.

The formula isolates first-time givers: (first-time donors from last year who also gave this year) / (total first-time donors from last year) x 100.

Sector benchmarks from the Fundraising Effectiveness Project put new donor retention at 19-26%. If 40 of the 150 prior-year donors were first-time givers and only 9 of them gave again, the new donor retention rate is 9 / 40 x 100 = 22.5%. That sits in the sector range but well below the overall 43.3%.

When new donor retention is low and overall retention is acceptable, the problem is the second-gift conversion, not the relationship with established donors. The fixes are operational: faster acknowledgment, an early second-ask, an onboarding sequence that ties the donor's gift to specific program outcomes.

### Multi-Year Cohort Retention

Donors in their second, third, and fourth+ years retain at progressively higher rates. Calculating retention by cohort year reveals where donors fall off.

Pull every donor by year of first gift. For each cohort, calculate what percentage gave again in the most recent year. The pattern usually looks like this: 22% retention in year two, 50% in year three, 65% in year four, and 75%+ for donors past their fourth year. The biggest cliff is between year one and year two.

The cohort view tells the development director where retention spending produces the highest return. Adding a major gift officer to steward five-year donors who already retain at 75% produces less marginal lift than adding a touchpoint between gift one and gift two for first-year donors retaining at 22%.

### Channel Retention

Online donors retain at lower rates than offline or major donors. Calculating retention by acquisition channel — online, direct mail, event, major gift — reveals which channels produce durable donors.

A peer-to-peer fundraiser who gave once because a friend ran a marathon may retain at 12%. A donor acquired through a long-form direct mail appeal may retain at 38%. A donor acquired through an in-person event tour may retain at 55%. The channel that produces the highest acquisition volume is rarely the channel that produces the highest retention.

When acquisition spending is concentrated in low-retention channels, total revenue can grow while the donor base hollows out. Channel retention reveals that pattern before it shows up in the bottom line.

## Industry Benchmarks

The Fundraising Effectiveness Project publishes annual sector benchmarks based on data from thousands of nonprofits.

- Sector average overall retention: 43-46%

- High-performing retention: 60% or above

- High-risk threshold: below 35%

- New donor (first-year) retention: 19-26%

- Recurring (monthly) donor retention: 80-90%

A retention rate below 35% means more than 65% of the donor base is replaced every year. Acquisition spending alone cannot solve that. Acquisition raises the top of the funnel while the bottom drains; the answer is closing the leak, not pumping more water through.

A recurring giving program is the highest-impact retention move available to most organizations. Recurring donors retain at 80-90%. Converting even 10% of one-time donors to monthly giving lifts overall retention by several points and stabilizes cash flow.

## Step-by-Step Calculation

Most CRM systems can produce the data needed for this calculation, but not all of them produce it cleanly. Here is the practical sequence.

1. Pull the donor list for the prior fiscal year. Use the donor record, not the gift record — a donor who gave three times last year counts as one donor, not three.

2. Pull the donor list for the current fiscal year. Same rule: one row per donor.

3. Match the two lists on a unique identifier (donor ID, not email or name). Email addresses change. Names get entered inconsistently. The donor ID is the only reliable join key.

4. Count the matches. That is the numerator.

5. Count the prior year list. That is the denominator.

6. Divide and multiply by 100.

In a spreadsheet, the match step is a VLOOKUP or INDEX-MATCH from one year's list against the other. It works but is error-prone, especially at scale or when the same donor appears under slightly different IDs from a CRM merge that did not fully complete.

A donor management CRM should generate this query in seconds, not require a manual export. If the current system cannot produce a LYBUNT (Last Year But Unfortunately Not This Year) report or calculate retention rate directly, that is a tooling gap. The number is the starting point for retention work, and a number that takes three hours to calculate gets calculated less often than it should.

## What to Do With the Result

Three actions follow the calculation, in order.

**Pull the LYBUNT list.** Every donor who gave in the prior fiscal year but has not yet given in the current year is a re-engagement priority. Donors within 12 months of their last gift are dramatically more reachable than donors who have been gone two or more years. The LYBUNT segment gets a personal outreach sequence, not a mass appeal.

**Calculate the value of a 5-point improvement.** If 150 prior-year donors averaged $250 per gift, moving from 43% retention to 48% retention means retaining 7.5 more donors per year. At $250 per gift, that is $1,875 in year one — and those donors continue giving in subsequent years, so the compounded value across five years is meaningful. For organizations with 1,000+ donors, the math scales into six figures quickly.

**Set a retention goal for the next fiscal year.** A 2-3 point improvement is realistic for an organization with no current retention strategy. A 5-point improvement requires investment in onboarding, recurring giving conversion, or major donor stewardship. A 10-point improvement means restructuring the development calendar around retention rather than acquisition.

## The Most Common Mistake

The single most common retention rate mistake is calculating it on transactions instead of donors.

A spreadsheet that counts gifts in 2024 and gifts in 2025, then divides one by the other, produces a number that looks like a retention rate but is not. A donor who gave three times last year and once this year shows up as three transactions versus one — a 33% "retention" that misrepresents what actually happened.

The correct calculation is donor-level, not gift-level. One row per unique donor in the prior year, one row per unique donor in the current year, match by donor ID.

This mistake is most common in organizations that pull retention numbers from accounting systems rather than donor management systems. Accounting tracks transactions; donor management tracks donors. The two systems answer different questions, and retention rate is a donor question.

## Why This Number Belongs on the Dashboard

Donor retention rate is a leading indicator for revenue stability. A rising retention rate shows up in next year's revenue with very little additional spending. A falling retention rate shows up two years later, when the cumulative effect of replacement-only acquisition catches up.

Boards rarely ask about retention rate, which is exactly why it should appear on every quarterly board report. Total dollars raised is the easy number. Donors retained is the durable number. Organizations that grow on retention compound. Organizations that grow on acquisition treadmill.

## Takeaway and What to Do This Week

Pull the donor lists for the last two fiscal years. Match them by donor ID. Calculate the rate. The full exercise takes 30 to 60 minutes if the CRM cooperates, longer if the data needs cleanup. Once the number is on paper, calculate the new donor retention sub-rate and the 5-point improvement value separately so the conversation with the executive director and the board can move from abstract concern to specific dollars.

Then build the LYBUNT list and set a date to begin re-engagement outreach. Most lapsed donors do not lapse for any specific reason — they simply do not get asked. The number will only move if the work moves first.
