# Net Asset Releases: The Accounting Entry Nonprofits Most Often Get Wrong

A finance director at a mid-sized nonprofit receives a $150,000 restricted grant in October. By November, the check has cleared and the grant agreement is signed. By December, the full $150,000 has been recorded as unrestricted revenue in the Statement of Activities. The organization looks financially stronger. The board is pleased. The auditor is not.

Recording the entire grant award as unrestricted income at receipt is the most consequential timing error in nonprofit accounting. It misrepresents the financial position, overstates operational flexibility, and creates audit exposure that follows the organization through the annual audit cycle and potentially longer. The correct treatment — a net asset release triggered only as qualifying expenditures are incurred — is what FASB ASC 958 requires and what every auditor of a grant-reliant nonprofit is specifically trained to test.

## What a Net Asset Release Actually Is

A net asset release is a reclassification entry, not new revenue. When a restricted grant is received, the funds enter the with-donor-restrictions net asset class. They sit there, committed but not yet deployed. As qualifying program expenditures are made against the grant, the restrictions are released — the funds transfer from with-donor-restrictions to without-donor-restrictions in the Statement of Activities. The total net assets of the organization do not change with the release entry; the composition does.

This matters because the two net asset classes carry different information for financial statement users. With-donor-restrictions shows what the organization has been entrusted to deliver. Without-donor-restrictions shows what the organization can deploy at its own discretion. A board member reading a Statement of Financial Position where all grant funds have been prematurely released into the unrestricted class is reading an inaccurate picture of organizational flexibility — and of obligation.

Under FASB ASC 958-210-45, there are two net asset classes. The old "unrestricted" and "temporarily restricted" and "permanently restricted" three-class model was replaced by FASB ASU 2016-14, effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2017. Organizations still using the old terminology in audited statements are presenting an accounting error, not just a style choice.

## Three Triggers for Release

Restrictions are released when one of three conditions is satisfied.

**Purpose restriction met.** The funds were spent on the activity specified in the grant agreement or gift letter. A grant restricted to "after-school tutoring for middle school students" releases its restriction dollar-for-dollar as qualifying tutoring program costs are incurred and documented. The release tracks expenditure activity in real time — it does not wait for the grant period to end, and it cannot outrun actual spending.

**Time restriction expired.** Some contributions specify a time period rather than a purpose: "these funds are for fiscal year 2026." When that period arrives, the time restriction is satisfied and the funds transfer to without-donor-restrictions — even if they have not been spent on any program. This is distinct from a purpose restriction. A contribution that is both time-restricted and purpose-restricted requires both conditions to be met before release.

**Combined restrictions both satisfied.** Grants that carry time and purpose restrictions simultaneously — federal grants are a common example — are released only when the grant period is active and qualifying expenditures are made. There is no shortcut: satisfying one condition does not trigger partial release on the other.

## The Journal Entry

The accounting entries for a net asset release appear in two coordinated parts.

The release entry moves the funds between net asset classes: debit Net Assets Released from Restrictions — With Donor Restrictions, and credit Net Assets Released from Restrictions — Without Donor Restrictions, for the amount released. This entry has no cash impact. It is a reclassification.

The expense entry records the program cost that triggered the release: debit the appropriate program expense account, and credit Cash or Accounts Payable. These two entries appear simultaneously in a well-structured accounting system. When an expense is coded to a restricted grant in the general ledger, the system should generate the release entry alongside the expense entry. Organizations using accounting systems that do not automate this must generate the release entries manually — but the entries must appear in the same period as the qualifying expenditure.

In the Statement of Activities, the release line appears in both columns. The with-donor-restrictions column shows a deduction — funds leaving that class. The without-donor-restrictions column shows an addition — funds entering the class — offset by the program expense incurred. The net change to without-donor-restrictions from the release and the related expense is zero. The Statement of Activities accurately reflects that grant funds were deployed toward the restricted purpose.

## The Four Timing Errors

**Releasing the full grant at receipt.** The most common and most damaging error. The entire award is recorded as unrestricted revenue when the check arrives. This inflates without-donor-restrictions net assets, makes the funds appear available for any use, and creates an audit finding when the grant is subsequently tested. Correcting it requires reversing the entry and restating prior-period financials if the error crosses a reporting period — a significant operational burden.

**Not releasing as expenditures are made.** The opposite problem: qualifying expenditures are coded and paid, but the release entries are never generated. The result is a growing gap between the restricted net asset balance and the actual unspent grant funds. At year-end, the accounting records show more in with-donor-restrictions than actually remains. Reconciliation at audit time requires tracing every qualifying expenditure back through the year to generate the missing entries — work that compounds in complexity with each passing month.

**Releasing based on budget rather than actual expenditures.** Some finance teams release restricted net assets based on the grant's budget schedule — releasing $25,000 per quarter on a $100,000 annual grant regardless of actual spending. This is incorrect. Releases must be driven by actual qualifying expenditures posted in the accounting system, not by the budgeted timeline. A quarter in which the program is under-spent should show a smaller release than a quarter in which spending ran ahead of schedule.

**Releasing before the grant period begins.** A federal grant covering fiscal year 2026, received and signed in November 2025, carries a time restriction that is not yet satisfied. The funds should remain in with-donor-restrictions until the grant period start date arrives, even though the award has been made and the check has cleared. Recording the income in the period of receipt is correct; releasing the restriction before the period opens is not.

## Documentation That Makes Audit Straightforward

Every net asset release should be traceable through a four-document chain.

The original grant agreement or gift letter establishes what the restriction requires — what activities qualify, what time period applies, what documentation the grantor expects. This document is the baseline against which every release entry is evaluated by an auditor.

The expenditure documentation for the costs that triggered the release — invoices, payroll records, time sheets — demonstrates that qualifying program work was done. For personnel costs charged to a federal grant, 2 CFR 200.430 requires that the documentation reflect actual time worked on grant-funded activities, not estimated or budgeted percentages. Reconstructed time records are a compliance risk.

The accounting entries showing the release and the related expense confirm that the reclassification was recorded correctly and in the right period.

A period-end reconciliation of the restricted fund balance before and after the release surfaces any discrepancy between what was spent and what was released. For organizations managing multiple restricted grants simultaneously, this reconciliation is the control that prevents the with-donor-restrictions balance from drifting out of alignment with actual unspent obligations.

## The Specific Risk for Grant-Reliant Organizations

Mid-sized nonprofits managing four to ten active restricted grants simultaneously face a specific compounding risk. Each grant has a different restriction, a different period, and a different release trigger. Personnel whose salaries are split across multiple grant-funded programs must have time documentation that allocates hours to the correct grant — and each allocation generates a separate release event when the expense is posted.

The common failure mode is annual: all of the year's qualifying expenditures are posted correctly, but the release entries are generated once at year-end rather than concurrent with the expenses. The Statement of Activities for the first three quarters of the year understates program activity and overstates the restricted net asset balance. When the auditor tests period-end balances against transaction-level records, the timing mismatch surfaces as a control finding.

The mechanics are not complicated. The discipline is. Each qualifying expenditure generates a release entry in the same period. The restricted fund balance declines in real time as program work is delivered. The Statement of Activities reflects, month by month, exactly what grant obligations have been satisfied and what remains.

## What to Do This Week

Pull the balance in net assets with donor restrictions. For each grant comprising that balance, confirm the unspent grant amount in the accounting system matches the restricted net asset balance attributed to that grant. A discrepancy is a missing release entry — and every missing entry is a prior-period adjustment waiting to happen.

If the reconciliation reveals a gap, generate the missing release entries for the relevant periods before the audit cycle begins. Document what expenditures triggered each release and attach that documentation to the journal entries.

GrantPipe tracks restricted fund balances at the grant level and generates release entries concurrent with expenditure posting, so the with-donor-restrictions balance and the unspent grant balance are always aligned. For finance directors who currently reconcile these manually at year-end, that automated linkage eliminates the most time-intensive pre-audit task.

# The SF-SAC Dual-Signature Trap: Why Single Audits Sit Unfiled Past the 30-Day Deadline

The single audit is complete when the auditor signs the reports. The filing is complete when the SF-SAC clears the Federal Audit Clearinghouse. Those two events are not the same, and the gap between them is where organizations routinely miss the 30-day deadline.

Most organizations know the deadline exists. Most believe they are complying with it. What they miss is that the SF-SAC requires two separate, authenticated actions — and the second one cannot happen until the first is finished. When the auditee certifying official signs on day 28 and the auditor gets around to certifying on day 33, the submission is late. The public record shows it. Awarding agencies see it.

## The Dual-Signature Process

The SF-SAC is not a single form submitted by a single party. Under 2 CFR 200.512, the reporting package submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse (fac.gov) requires both the auditee certifying official and the auditor to sign — separately, through their own FAC accounts.

The sequence is fixed. The auditee certifying official (typically the executive director or CFO) creates the submission in FAC, enters all required organizational and federal awards data, uploads the reporting package documents, and electronically signs the auditee certification. This action triggers a notification to the auditor. The auditor then independently logs into FAC, reviews the submitted data, and certifies the auditor section. The submission is not complete — and FAC will not mark it accepted — until both signatures are in place.

This is the single most common source of missed SF-SAC deadlines. Organizations submit the auditee portion and assume the auditor will handle the rest automatically. The auditor receives an email. The email may sit in a queue. The 30-day window closes.

## The Deadline Math

Under 2 CFR 200.512(a)(1), the submission deadline is the earlier of two dates: 30 days after the auditor's report date, or 9 months after the end of the fiscal year.

For a December 31 fiscal year end with an audit report dated April 15, the deadline is May 15 — the 30-day rule controls, and the 9-month deadline (September 30) is later.

For a June 30 fiscal year end with a report dated February 28, the 30-day deadline (March 30) is essentially concurrent with the 9-month deadline (March 31). Both land in the same window, but the 30-day rule controls.

The FAC timestamp records when the submission is fully complete — both signatures in place. This matters because "I submitted my portion on time" is not a defense. The submission date for public record purposes is the date the final signature is received.

OMB's 2024 revision to the Uniform Guidance (89 FR 30046) added provisions allowing federal awarding agencies to impose additional conditions on recipients with late or incomplete single audit submissions. The FAC itself does not impose a monetary penalty, but late filings are publicly searchable. Program officers see them.

## FAC Account Requirements

The FAC's 2023 transition from Census to GSA management (now at fac.gov) introduced Login.gov as the authentication mechanism for both parties. This created a new class of delay for organizations submitting their first single audit.

The auditee certifying official must have a Login.gov account. Identity verification through Login.gov can take 3–5 business days. For first-time filers, account setup should happen during audit fieldwork — not after the report is signed. FAC also requires a separate auditee authorization step that links the certifying official to the organization.

The auditor must be registered in FAC as an audit firm, and the individual CPA certifying must have a Login.gov account linked to that firm. Many audit firms pre-register during planning; many do not. Confirming auditor registration status before the report is signed eliminates a common last-week scramble.

The practical rule: both parties should have active FAC accounts and confirmed access before audit fieldwork begins. Treating account setup as a post-audit administrative task is how organizations find themselves doing identity verification with nine days left in the 30-day window.

## What the SF-SAC Contains

The SF-SAC is a data collection form, not the audit itself. It summarizes the audit in a structured format that allows oversight agencies and the public to search, compare, and monitor single audit results across thousands of organizations.

The form requires: general organizational information (EIN, UEI, fiscal year end, audit type, total federal expenditures); financial statement information including audit opinions and any going concern disclosures; federal awards data — each Assistance Listing Number, program name, expenditures, and whether the program was identified as a major program; findings information including finding reference numbers, types, federal program ALNs, questioned cost amounts, and whether findings are repeats; and the auditee and auditor certifications.

All data entered in FAC must be consistent with the uploaded reporting package documents. FAC runs limited automated validation, but inconsistencies between the SF-SAC data entries and the uploaded reports surface during oversight agency review. A finding numbered "2026-001" in the data field and "Finding 1" in the uploaded schedule causes rejection.

The Federal Audit Clearinghouse received approximately 30,000 single audit submissions in FY2023. Every one of them is publicly searchable at fac.gov.

## Common Errors That Delay Acceptance

Five errors account for most SF-SAC delays:

**Mismatched report dates.** The date entered in FAC must exactly match the date on the signed audit report. A one-day discrepancy triggers rejection. This sounds trivial. It happens regularly when the auditee enters the date from a draft report rather than the final signed version.

**Password-protected PDFs.** FAC requires accessible PDFs — not password protected, not encrypted. PDF/A compliance is required. Large documents should be compressed before upload; file size limits apply. Organizations that generate their reporting package from accounting software exports often produce PDFs that fail FAC's upload validation on the first attempt.

**Inconsistent finding numbers.** Finding reference numbers in the SF-SAC data entry must match the numbering in the uploaded schedule of findings exactly. If the data field reads "2026-001" and the document reads "Finding 2026-1," the submission fails validation.

**Missing corrective action plan.** Every finding requires a corresponding corrective action plan entry and an uploaded CAP document. Under 2 CFR 200.511(c), the CAP must include the finding number, the auditee's position, the specific corrective action, the responsible party, and the expected completion date. A finding without a complete CAP prevents submission completion. Vague responses — "management will strengthen controls" — may pass FAC's technical validation but create problems when awarding agencies review the substance.

**Auditor delay.** This is the most common reason deadlines are missed. After the auditee certifying official signs, the auditor receives an email notification to log in and certify. If that email is not acted upon within the remaining window, the submission stalls. The fix is coordination: before the auditee signs, confirm explicitly with the auditor what date they will certify. Build the certification date into the submission timeline. Do not treat it as a follow-on task.

## The Repeat Finding Risk

A finding that appears in two consecutive single audit cycles is treated differently by awarding agencies than a first-time finding. Repeat findings trigger specific conditions under 2 CFR 200.208 — prior approval for draws, enhanced monitoring, or high-risk designation. These conditions persist until the awarding agency is satisfied that the underlying problem has been resolved.

Breaking a repeat finding pattern typically requires more structural change than the corrective action plan for the first finding suggested. New staff, new systems, documented policy changes, or external controls review. Organizations that produce corrective action plans that address symptoms rather than causes produce repeat findings.

The SF-SAC data at fac.gov makes repeat findings visible across organizations and years. Program officers review this history when making funding decisions.

## The Single Most Preventable Outcome

Late SF-SAC submissions are overwhelmingly preventable with one practice: treat the auditor certification as a calendared commitment, not an assumption.

After the audit is complete and the report is signed, schedule the auditee certification date and the auditor certification date before either party acts. Confirm both dates with the auditor in writing. The auditee certifies first. The auditor certifies on the agreed date — at least three to five business days before the deadline, to allow for corrections if something fails validation.

The organizations that miss the 30-day window almost always had enough time. They ran out of coordination, not calendar.

## The Common Mistake

The single most common failure is treating the SF-SAC as an administrative task to complete after the audit is done, rather than a parallel process to coordinate during the audit's final phase.

The consequence is predictable: the report is signed, everyone breathes, and then someone initiates FAC access setup, discovers the auditor is not registered, realizes the PDF from accounting software is password-protected, and starts scrambling with 10 days left in the window. Ten days is not enough time to recover from all three of those simultaneously.

Start the process before the report is signed. Confirm FAC accounts, auditor registration, and document format before fieldwork is complete. The administrative setup is not complicated. The timing is.

## What to Do This Week

If your fiscal year ends in the next six months, confirm two things now: that your certifying official has an active Login.gov account linked to your organization in FAC, and that your audit firm is registered in FAC with at least one active Login.gov credential. If either is missing, initiate setup before audit fieldwork begins.

If your single audit is already in progress, schedule the auditee and auditor certification dates explicitly — in writing, with the audit firm — before the report is issued. This one step eliminates the most common source of missed deadlines.

Booking a pledge write-off as bad debt expense is one of the most common accounting errors in nonprofit finance — and under FASB ASC 958, it is wrong.

The correct entry debits the allowance for uncollectible pledges and credits the pledge receivable. The write-off reduces the contra-asset and eliminates the receivable. It does not create a new expense on the Statement of Activities.

This matters because most accounting staff coming from for-profit environments do exactly the opposite. The for-profit instinct is a debit to bad debt expense — which is not the correct account under ASC 958-605.

The complication is the allowance itself. If the organization set the allowance to zero when the pledge was recorded, the write-off has nowhere to absorb: it becomes a direct charge to contribution revenue, reducing the current period's reported contributions.

Multi-year pledges add a second entry that gets missed: the unamortized present-value discount attributable to the written-off portion must also be eliminated per ASC 958-605-30-6. Leaving the discount in place after the receivable is gone overstates the discount contra-asset.

Auditors testing pledge receivables will sample write-offs and look for: the original pledge documentation, payment history, collection effort evidence, the collectibility assessment memo, and approval at the threshold specified in your policy.

The SF-425 Federal Financial Report is not a routine form. It is a compliance obligation submitted under the False Claims Act, and one specific error accounts for most of the findings it generates.

Line 10f — Federal Share of Expenditures — must show cumulative expenditures for the entire period of performance, from day one of the award through the last day of the reporting period. Not just the current quarter. Cumulative.

If your grant started October 1 and you are submitting the March 31 quarterly report, line 10f must show total expenditures from October through March. An agency receiving reports that appear to show expenditures declining or fluctuating rather than steadily accumulating will flag the discrepancy.

The final SF-425 is due no later than 120 calendar days after the period-of-performance end date. Some agencies specify shorter deadlines in the notice of award. The final report must reconcile exactly to your general ledger — a discrepancy is a compliance finding in the financial reporting area of a single audit and prevents award closeout.

Line 10g (unliquidated obligations) should be zero on the final report: all obligations should be liquidated before submission.

Line 10j (program income) requires reporting and accounting for any gross income earned directly as a result of federally funded activities, per the method specified in the award.

A wrong number on the SF-425 is not a clerical error in a program monitor's view. It is a finding.

CRM migrations fail at the field mapping step or the data quality step — not the software step.

The field mapping problem is structural: every data element in the source system needs a documented destination in the target, a defined transformation if formats differ, and a validation rule that confirms the migration succeeded. Skip that step and the errors surface after go-live, when fixing them disrupts live operations.

The data quality problem is older than the migration. Most source systems contain years of accumulated quality problems — duplicate contacts, blank required fields, inconsistent fund designation naming, phone numbers in five formats — that transfer directly into the new system if not addressed first.

The pre-migration data audit should take two to three weeks. Target zero duplicate contacts by primary identifier. Run a report of records where required fields are blank in the target system. Establish a merge rule for duplicates before you start. Decide which records to migrate (active donor records, five to seven years of giving history, active grants) versus exclude (closed grants older than five years, test records, deprecated fields with no current use).

Post-migration validation requires record count reconciliation, a random sample of 20 donor giving histories, and financial validation confirming total giving history in the target matches the source for the same period.

# How to Justify Nonprofit Software Costs to Your Board

The most common reason nonprofit software budget requests fail is not cost. It is framing.

Executive directors who present CRM software as a technology upgrade get a technology conversation with their board. That conversation typically ends in one of two ways: board members who are not technology-inclined vote against it on instinct, or board members who are technology-inclined start asking about integrations, data migration timelines, and API compatibility. Neither conversation produces an approved budget line.

The requests that get approved make the cost of the status quo visible before introducing a solution.

## The Current Process Cost

Before writing a budget memo, calculate what the manual process costs your organization right now. This is the step most executive directors skip, and it is the number that matters most to a board vote.

Count the staff hours per month devoted to tasks the software would handle: gift entry, donor record maintenance, grant reconciliation, funder report preparation, board report generation, pledge tracking. Multiply by the fully-loaded hourly rate of each staff member doing the work. The loaded rate includes salary, employer payroll taxes, and benefits — typically 25 to 35 percent above base salary.

If your development associate spends 15 hours per month on tasks a CRM would automate, and their fully-loaded cost is $28 per hour, that is $420 per month or $5,040 per year in staff time devoted to work a $200 per month software platform handles. The software pays for itself in five months.

This calculation is not theoretical. It requires 30 minutes with your development staff and a count. Most executive directors who do this are surprised by the total. Manual processes accumulate gradually — no one notices that gift entry takes six hours per month until someone tracks it. If multiple staff members maintain overlapping manual records (one person maintaining a donor spreadsheet, another a grant tracking spreadsheet, a third reconciling them for board reports), count all of it.

## The Compliance Risk Argument

Manual grant tracking in spreadsheets creates audit exposure. The cost of an audit finding is not the auditor's billable hours — it includes staff time responding to the finding, implementing corrective actions, documenting those actions, communicating with funders, and potentially repaying funds the organization cannot document as properly allocated.

For organizations managing $500,000 or more in active restricted grants, the insurance value of software that maintains compliance documentation automatically is a legitimate budget argument. You do not need to have experienced a finding to make it. The risk exists in every organization tracking restricted funds in a shared spreadsheet without version control or access logging.

Federal grants above $1,000,000 in annual expenditure trigger the Single Audit requirement under 2 CFR 200.501 of the Uniform Guidance. Organizations approaching that threshold cannot afford documentation gaps. The audit will test whether restricted funds were allocated to specific program expenses — and a spreadsheet that multiple staff members have edited over 18 months is not a reliable audit trail.

Frame this concretely for your board: "We currently track three active federal grants totaling $420,000 in a shared spreadsheet. If an auditor finds we cannot document how restricted funds were allocated to specific program expenses, we face corrective action requirements and potential repayment." That is a risk mitigation argument. It is not a technology pitch.

## Total Cost of Ownership, Not the Monthly Fee

The monthly license fee is the wrong number to present to your board — especially if your organization has ever been in a Salesforce or Blackbaud conversation. Those enterprise platforms have license costs that look manageable and total cost of ownership that most mid-sized nonprofits do not model until after implementation is underway.

Purpose-built nonprofit CRMs — Bloomerang, Keela, Little Green Light, GrantPipe — have a total cost of ownership that is close to the license fee. No implementation consulting, no required add-ons, no mandatory training packages. A platform at $200 per month has a three-year TCO of approximately $7,200.

Salesforce with the Nonprofit Success Pack looks affordable on a per-license basis — approximately $36 per user per month through TechSoup discounts. Implementation through a consulting partner typically runs $30,000 to $100,000 depending on configuration complexity. Annual administration costs add $10,000 to $25,000 if you need a dedicated Salesforce admin or ongoing consultant hours. The three-year TCO for Salesforce at a mid-sized nonprofit is often $60,000 to $150,000.

Blackbaud products carry multi-year contracts with annual fees ranging from $6,000 to $24,000 or more, plus implementation fees and data migration charges.

When you present a $200 per month platform alongside a Salesforce three-year TCO of $80,000, the comparison reframes the request. Your board is not deciding whether to spend $2,400 per year on software. They are deciding between a $7,200 investment and an $80,000 investment — or continuing a manual process that already costs more than $5,000 per year in staff time and carries audit exposure.

## The Three-Number Budget Request

Board members read in volume. A software budget request that requires 15 minutes to read competes with everything else in the board packet. The format that works is one page with four sections.

**Current state.** What the manual process costs per year in staff time and what compliance risks it creates. Use specific numbers. "Our development team spends 18 hours per month on tasks this software automates, at a loaded cost of $6,048 per year" is stronger than "significant staff time." Specific numbers earn credibility. Vague estimates invite skepticism.

**Proposed solution.** What the software does, at what annual cost. Name the platform and the pricing. "$2,400 per year, no implementation fee, month-to-month pricing" is a complete cost statement. Avoid feature lists — they look like a technology pitch.

**Net benefit.** Staff hours recovered per year, compliance risk reduced, and any new capabilities. Quantify what you can. "Recovers approximately 216 staff hours per year and maintains audit-ready grant documentation automatically" is a statement a board can evaluate.

**Decision requested.** "Approve $2,400 in annual software budget for donor and grant management." A clear ask with a specific number is easier to approve than an open-ended technology discussion.

Vendor comparison detail, pricing tables, and feature grids belong in an appendix. The one-page format forces the most important information forward and does not ask board members to parse product documentation.

## Common Mistake: Leading With Features

The most frequent budget request failure is leading with what the software does rather than what the current process costs.

"This CRM has automated acknowledgment letters, a grant pipeline dashboard, a donor retention module, and a real-time compliance calendar" is a feature list. It describes the software, not the problem.

"Our development team currently spends 12 hours per month preparing monthly donor reports manually. This software generates those reports automatically. At a loaded cost of $28 per hour, we are spending $4,032 per year on work a $2,400 per year platform handles" is a cost comparison. It describes the operational decision.

The feature list triggers a technology evaluation. The cost comparison triggers an arithmetic conversation. Boards that approve technology budgets are making operational decisions. Boards that reject technology budgets are usually responding to requests that sounded like preferences.

## The 90-Day Trial as a Lower-Friction Path

For boards that are genuinely uncertain rather than resistant, a 90-day trial with defined success criteria is the lowest-friction approval path. Month-to-month pricing on most purpose-built platforms makes this possible without a long-term commitment.

Define the criteria before the trial starts. The software must generate a compliance report for any active grant in under 10 minutes. It must reduce gift entry time by at least 50 percent. It must produce the quarterly donor retention report without manual preparation. Those are measurable outcomes, not impressions.

A time-bounded trial with measurable criteria is easier to approve than an open-ended budget commitment. It also gives development and finance staff enough time to evaluate the platform under real working conditions rather than in a vendor demo. If the trial succeeds against the criteria, the annual budget request is straightforward — 90 days of operational data supports it. If it does not, you have avoided a multi-year commitment.

## After the Vote

If the budget is approved, schedule a six-month review checkpoint where you report back on actual staff hours recovered and compliance improvements. Boards that see follow-through on technology investments approve future requests more readily. Boards that approve software that disappears from the agenda become skeptical of the next request.

If the budget is not approved, ask specifically what would need to change. Cost concern: propose a lower-tier plan or the trial structure. Uncertainty about fit: define measurable success criteria and propose a bounded evaluation. General technology hesitancy: reframe around compliance risk and staff time, and ask whether the board would like to see documented manual process costs from the next quarter before deciding.

Most budget rejections are not permanent. They are requests for better information, presented differently. The average nonprofit spends less than 3 percent of its budget on technology, compared to 5.85 percent for for-profit companies, and 45 percent of nonprofits report spending too little. The gap is not board resistance to technology. It is that technology requests rarely arrive in a form that makes the investment case clear enough to approve.

Myth: a nonprofit on cash-basis books can report to federal agencies the same way it reports internally.

Reality: federal grant reporting is accrual-only, under 2 CFR 200.302(b)(3).

The SF-425 Federal Financial Report is the clearest proof. Block 10e captures accrued expenditures — costs incurred but not yet paid. Block 10g captures unliquidated obligations. A cash-basis organization that enters only cash disbursements on Block 10e is underreporting federal expenditures, even if the books look correct internally.

Under FASB ASC 958, audited nonprofit financial statements must also be on accrual. Form 990 preparation follows the same standard.

The practical fix for a cash-basis organization: at each reporting date, identify unpaid vendor invoices, calculate any pay-period proration for accrued wages, isolate grant receivables not yet submitted for reimbursement, and document the cash-to-accrual reconciliation in a worksheet retained with the FFR.

Missing reconciliation worksheets are one of the more reliable indicators of accounting control weaknesses in single audits.

Cash books and federal reporting can coexist. The bridge is documented, repeatable, and auditable.

A post-closeout cost transfer on a federal grant requires written authorization from the awarding agency before any journal entry is booked.

That is the step most organizations get wrong: they discover the misposting, assess it, and move the cost — then ask permission. That sequence creates a second compliance problem on top of the original one.

Under 2 CFR 200.344, grantees have 120 calendar days after the period of performance ends to liquidate obligations and submit final reports. A transfer discovered after that window closes is in different territory.

The correct sequence: document the specific cost and why it needs to transfer, confirm whether the 120-day window is still open, notify the federal program officer and grants management specialist in writing, submit a formal prior approval request package with original expenditure documentation, wait for written authorization (typically 30 to 90 days depending on the agency), then book the entry.

If the transfer changes figures on the final SF-425, an amended FFR must be submitted.

Program officers are helpful. Verbal concurrence from a program officer is not written authorization from a grants management specialist. The distinction matters.

# How to Build a Grant Prospecting Workflow That Does Not Waste Staff Time

A development director at a $3M nonprofit once described her prospecting process as "structured panic." Every quarter, she opened the same grant databases, exported the same opportunity lists, circulated spreadsheets, and watched the team spend two weeks chasing funders who had never funded organizations like theirs. Applications went out. Most heard nothing back. The ones that did come back as awards were often the most administratively expensive grants in the portfolio.

The prospecting process looked busy. It was not producing results proportional to the effort.

That problem is not unusual. It is the predictable outcome of treating grant search as a volume exercise rather than a qualification system.

## The Volume Trap

Grant prospecting feels productive when teams are active — building funder lists, subscribing to alerts, bookmarking opportunities, attending webinars about federal funding priorities. The metric that feels meaningful is pipeline count: how many opportunities are in the funnel.

Pipeline count is the wrong metric. What matters is how many qualified opportunities are in the funnel — ones where the organization's mission, geography, eligibility, award size, and operational capacity align with the funder's requirements.

Without explicit qualification criteria, teams research opportunities that were never a fit. They write letters of inquiry to funders that only award to organizations with narrower missions, larger budgets, or service populations the nonprofit does not reach. They spend three weeks on a federal application for an award they cannot administer without hiring two additional staff members.

The fix is not working harder. It is qualifying earlier.

## The 4-Stage Grant Prospecting Framework

A grant prospecting workflow that protects staff time has four stages: internal definition, qualification gates, ranked scoring, and pre-award capacity check. These run in sequence. Skipping to scoring without qualification first, or starting the search without internal definition, is where time gets lost.

**Stage 1: Internal Definition**

Before opening any grant database, the organization needs clarity on what it is actually prepared to fund and operate. That clarity covers:

- Program areas — what specific activities can be credibly presented to funders as the work

- Service geography — exact service area, because many funders have geographic restrictions that disqualify applicants from outside specific regions or jurisdictions

- Realistic award size — both a floor and a ceiling; awards too small do not justify administrative overhead, awards too large exceed operational capacity

- Staffing capacity — whether the team can actually manage a new grant's reporting burden alongside existing awards

- Reporting tolerance — some grants require quarterly federal financial reports, time-and-effort certifications, and participant-level data collection; some organizations cannot sustain that without a dedicated grants manager

Organizations that skip internal definition start from the funder's criteria rather than their own. That reversal is how reverse-engineering begins: "This funder looks interesting — can we make our work fit their priorities?" That question rarely produces strong applications.

**Stage 2: Qualification Gates**

After internal definition, the search can begin — but qualification must come before any scoring. Basic qualification gates eliminate weak-fit opportunities before they consume research time.

Qualification gates for a mid-sized nonprofit typically include:

- Mission fit — does the funder's stated priorities match the organization's actual programs, not just broadly related issue areas

- Geography fit — does the funder award in the organization's service area

- Eligibility — does the organization meet the legal, financial, and operational eligibility requirements (501(c)(3) status, minimum budget size, required certifications)

- Timeline fit — is the deadline achievable given the current application workload, and does the award start date align with program planning cycles

- Award size fit — is the typical award range within the boundaries established in the internal definition stage

- Reporting burden — what does the funder require after award: financial reports, program reports, site visits, data collection, subrecipient monitoring

The last gate — reporting burden — is where most prospecting processes have a gap. A grant that looks attractive on mission and size can still be a poor fit if the post-award compliance requirements exceed what the organization can sustain.

This matters particularly for federal awards. A 21st CCLC federal grant requires quarterly attendance reporting and annual academic outcome data. A federal workforce development award under 2 CFR Part 200 requires cost-reimbursement billing, time-and-effort certifications for grant-funded personnel, and potentially single audit exposure if the award pushes federal expenditures above $1,000,000. These requirements do not diminish after the award is received. They increase in consequence if mismanaged.

Weak opportunities that fail any gate should be documented and discarded quickly, not set aside for later review. "Set aside for later" becomes a permanent holding pattern.

**Stage 3: Scored Ranking**

After qualification, the surviving opportunities can be ranked. Scoring at this stage is useful because the team is comparing options that already meet baseline criteria — mission fit, eligibility, timeline, and reporting capacity are established. Scoring distinguishes among viable opportunities, not all opportunities.

A simple scoring model is more useful than a complex one. Consistency matters more than mathematical precision. The factors worth scoring:

- Likelihood of award — based on the funder's history with organizations of this type and size, past award data where available, and whether the organization has an existing relationship with the funder

- Strategic importance — whether the award advances a program priority, a geographic expansion, or a relationship with a funder the organization wants to cultivate over multiple cycles

- Award size — weighted for the organization's capacity

- Timing — whether the award cycle aligns with program planning and cash flow needs

- Operating burden after award — a lower score for awards that carry high administrative complexity relative to their dollar value

A ranking method the team trusts is more important than the specific numerical weights. The ranking exists to make the "apply or pass" decision easier and more consistent across the team.

**Stage 4: Pre-Award Capacity Check**

Before any application is submitted, the organization should answer one question that prospecting teams routinely skip: could we actually run this grant if we won it?

That question has financial and operational dimensions. Financially: is the award a cost-reimbursement structure (which requires fronting costs and waiting for reimbursement) or an advance payment structure? Does the organization have the cash flow to front costs on a cost-reimbursement award? Operationally: does the grant require a dedicated program coordinator? Will the finance team be able to support the reporting cadence without hiring? If the award has a match requirement, is documented match available from allowable sources?

Finance staff should have a voice in this stage. Development teams evaluate grants on mission and likelihood. Finance teams evaluate grants on operational sustainability. The organization that applies for every attractive grant without filtering for operational capacity wins awards it cannot administer well — and administering them poorly creates audit findings, strained funder relationships, and compliance exposure that costs more than the award was worth.

## Common Mistakes

**Researching without qualifying.** Opportunity research is open-ended by nature. Without qualification gates, teams keep going because there is always one more funder to review. Time-boxing each stage — a defined research window, a qualification pass with a deadline, a shortlisting session — protects against prospecting becoming a permanent background project.

**Scoring before cutting.** Ranking 80 opportunities instead of the 15 that survived qualification wastes time and produces a ranked list that still requires another round of triage. Qualify to a manageable number, then score.

**Ignoring post-award capacity at prospecting time.** The award's administrative burden does not become relevant only after the award letter arrives. It should be part of the qualification gate. Development directors who prospect without finance input on operational costs often deliver awards that create internal strain — not because the grant was wrong for the mission, but because it was wrong for the current staff capacity.

**Treating pipeline count as a success metric.** A pipeline of 40 opportunities where 35 are weak fits is not 40% more valuable than a pipeline of 10 strong fits. It is more expensive and less productive.

## What a Disciplined Workflow Produces

A grant prospecting workflow that runs these four stages produces something specific: a shortlist of qualified opportunities, documented reasons for disqualifying weak fits, a ranking method the team can apply consistently, and a visible handoff point into application planning.

That handoff point matters. Prospecting should not end with "this looks promising." It should end with a decision: apply or pass, with reasoning that both development and finance understand.

Organizations that build this discipline find that their application rates drop and their award rates rise. They spend less time writing applications for grants they were never going to win, and more time preparing strong submissions for funders where the fit — mission, eligibility, capacity, and timing — is genuine.

For mid-sized nonprofits with lean development teams, that is the better operating model. Prospecting quality is not about finding more opportunities. It is about finding the right ones and being disciplined enough to pass on the rest.

## What to Do This Week

Map the current prospecting process against the four stages above. Where does the team currently spend most of its research time — before or after qualification? If opportunities are being scored before they are qualified, the next prospecting cycle can start with a qualification pass instead. If internal definition has not been documented formally, a one-hour conversation with development and finance to establish the award size range, reporting tolerance, and capacity constraints pays dividends for every prospecting cycle afterward.

GrantPipe connects the grant tracking that begins at award to the donor and funder records that matter in prospecting — so the pipeline you build feeds directly into the compliance and reporting workflow after an award is won. One operating record, not a pre-award system and a post-award system maintained separately.

Myth: if a cost is in the grant budget, it is allowable on a federal award.

Under 2 CFR Part 200, every cost charged to a federal grant must pass three separate tests simultaneously. A cost can appear in the approved budget and still be disallowed.

Test 1 — Allowability: the cost must not be explicitly prohibited under 2 CFR 200.420–200.475. Alcoholic beverages (200.423), entertainment (200.438), lobbying (200.450), and fundraising costs (200.442) are never allowable — regardless of what appears in the budget.

Test 2 — Allocability: the grant must have actually benefited from the cost. Charging 100% of a shared cost to one grant when multiple programs benefited is a common allocability error, even when the total amount is small.

Test 3 — Reasonableness: would a prudent person pay this amount for this good or service in the ordinary course of business? Above-market contracted services, procurements without competitive quotes above the micro-purchase threshold, and equipment that exceeds program requirements can produce partial disallowances based on reasonableness alone.

Budget approval does not substitute for any of these three tests. Document each cost on its own merits at the time of the transaction.

The most common subaward budget modification error is not forgetting to file paperwork. It is approving a change before checking who actually has the authority to approve it.

Under 2 CFR 200.308(e)(4), pass-through entities can approve direct cost transfers across budget categories without federal prior approval — but only when the transfer does not exceed 10% of the total award budget and does not alter the project scope. That threshold is calculated against the total federal award, not the category being modified.

An organization with a $500,000 award can transfer up to $50,000 across categories on its own authority. Beyond that, a written request must go to the federal program officer before the subrecipient incurs costs under the new budget.

Approving first and seeking federal sign-off after is itself a compliance violation. Expenditures incurred under an unauthorized modification may be questioned or disallowed.

The second-most common error: treating a reallocation that funds an activity not in the original scope as a routine budget transfer. If the modified budget funds something new, federal prior approval is required regardless of the dollar amount.

Federal prior approval timelines vary by agency — HHS Grants Management often responds within 30 days; DOJ and HUD can take 60 to 90 days. Build those timelines into every subaward monitoring calendar from award day.

# What Donor Retention Reports Should Actually Tell Your Board

The quarterly board packet lands and the development director flips to the fundraising page. Total gifts received: $312,000. Same slide as last quarter, different number.

That number does not tell the board whether the donor base is healthy or eroding. It does not distinguish between an organization that retained 70% of its donors and grew revenue from existing relationships versus one that retained 35% and spent heavily on new acquisition to offset losses. Both can show identical totals in a given quarter.

The metrics below take roughly the same time to report as total revenue, assuming the CRM tracks giving history year over year. They produce fundamentally different board conversations.

## Why Total Revenue Conceals the Real Picture

The Fundraising Effectiveness Project has consistently documented that nonprofits in aggregate lose more donors than they gain each year. The organizations that grow despite this pattern retain existing donors at above-average rates. The ones that stagnate or decline are often replacing lapsed donors with new acquisition — which costs money and masks the structural problem in the revenue line.

A board that sees only total revenue cannot ask the right questions. "How do we grow revenue?" is not the same question as "why did we retain 38% of general donors last quarter and what specifically are we doing differently?" The first question produces strategy conversations. The second produces corrective action.

Donor retention rate is the single most useful leading indicator of long-term revenue stability. An organization with strong current revenue but declining retention is heading for a funding gap that the revenue number will not reveal until it arrives. Boards that track retention quarterly can intervene before the gap materializes.

## The Four Metrics That Matter

**Overall retention rate, with year-over-year trend.** The calculation is straightforward: donors who gave this year who also gave last year, divided by total donors who gave last year. The sector average is approximately 45%, meaning more than half of donors from any given year do not return the following year. Organizations above 60% have strong donor relationship programs.

The trend matters as much as the rate. Retention at 48% this year versus 46% last year looks like minor improvement. If retention was 55% three years ago, the year-over-year comparison is misleading — the trend is downward. Present retention on a rolling view covering the past four quarters or twelve months.

**Retention rate segmented by giving level.** Most organizations track at least three segments: major donors (typically $1,000+ annually), mid-level ($250–$999), and general (under $250). Each segment has a different expected range and a different response if it falls below it.

Major donor retention should be 80% or higher. If it drops below that threshold, the board needs to know immediately — major donors typically represent a disproportionate share of total revenue. Mid-level retention in the 50–60% range is strong; this segment often represents the largest improvement opportunity because mid-level donors respond to personal outreach but rarely receive it. General donor retention at 40–50% is sector average; below 35% signals a systemic problem with acknowledgment timing, communication frequency, or impact reporting.

Segmented retention shifts the board conversation from "how is fundraising going" to "which specific segment needs attention and what should change." That is a board-level strategy conversation.

**LYBUNT count with estimated recapture value.** LYBUNT — Last Year But Unfortunately Not This — identifies donors who gave in the immediately preceding year but have not given in the current year. They have a recent relationship with the organization. Recapture rates for LYBUNT donors targeted with specific outreach are typically 15–25%.

The board does not need the acronym. They need the translation: "We have 200 donors who gave last year and have not yet given this year. At their average prior gift of $150 and a 20% recapture rate, a targeted campaign could recover approximately $6,000." A board that sees a dollar figure can decide whether to fund a recapture initiative. A board that sees a percentage cannot.

SYBUNT donors — Some Years But Unfortunately Not This — gave in prior years but not the most recent year. Their connection is more distant; recapture rates run 5–10%. The pool is larger. SYBUNT recapture requires a different approach: reintroduction to current work, not a renewal ask. Both counts belong in the quarterly report because they represent different revenue opportunities with different outreach strategies.

**Average gift size, with trend.** An average gift increase from $180 to $195 looks positive in isolation. If that increase is driven by a single large gift while median gift size is declining, the trend data reveals it. Present average gift size with a year-over-year comparison and a rolling view. When average gift is rising alongside retention, the donor relationship is deepening. When average gift is rising while retention is declining, the organization is becoming more dependent on fewer, larger donors — a concentration risk the board should understand.

## The Framework: Four Numbers, One Narrative, One Table

Board members read in volume. A donor retention report that requires 15 minutes of close reading will not receive careful attention in a board meeting.

The format that works: one page, four key metrics at the top in dashboard layout, one paragraph of narrative context in the middle, and a segmented retention table at the bottom. Supporting detail — the full donor list, gift-by-gift breakdown, LYBUNT roster — goes in an appendix available on request.

The top section is four numbers with context: total active donors (with year-over-year change), overall retention rate (with trend direction), LYBUNT count with estimated recapture value in dollars, average gift size (with trend direction).

The narrative paragraph is specific, not general. Not "fundraising is strong" but "major donor retention declined 8 points to 74%. Three major donors from the capital campaign cycle completed their pledges and have not renewed at a sustaining level. The development director recommends personal outreach to all three within 30 days." The board can act on a specific recommendation. They cannot act on a status summary.

The segmented table shows retention rate for major, mid-level, and general donors with year-over-year comparison. Three rows, three columns. Preparation time under 30 minutes if the CRM tracks the data.

## The Most Common Mistake: Annual Reporting

Annual donor reports arrive too late to change course within the fiscal year. If retention drops 8 points in Q1 and the board does not see it until the annual report in Q4, nine months of corrective action opportunity is gone.

Quarterly retention reporting gives the board advance notice: approve a recapture campaign before the window closes, question a development strategy that is producing declining results, or reallocate resources between acquisition and retention before the budget cycle ends. The preparation overhead is minimal if the CRM tracks the data — approximately 1–2 hours per quarter to pull the numbers, write the narrative paragraph, and format the board packet page.

If the current reporting cadence is annual, the practical starting point is adding a single quarterly one-page retention summary to the next board meeting agenda. It does not require restructuring the entire board reporting process.

## Translating Retention Into Dollars for Board Decisions

Finance boards are comfortable with dollar figures and uncomfortable with sector benchmarks. Lead with the financial consequence, not the metric.

"Our retention rate is 48%" produces a note in the board minutes. "Roughly half our donors from last year did not give again, which represents approximately $48,000 in revenue we need to replace through new acquisition or lapsed donor outreach — and new acquisition costs money to produce" produces a decision about strategy.

The calculation takes 90 seconds: total lapsed donors multiplied by average prior gift equals the revenue gap. Run it every quarter as part of the standard retention summary. When the board consistently sees the dollar consequence of retention trends, they develop the intuition to ask better questions about development strategy — including questions about whether acquisition spending is efficiently replacing lapsed revenue or merely obscuring a systemic retention problem.

## What the CRM Should Do Automatically

Generating these four metrics should take under an hour if the CRM tracks donor history and year-over-year giving. Platforms with native retention reporting — automatic retention rate calculation, LYBUNT and SYBUNT identification, giving-level segmentation, rolling trend views — eliminate the manual work of exporting two years of donor lists, matching records in a spreadsheet, and calculating who is missing.

If pulling a segmented retention report from the current system takes more than an hour, that is a platform limitation worth factoring into the next CRM evaluation. Board-ready donor reporting is a basic function, not an advanced feature. CRMs that require a consultant or custom report builder to produce retention segmentation by giving level have an ongoing cost embedded in every board meeting.

The capabilities to verify before selecting a platform: automatic retention rate calculation with year-over-year comparison, LYBUNT and SYBUNT identification from giving history, giving-level segmentation without manual filtering, rolling twelve-month or four-quarter trend views, and exportable formatting that fits a one-page board packet without reformatting.

## One Practical Change for the Next Board Meeting

If none of these metrics are currently in the board packet, the lowest-friction starting point is the LYBUNT count with a dollar estimate. Export last year's donor list and this year's donor list, match on email address, count the ones in last year's list who are absent from this year's, multiply by average prior gift, and add two sentences to the current board narrative.

That single addition shifts the board's understanding of development performance from revenue received to relationship health. From that starting point, segmented retention and trend data follow naturally as reporting cadence and CRM capability allow.

GrantPipe calculates retention rate automatically, segments by giving level, and identifies LYBUNT and SYBUNT donors from giving history — so the quarterly retention summary takes minutes to pull rather than hours to construct. If your current system cannot produce this view efficiently, that limitation has a cost worth accounting for in the next platform review.

"Management decision" has a specific legal meaning in federal grant compliance that differs from ordinary usage.

Under 2 CFR 200.521, a management decision is the written determination issued by a federal awarding agency or pass-through entity in response to a finding from a single audit.

The federal agency has six months from the date the audit is accepted by the Federal Audit Clearinghouse to issue it.

The management decision either accepts the finding as written, modifies its scope, or in rare cases disputes it. For questioned costs, it determines whether those costs are allowable or must be repaid. For internal control or compliance findings, it establishes the required corrective actions and the timeline for completion.

Once issued, the corrective actions become tracked obligations. Status is reported in the Summary Schedule of Prior Audit Findings in every subsequent single audit until the finding is resolved. If the deadline passes and corrections are not complete, the finding may be characterized as a repeat finding in the next audit — treated as more serious than a new finding.

Organizations that disagree have appeal rights, but appeals must generally be filed within 60 to 90 days of receiving the management decision.

Most finance teams know what a finding is. Fewer know exactly what triggers the six-month clock.

# Restricted Fund Tracking: Where Nonprofits Lose Control and What to Do About It

A program coordinator who works 60% on one grant and 40% on another has a compliance obligation most organizations do not have a reliable system to fulfill. The time split must be documented. The allocation must be updated if responsibilities shift. The payroll charges must map to the correct fund code, pay period by pay period, for the full grant term. When an auditor samples personnel costs three years after the fact, the organization either produces that documentation or explains a finding.

This is not a software problem or a staffing problem, though both are factors. It is an operational problem that most nonprofits underestimate until it surfaces in an audit finding, a disallowed cost, or a funder relationship that does not survive the compliance review.

## What Restricted Funds Actually Require

Restricted funds are assets whose use is limited by an external donor or funder condition. The accounting standard is FASB ASC 958, which separates nonprofit net assets into unrestricted, temporarily restricted, and permanently restricted categories. For most mid-sized nonprofits managing active grant portfolios, the day-to-day challenge is temporary restrictions: a federal workforce development grant limited to specific job training activities, a foundation health grant limited to a defined service population, a state housing grant with approved budget categories and allowable cost definitions that differ from the organization's own cost structure.

The compliance obligation is not ambiguous. Restricted funds must be spent on what the funder approved. They must be tracked separately from unrestricted operating funds. They cannot cross-subsidize each other without documented allocation methodology. And they must generate the documentation that supports funder financial reports and withstands audit testing.

The failure mode is not usually deliberate misuse. It is a system that cannot enforce the rules automatically, combined with staff who are working too fast to catch the errors before auditors do.

## The Three Operational Breakdowns

**Personnel cost allocation.** Staff costs present the largest restricted fund tracking risk. A program coordinator whose time is split across two grants cannot simply appear on one grant's payroll. Monthly personnel activity reports — not semi-annual certifications, which apply only to single-program employees — must document 100% of that person's compensated time, allocated to the correct funding source for each pay period. If responsibilities shift mid-year, the allocation percentages must be updated prospectively and documented. Payroll systems do not track grant allocations by default. Someone must create, maintain, and update that tracking system. When the person who owned the spreadsheet leaves, the system often goes with them.

**Shared cost allocation.** Office supplies, software subscriptions, telephone, facility costs — these benefit multiple programs simultaneously. Organizations charge these to grants using an indirect cost rate or a cost allocation methodology. The methodology must be documented, consistently applied, and defensible under audit. Federal grantees without a negotiated indirect cost rate agreement (NICRA) may use the de minimis rate of 15% of modified total direct costs under 2 CFR 200, but choosing the de minimis rate requires a documented election and consistent application. Organizations that use different methodologies in different years, or that cannot produce the documentation underlying their allocation, create audit exposure on what should be a routine compliance item.

**Timing gaps between spending and reconciliation.** A restricted grant is received in month one. Personnel expenses accumulate in months two through twelve. Vendor invoices for approved program activities arrive throughout the year. By the time someone reconciles the grant budget in month six — or month twelve, if reconciliation only happens at report time — connecting each expenditure to the correct fund requires reconstructing decisions made months earlier. The longer the gap between spending and reconciliation, the higher the error rate. The MacArthur Foundation's indirect cost study found that the minimum indirect cost rate associated with financially healthy organizations is 29%, yet most funders reimburse far less. Organizations managing grants with inadequate tracking tools end up absorbing costs that were legitimately chargeable to grants — not because the costs were ineligible, but because the documentation did not exist to claim them.

## What Audit Failure Costs

The Nonprofit Finance Fund's 2025 State of the Nonprofit Sector Survey found that 36% of nonprofits ended FY2024 with an operating deficit — the highest rate in a decade. Cash constraints make the cost of audit findings particularly acute.

For federal grants, a finding that restricted funds were used outside their approved purpose can result in questioned costs: the funder refuses to reimburse those expenses and may demand repayment of amounts already disbursed. Significant findings can result in suspension of future funding, additional monitoring requirements, or debarment from federal programs.

For foundation grants, the consequence is almost always relational: required repayment and loss of the grantor relationship. Foundation program officers communicate with peer funders. A compliance failure that becomes part of the organization's reputation in a funding community affects grant prospects beyond the single funder involved.

The consistent pattern: the cost of correcting a compliance failure after audit is higher than the cost of tracking correctly throughout the grant period. Organizations that run the math on staff time spent on post-audit remediation, required repayments, and lost funding relationships consistently find the upstream investment in systems would have been cheaper.

## The Three-System Problem

The root cause of most restricted fund tracking failures is architectural. Accurate fund tracking requires connecting three systems that typically do not communicate: the accounting system, which holds the general ledger and fund codes; the grant management system, which tracks award terms, budget categories, and funder requirements; and the HR or payroll system, which processes personnel costs without grant allocation logic.

In the absence of a connected system, organizations build manual bridges: the spreadsheet that translates payroll to grant allocations, the shared drive where invoices are filed without a consistent naming convention, the monthly email from the grants manager that produces the reconciliation the finance director needs for SF-425 preparation. Each bridge is a failure point. When the grants manager is out or transitions roles, the bridge fails. When a budget modification is approved by the funder but not propagated to the tracking spreadsheet, the bridge fails. When the accounting system year-end close happens before the grant reconciliation is complete, the bridge fails.

Purpose-built grant compliance software creates the connection architecture directly. Each grant award links to its approved budget categories. Expenditures are recorded against the correct grant as they occur rather than being allocated retroactively. Personnel activity reports tie personnel costs to fund codes at the time payroll is processed. The fund balance visible to the development director matches the fund balance in the accounting system because they are drawing from the same data source.

## The Monthly Reconciliation Practice

The operational fix is not primarily a software purchase. It is a practice change that software can support. The practice: reconcile every active restricted fund monthly, not quarterly and not at report time.

A monthly reconciliation does four things. It catches misallocated expenditures while the transactions are recent and correctable, before they compound over multiple months. It produces the running budget-to-actual comparison that makes SF-425 preparation a confirmation exercise rather than a reconstruction project. It flags pending expenses that need to be reviewed for allowability before they are processed rather than after. And it creates the documentation record that demonstrates the monitoring occurred — which auditors treat as evidence of a functioning compliance system, not just data in a ledger.

The specific steps of a defensible monthly reconciliation:

1. Pull a fund-specific expenditure report from the accounting system for the period.

2. Compare line by line against the approved budget, by category.

3. Identify any expenditures that appear in the wrong budget category or that exceed approved category amounts.

4. Document corrections needed and the date corrections were submitted.

5. Confirm that personnel allocations for the period match approved effort percentages.

6. Update the remaining-balance calculation for each budget category.

7. File the reconciliation as a dated document with the grant file.

Organizations that complete this practice consistently find that grant closeout becomes a verification step rather than a month-long reconstruction.

## The Most Common Single Failure

Across audit findings involving restricted funds, the most common single failure is not misuse of funds. It is missing documentation of allowable expenditures. The expense was legitimate. The cost category was correct. The fund had budget remaining. The organization simply cannot produce the invoice, the time record, or the approval evidence that connects the expenditure to the grant.

The consequence is the same as actual misuse from the auditor's perspective: a questioned cost. The organization must either produce the missing documentation — if it exists somewhere — or accept the disallowance.

The fix is documentation discipline at the point of expenditure, not at audit time. Every charge to a restricted fund should have a source document that travels with it into the grant file: the invoice for vendor costs, the payroll register excerpt for personnel costs, the business purpose justification for travel. When the document is filed at the time the expense occurs, the audit response is retrievable in minutes. When it is not filed, the response requires weeks.

## What to Do This Week

If your organization manages active restricted grants, three actions create immediate risk reduction.

Pull the current budget-to-actual for each active grant today, from the accounting system, not from a spreadsheet. If the two sources do not match, the reconciliation gap is the first priority.

Verify that personnel allocation percentages in payroll match what is documented in each grant's file. A discrepancy means either the payroll allocation is wrong or the documented allocation is out of date — either way, it is an audit exposure that is better corrected now than explained later.

Confirm that the grant file for each active award contains the pre-award risk assessments, sub-award agreements, and SAM.gov debarment checks required under 2 CFR 200.332 for any subrecipients. These are among the most frequently requested documents in single audit testing, and they must have existed at the time the sub-award was made, not be assembled retroactively.

GrantPipe connects the donor CRM, grant lifecycle management, and restricted fund tracking in one system — so the reconciliation that currently requires three systems and a reconciling spreadsheet runs against a single data source. For organizations managing five or more active grants simultaneously, that integration is what separates compliant operations from a recurring audit finding.
