"Payroll allocation errors are rare." They are the opposite: they appear in roughly 25% of single-audit engagements every year.

The HHS Office of Inspector General cross-cutting findings report identifies payroll allocation as a persistent top-five single audit finding. The reason is structural, not negligent.

Most nonprofits run payroll in ADP or QuickBooks. The grants manager maintains a separate spreadsheet showing how each employee's time should split across awards. Finance makes journal entries to move costs to grant-specific accounts. Time-and-effort certifications live in a shared folder somewhere.

At audit time, the auditor needs three things: the certification, the allocation entry matching the certification, and the payroll register confirming the gross pay amount. Reconciling those three sources — for every employee, every month, every award — is where the gaps appear.

The 2024 revision to 2 CFR 200.430 clarified explicitly that budget-based allocations without after-the-fact verification remain non-compliant. Organizations that entered allocations at planned percentages rather than certified actual percentages have a finding waiting for them.

The fix is not more spreadsheet columns. It is linking the allocation entry, the certification, and the payroll register so the comparison happens before the auditor does it.

Before you submit an Indirect Cost Rate proposal, run this check: does every number in your cost pool and allocation base trace directly to a line in your audited financial statements?

If the answer is anything other than yes, the cognizant agency will return the proposal without negotiating.

The ICR proposal process under 2 CFR 200.414 starts earlier than most organizations realize. There is a threshold decision before any paperwork: if your actual indirect rate is below 10%, the de minimis rate under 2 CFR 200.414(f) likely beats the NICRA. No proposal, no negotiation, no annual renewal. For organizations under $1–2M in federal funding with modest indirect costs, the administrative savings outweigh the marginal recovery difference.

When a NICRA does win — typically when actual indirect rates run 15% or higher — the math is concrete. On $2M of Modified Total Direct Costs, a 15% rate recovers $300K versus $200K at de minimis. A $100K annual difference justifies the 40–80 hours of first-time proposal effort.

The rate type choice is separate from the rate level. Fixed-with-carryforward is the most common structure for mid-sized nonprofits: the rate is set in advance, variances roll into the next period rather than triggering retroactive adjustments, and the administrative burden is manageable.

The cognizant agency for most nonprofits without a dominant single federal funder is HHS Division of Cost Allocation. First-time negotiations take 90–180 days from submission. Plan accordingly.

A federal grant drawdown is not automatic. The awarding agency loads the grant funds into a payment system — usually ASAP, the Automated Standard Application for Payments — and the grantee must actively request disbursement.

ASAP processed more than $700 billion in federal disbursements in fiscal year 2023. Every one of those transactions started with a grantee initiating a request.

Under 2 CFR 200.305, two payment methods govern when the request can happen.

Advance payment releases funds before expenses are incurred — the grantee requests an amount projected to cover the next 30 days. The advance must reconcile against actual expenses, and any excess must be returned promptly. Most mid-sized nonprofits use advance payment because they cannot float payroll while waiting for reimbursement.

Reimbursement releases funds after expenses are posted in the accounting system. The grantee documents the costs, runs an expenditure report, and requests the documented amount. Impossible to over-draw when the request is based on posted actuals.

Three things create drawdown problems: over-drawing (requesting more than posted allowable expenses support), under-drawing (leaving documented costs without requesting reimbursement — which can trigger automatic deobligation near award end dates), and drawing against unallowable costs.

None of these are exotic compliance failures. They are the predictable result of drawdown schedules that fall out of sync with actual expenditure records.

# How to Negotiate a Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA): A Practical Guide for Nonprofit Finance Teams

A nonprofit receiving $2 million in federal awards and charging indirect costs at the 15% de minimis rate recovers $200,000. The same organization with a negotiated indirect cost rate of 18% recovers $360,000. That $160,000 difference funds staff time, facilities, and administration that would otherwise come out of unrestricted reserves — or not be funded at all.

The gap between those two outcomes is a NICRA: a Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement issued by a cognizant federal agency. The decision to pursue one — or to stick with the 15% de minimis rate under 2 CFR 200.414(f) — is one of the most consequential financial decisions a federally funded nonprofit makes. Most organizations make it by default rather than by calculation.

## The First Decision: NICRA or De Minimis

Before preparing any proposal, the calculation comes first. Under 2 CFR 200.414(f), an organization that has never had a negotiated indirect cost rate may elect the de minimis rate of 15% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC). No proposal, no cognizant agency review, no annual renewal required. The election can be used indefinitely.

The de minimis rate wins when actual indirect costs are close to or below 15% of MTDC. For organizations with modest administrative structures relative to their direct program spending, chasing a negotiated rate produces marginal additional recovery that does not justify 40–80 hours of initial proposal work.

The NICRA wins when actual indirect costs run materially higher. A practical threshold: if the organization's actual indirect rate is 13–15% or above, the NICRA pays for itself within two to three years. Below that, the de minimis is often the more pragmatic path.

The 2024 revision to 2 CFR 200 also extended de minimis eligibility significantly. Some organizations that previously had to submit ICR proposals can now elect de minimis instead. It is worth confirming current eligibility before starting a proposal.

## Identifying the Cognizant Agency

The cognizant agency is the federal entity responsible for reviewing and issuing the rate agreement. For most nonprofits, it is determined by a single rule: the federal agency providing the largest direct dollar amount of funding.

In practice, that means HHS handles most nonprofits. The Division of Cost Allocation (DCA) within HHS's Program Support Center is the functional office. The Department of Education handles educational organizations with significant federal education funding. USDA handles organizations with agricultural or rural program focus.

If an organization receives only pass-through federal funding — federal money flowing through a state agency or intermediary — HHS DCA typically serves as the cognizant agency by default, since there is no direct federal funder to assume the role.

This matters practically because different cognizant agencies have different submission portals, different documentation checklists, and different response timelines. HHS DCA accepts electronic submissions and has published checklists. First contact with the relevant agency should happen before the proposal is assembled.

## The Three-Part Framework: Pool, Base, and Documentation

Every ICR proposal rests on three technical elements. Getting these right determines whether the proposal moves or gets returned.

**The Cost Pool**

The indirect cost pool contains all organizational costs that benefit multiple programs and cannot be directly assigned to a specific federal award. Common indirect costs include general administration (executive leadership, finance, HR, legal), facilities costs (rent, utilities, depreciation on shared space), IT and communications infrastructure, and board-related expenses.

What does not belong in the indirect pool: any cost that can be specifically identified with a particular award. A program coordinator whose time is tracked to specific grants is a direct cost, not an indirect one. Facilities costs for a space used exclusively by a single program belong direct. Organizations that commingle these categories — or that charge as indirect any cost that is inconvenient to track directly — will face challenges during review.

**The Allocation Base**

The allocation base is the denominator against which indirect costs are spread. The standard base is Modified Total Direct Costs. MTDC includes direct salaries, fringe benefits, materials and supplies, services, travel, and the first $50,000 of each subaward. MTDC excludes equipment, capital expenditures, rental of real property, student aid, and the portion of each subaward exceeding $25,000.

The base must be complete and consistent. Organizations that include some direct salaries but exclude others without documented justification will face scrutiny. The cognizant agency verifies that the base captures all relevant direct costs and that exclusions are defensible.

**The Documentation Package**

A complete submission includes: audited financial statements for the base year, IRS Form 990, personnel time allocation records, a written indirect cost allocation methodology, rate calculation worksheets that tie to the audit, a complete list of federal awards with amounts by agency, and a Certificate of Indirect Costs signed by an authorized official (typically the CEO or CFO).

The reconciliation between the proposal and the audited financial statements is the most critical element. Every number in the cost pool and base must trace to a specific line or schedule in the audit. Unreconciled submissions are returned without negotiation. This is not a technicality — the purpose is to ensure the proposal reflects actual costs, not estimated ones.

## Choosing the Rate Type

Four rate types exist, and the choice affects administrative burden for years after the NICRA is issued.

**Provisional rates** are temporary, used until a final rate is negotiated. They are common for first-time submissions while the initial review is pending. Provisional rates create uncertainty because retroactive adjustment is possible once the final rate is set.

**Predetermined rates** are fixed and not retroactively adjusted. They provide budget certainty for both the organization and its federal awarding agencies. The downside: if actual indirect costs exceed the predetermined rate, the difference is not recovered.

**Fixed-with-carryforward rates** are set in advance, but variances between the negotiated rate and actual costs carry into the next period's rate calculation rather than requiring retroactive adjustment. For most mid-sized nonprofits, this is the practical sweet spot: rate certainty in the current period, with over- or under-recovery settling out over time.

**Final rates** are established retroactively once actual costs are known. They provide precision but require keeping awards open until the final rate is resolved — administratively heavy for organizations managing multiple overlapping grant periods.

## The Submission and Negotiation Process

Submission deadlines are typically 180 days after fiscal year-end. Extensions are available if requested in advance from the cognizant agency.

After submission, expect the agency to ask clarifying questions and request additional documentation. Common focus areas: justification for specific cost allocations, support for personnel time records, and verification that excluded costs were correctly treated. Responses should be prompt and documented in writing.

First-time negotiations typically run 90–180 days from submission to rate issuance. Renewals of established NICRAs are faster — often 30–60 days. Organizations with clean audits, well-documented cost allocation methodology, and complete submissions move through the process fastest. Every response to an agency question that requires back-and-forth adds weeks.

Once the rate letter is issued, it specifies the rate, the allocation base, the rate type, and the effective period. Pass-through subrecipients of the organization's federal awards may use the NICRA for their own indirect recovery if subaward terms permit.

## The Most Common Failure: Mixing Direct and Indirect Costs

The single most frequent reason ICR proposals are returned or challenged during negotiation is mixed classification: costs that belong in the direct category appear in the indirect pool, or vice versa, without time-study support or documented methodology.

The most common specific version: a program director whose time benefits multiple grants and organizational activities is charged entirely to indirect costs for administrative convenience, rather than being tracked to specific awards through documented time allocation. The cognizant agency treats undocumented mixed-function salaries charged to indirect costs as a red flag.

The remedy is a written indirect cost allocation methodology — not a theoretical policy document, but an operational one that specifies how each expense category is classified, how staff time allocation is determined (time study, periodic allocation, after-the-fact certification), and how shared costs like IT and facilities are handled. This document is reviewed annually and during every ICR negotiation. Organizations that cannot produce it face extended review cycles.

## What to Do This Week

Organizations currently using the de minimis rate should run the calculation: what is the actual indirect cost rate based on the most recent audited financials? If it is at or below 10%, de minimis is likely correct. If it is 15% or higher and federal funding is $1M or more, a NICRA negotiation is worth modeling.

Organizations with an existing NICRA should confirm the rate letter expiration date. If renewal is due within the next 90 days, the submission should already be in progress. If it lapses without renewal, the organization falls back to de minimis — which may be acceptable, but should be a deliberate choice rather than an oversight.

For organizations beginning the NICRA process for the first time, GrantPipe maintains the cost pool, allocation base, and reconciliation records needed for an ICR proposal on a continuous basis — so annual renewal is a refresh rather than a full rebuild from the accounting system. The 15% de minimis election is tracked per award with automatic MTDC base calculation, and the audit trail captures the documentation needed to support either path under review.

The TCJA silo rule turned Form 990-T compliance into a fundamentally different problem for nonprofits with multiple revenue streams.

Before 2018, a nonprofit with a money-losing bookstore and a profitable parking lot could net those activities. Under IRC Section 512(a)(6) — effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2017 — each unrelated trade or business is calculated separately. The bookstore loss stays in the bookstore silo. The parking lot income is taxed at 21%.

Six steps govern 990-T preparation under the current rules.

Identify unrelated activities: all three elements must be present — trade or business, regularly carried on, and not substantially related to exempt purpose. Gross income of $1,000 from any single silo triggers the filing obligation, even if aggregate UBI nets to zero.

Assign each activity to a silo using its 6-digit NAICS code. Activities within the same code may combine.

Calculate UBTI per silo: subtract directly connected expenses, apply Section 512(b) modifications (dividends, interest, and passive rents are excluded — not deducted, excluded entirely).

Apply pre-TCJA NOL carryforwards: these remain aggregate offsets against total UBTI. Post-TCJA NOLs are silo-specific and can only offset future income in the same silo.

File a separate Schedule A for each silo with $1,000 or more of gross income. The main 990-T aggregates them.

File by the 15th day of the 4th month after fiscal year-end. Pay estimated taxes quarterly when expected liability exceeds $500. Late-filing penalties start at 5% per month, up to 25%.

# How to Prepare a Clean SEFA Before Your Single Audit Begins

The finance director at a $2.8 million nonprofit received the auditor's fieldwork schedule in October. The engagement would begin in three weeks. The SEFA — the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards — was not prepared. It had never been prepared before. The prior year, an outside consultant had assembled it at the last minute from bank records and grant files, and the auditor had spent two days requesting clarifications before the document was accepted.

That scenario plays out every year at organizations that treat the SEFA as an audit deliverable rather than a year-round financial document. The cost is measurable: extended fieldwork, higher audit fees, and — in the worst cases — findings that appear in the Federal Audit Clearinghouse and require corrective action plans.

Incomplete SEFA preparation is among the five most common Single Audit findings identified by GAO in its April 2024 analysis (GAO-24-106173). The same analysis linked $1.17 trillion of federal award spending from 2017 through 2021 to severe and persistent Single Audit findings. This is not a paperwork problem. It is a financial controls problem with public consequences.

## What the SEFA Actually Does

The SEFA lists every federal award expended during the fiscal year. It is organized by federal agency and by Assistance Listing Number (ALN) — the same number previously called the CFDA number, now maintained in SAM.gov. Each line shows the pass-through entity if the award came through a state or local government, the total amount expended during the fiscal year, and any amounts passed through to subrecipients.

This document determines the scope of your Single Audit. The auditor uses it to identify Type A programs — those large enough to require testing under the dollar threshold in 2 CFR 200.518 — and to select major programs for compliance testing. A clean, accurate SEFA narrows audit scope. A SEFA with missing awards, misclassified pass-throughs, or totals that do not reconcile to the financial statements expands scope and generates questions that delay the audit.

The current Single Audit threshold is $1,000,000 in federal expenditures in a fiscal year under the 2024 revisions to 2 CFR Part 200, effective for fiscal years ending September 30, 2025 or later. Organizations should update their monitoring and confirm fiscal-year applicability with their auditor.

## The Four-Part SEFA Framework

### Part 1: Federal Award Inventory

The foundation of the SEFA is a complete list of every federal award active during the fiscal year. This means direct federal grants, cooperative agreements, and — critically — awards received as sub-awards from pass-through entities.

Pass-through awards are where organizations most often go wrong. A grant received from the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services for a mental health program may be a pass-through of federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) funds. The grant agreement from DHHS may not make this obvious. The SEFA must list this award under the prime federal agency (HHS/SAMHSA) and disclose NC DHHS as the pass-through entity — not list it as a state grant.

The practical step: capture pass-through status at award acceptance, not at SEFA preparation time. When a new grant agreement arrives, read it for any mention of the federal program, ALN number, or pass-through entity. Document that information in your grant record. Trying to reconstruct federal origin at year-end from a stack of grant agreements is how SEFA preparation takes 40 hours instead of 8.

### Part 2: General Ledger Grant Coding

The SEFA totals must be supported by general ledger detail. For every award on the SEFA, there must be a corresponding set of expense transactions in the accounting system showing what was charged against that award during the fiscal year.

This is where the difference between real fund accounting and a workaround becomes operational. An accounting system with grant-level coding — whether through restricted fund accounts, project codes, or dimensions — produces SEFA data with a single export. The totals per grant reconcile to the ledger automatically because the ledger was coded to grants throughout the year.

QuickBooks Classes are the most common workaround in this space. Classes track expenses by category but do not maintain fund balances. A Class report shows total spending under a label. It does not maintain the fund account, does not automatically reconcile to the Statement of Activities, and does not document the release-from-restriction event required under FASB ASC 958. For the SEFA specifically, Class data is usable if grant-level Classes were maintained. But when expenses were coded only to functions (Program, Management, Fundraising), the SEFA must be reconstructed transaction by transaction.

### Part 3: Pass-Through Identification and Subrecipient Disclosure

Two separate disclosures are required under 2 CFR 200.510:

For awards received as sub-awards, the SEFA must identify the pass-through entity by name and UEI, and show the prime federal agency and ALN.

For amounts your organization passed through to subrecipients, the SEFA must disclose the total per federal program. This is a required line item, not an optional footnote. If your organization acts as a pass-through entity — administering a CDBG subaward from a jurisdiction, for example, and regranting to a smaller nonprofit — the amounts passed through must appear on your SEFA.

These two disclosures are not symmetric. One documents where your award came from. The other documents where you sent federal dollars downstream.

### Part 4: Reconciliation to the Statement of Activities

The grand total of federal expenditures on the SEFA must reconcile to federal revenue recognized on the Statement of Activities. This reconciliation is prepared by the auditee, reviewed by the auditor during fieldwork, and expected to be documented before fieldwork begins.

Common reconciling items include unearned federal revenue (cash received but not yet expended), prior-year receivables collected and expended in the current year, and timing differences on multi-year awards. Each item must be documented — a line in a reconciliation schedule with a brief explanation.

Auditors will ask for this documentation. If it is not prepared, the auditor prepares it during fieldwork, at your expense.

## The Common Mistake That Generates Findings

The single most common SEFA error is pass-through misclassification. An organization lists a state agency grant under the state agency. The auditor identifies the federal program underlying the award. The SEFA is corrected, but the finding is documented: the organization lacked controls to identify federal pass-through awards at intake.

The consequence is not just a finding note. The finding appears in the Federal Audit Clearinghouse, visible to every federal funder and pass-through entity that reviews your organization's compliance history. It must be addressed in a corrective action plan. If the same error appears in subsequent years, it escalates from a deficiency to a material weakness.

The correction is straightforward but must happen upstream: at the point of award acceptance, not at year-end.

## What the Auditor Needs and When

Deliver the SEFA draft to your auditor at least 30 days before fieldwork begins. This timeline is not arbitrary. The auditor uses the SEFA to determine major programs, draft compliance testing procedures, and allocate fieldwork hours. A late SEFA compresses the auditor's preparation, increases the chance that the auditor identifies errors during fieldwork rather than in advance, and extends the engagement timeline.

The draft should be complete: all awards, all pass-through disclosures, all subrecipient pass-through amounts, and a documented reconciliation to the Statement of Activities. A SEFA delivered 30 days before fieldwork with one reconciling item still outstanding is better than a SEFA delivered one week before fieldwork with clean numbers.

## Building the Habit Before Year-End

The organizations that prepare clean SEFAs quickly are not doing more work at year-end. They are doing smaller, consistent work throughout the year.

Three practices drive clean SEFA preparation:

Capture ALN numbers at award acceptance. Every grant agreement should be reviewed for the federal program identifier before it is filed. This takes five minutes at intake and saves hours at year-end.

Maintain grant-level coding in the general ledger. Expense transactions should reference the specific grant throughout the year. Even in a simple system, a project code or restricted fund designation by grant produces the year-end extract without reconstruction.

Reconcile grant totals to the general ledger quarterly. A quarterly review of spending by grant versus the ledger catches coding errors — costs charged to the wrong grant, costs coded to function without grant attribution — while the year is still open. Correcting a misposted expense in August is a two-minute journal entry. Correcting it in November during SEFA preparation, when the award may have already entered closeout, is a compliance event.

## What to Do This Week

If your fiscal year ends in the next six months, pull your federal award inventory now. List every active award with its ALN number and pass-through entity. Check each one against your general ledger coding — can you trace every expense back to the specific award? If not, identify where the gaps are and close them before year-end.

If your fiscal year recently ended and SEFA preparation has not started, start with pass-through identification. Confirm which awards are federal and under which prime agency each one belongs. That determination drives everything else on the document.

# Cash vs. Accrual Accounting for Nonprofit Grants: What Your Books Are Actually Telling the Auditors

A nonprofit runs its books on a cash basis. The development director submits an SF-425 Federal Financial Report each quarter. The numbers look reasonable. The auditors arrive for the single audit and ask for the reconciliation worksheet that ties the cash-basis ledger to the accrued expenditure figures on the FFR.

There is no worksheet.

This scenario plays out at mid-sized nonprofits with federal awards more often than the sector talks about publicly. The gap between how an organization manages its internal books and what federal grant reporting actually requires is one of the more reliable predictors of single audit findings. And it is almost entirely avoidable.

## The Requirement That Does Not Negotiate

Federal grant reporting is accrual-basis. This is not a preference or a recommendation. It is a requirement under 2 CFR 200.302(b)(3), which mandates that non-federal entity financial management systems permit the tracing of funds to a level of expenditure adequate to establish that funds have not been used in violation of the restrictions and conditions of the federal award.

Cash-basis records cannot meet that standard when there are unpaid vendor invoices, earned-but-unpaid wages, or incurred-but-unreimbursed costs sitting at any period end.

The SF-425 Federal Financial Report makes this concrete. Block 10e asks for total federal share of expenditures — which includes both cash disbursements and accrued expenditures. An organization that submits only its cash disbursements in Block 10e is underreporting federal expenditures, even if it does not realize it.

This matters beyond the quarterly paperwork. Auditors test the FFR against the general ledger. If cumulative FFR expenditures consistently match cash disbursements with no accruals ever appearing, that pattern is an audit signal — not because accruals must exist in every period, but because the absence of any accruals across multiple periods is statistically unlikely for most organizations.

## The GAAP Layer

FASB ASC 958, Not-for-Profit Entities, adds a second layer. All audited nonprofit financial statements must be prepared on an accrual basis. This means:

Net assets are classified into two categories: with and without donor restrictions. Revenue is recognized when earned, not when cash arrives. Expenses are recognized when incurred, not when paid.

An organization that maintains internal cash-basis books and produces audited financials is running two parallel records: the working cash books and the accrual conversion the CPA prepares at year-end. This dual-maintenance model is common and functional. The risk is that the accrual conversion happens once a year, is never tested during the year, and produces a version of the financials that may not reconcile cleanly to the quarterly FFRs submitted throughout the year.

The Form 990 adds a third layer. IRS instructions require accrual-basis financial data for 990 preparation. Organizations using cash-basis books must reconcile to accrual for 990 filing — another conversion step where errors accumulate if the process is not documented.

## The Grant Revenue Recognition Framework

Understanding when to recognize grant revenue is a separate question from understanding the accounting basis. Under FASB ASC 958-605, recognition depends on the nature of the grant.

**Unconditional, purpose-restricted grants** are recognized as restricted revenue when the grant agreement is executed. The cash may not arrive until months later — a grant payable by quarterly reimbursement may not result in a cash receipt for 90 days. Under accrual basis, the revenue accrues at the point of an enforceable right. The organization has an asset (grant receivable) and revenue (restricted contribution) before any money moves.

**Conditional grants** are recognized as revenue when conditions are substantially met. A grant advance received before conditions are overcome is deferred revenue — a liability, not income. The cash was received; the revenue has not been earned. When qualifying costs are incurred, the deferred revenue is released to grant revenue on the statement of activities.

**Government grants structured as exchange transactions** may follow ASC 606 rather than ASC 958-605, depending on whether the relationship is a contribution or a fee for services. This distinction affects timing and classification. Getting it wrong produces either revenue overstatement (recording a fee-for-service contract as a contribution) or understatement (deferring revenue that should be recognized at contract execution).

The grant agreement's terms govern the analysis — not the organization's preference or prior practice.

## The Cash-to-Accrual Conversion: Four Required Adjustments

An organization that maintains cash-basis books and must report on an accrual basis for each FFR needs to perform the following adjustments at every reporting date. This is not optional or theoretical. It is what federal auditors will test.

**Adjustment 1: Accounts payable and accrued liabilities.** Identify all vendor invoices received and approved but not yet paid. These are accrued expenditures under accrual basis. Add these to the expenditure figure for the reporting period.

**Adjustment 2: Accrued payroll.** If a pay period crosses the FFR reporting date, the earned but unpaid wages belong in accrued expenditures. Calculate the proration. For semi-monthly payroll on a period that ends on the 15th and 30th, a quarterly FFR due on the last day of the month will typically have a half-payroll accrual to include.

**Adjustment 3: Grant receivables.** Costs incurred and reportable to the funder but not yet submitted for reimbursement are grant receivables — an asset under accrual basis. These costs are expenditures in the current period even if the reimbursement request has not been submitted. Organizations on a cost-reimbursement award that draw funds monthly may have two weeks of unsubmitted costs at any reporting date.

**Adjustment 4: Deferred revenue.** Cash advances received for conditional grants should not be included in accrual-basis revenue until conditions are met. If a grant advance was received in the prior quarter for a conditional award where conditions have not been substantially met, that advance is still deferred revenue.

Each adjustment must be documented in a reconciliation worksheet that ties the cash-basis ledger total to the accrual-basis figure used in the FFR. The worksheet is audit evidence. Its absence is a finding.

## The Most Common Error in Practice

Organizations that manage their books in QuickBooks — or any general ledger configured to cash basis — often discover the gap during a single audit rather than during their normal reporting process.

QuickBooks set to cash basis does not capture accounts payable accruals or grant receivables correctly. Reports run from a cash-basis QuickBooks file show only cash disbursements. If those figures go onto an SF-425 without adjustment, the FFR is understated.

The fix is straightforward in principle: configure QuickBooks to accrual basis. This enables accounts payable tracking, accounts receivable tracking, and the ability to run both cash-basis and accrual-basis reports for comparison. An organization with federal awards that is running QuickBooks on cash basis is creating unnecessary reconciliation risk every reporting cycle.

Organizations that have been running cash-basis books for years often resist the configuration change because the existing reports are familiar and the prior-year financials were prepared on cash basis. The transition is manageable. It requires reconciling the opening balances at the transition date, training the bookkeeping staff on the accrual entries, and building the documentation habit before the next FFR is due.

## The Single Audit Connection

Discrepancies between cash-basis books and accrual-basis FFR submissions are one of the more reliable indicators of accounting control weaknesses in single audits. Not because auditors are looking for procedural failures — they are looking for evidence that the organization's financial management system can actually demonstrate that federal funds were spent in accordance with the award terms.

A clean reconciliation worksheet, produced at each reporting date, documented with source records, and retained in the grant file, is the evidence that the accrual-basis FFR was derived properly. It is also what makes the conversation with auditors short and uneventful rather than extended and documented in a finding.

The organizations that find themselves in single audit findings related to accounting basis are almost never committing intentional misrepresentation. They are organizations that did not build the conversion documentation habit, assumed the cash figures were close enough, or did not know the accrual requirement existed until an auditor asked about it.

## What to Do This Week

If your organization has federal awards and uses cash-basis books, the action items are clear.

First, identify the accounting basis in your general ledger and confirm whether your QuickBooks or equivalent system is configured to cash or accrual. Second, pull the most recent FFR submitted and compare the federal expenditures figure to the cash disbursements in your general ledger for the same period. If they match exactly — with no accruals ever appearing in Block 10e — you have a gap to close. Third, build the reconciliation worksheet for the current reporting period, even if a submission is not imminent. Document the four adjustments and retain the worksheet with the grant file.

If the reconciliation reveals a discrepancy with prior FFR submissions, discuss the scope of the issue with your auditor before self-reporting. Errors in prior FFR submissions are correctable through amended filings; the process is more manageable when it is documented and disclosed proactively.

If your current process relies on a manual conversion built in a spreadsheet each quarter, that is worth fixing before the next single audit cycle begins.

VAWA confidentiality is not a best practice. It is a federal prohibition.

Section 13925(b)(2) of the Violence Against Women Act bars any VAWA grantee from disclosing personally identifying information about a service recipient — to funders, federal systems, or any third party — without informed, written, reasonably time-limited consent.

PII under VAWA includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and any information that could be used to identify or locate an individual.

Most commercial CRMs are not configured to honor this rule by default. If a funder, federal program officer, or support staffer can access your client records through shared logins or integrations, that system may already be out of compliance.

Intentional violations carry consequences: funding termination, OIG referral, and civil liability.

The VAWA 2022 reauthorization (Pub. L. 117-103, Division W) strengthened these protections and extended them explicitly to tribal organizations and LGBTQ+ survivors.

The PMT portal receives aggregate service counts — never individual client records. That distinction is not a technicality. It is the architecture.

Most organizations updated their journal entry practices after FASB ASU 2020-07. Far fewer updated their footnote disclosures.

ASU 2020-07 — effective for fiscal years beginning after June 15, 2021 — requires nonprofits to present contributed nonfinancial assets as a separate line and disclose by category: the valuation technique, fair value hierarchy level, whether assets were monetized or used directly, and any donor restrictions.

The footnote is not the same as the general contributions policy note that existed before.

Common gaps after adoption: organizations list food donations as "valued at fair value" without stating they used USDA wholesale prices as the basis. Or they disclose that legal services were received without identifying that the value used was the attorney's standard billing rate.

Under 2 CFR 200.306, in-kind contributions used as federal grant match must be valued using comparable market prices with documentation that is verifiable by auditors.

Stale valuations from the year a recurring in-kind relationship began — the law firm that has donated services for three years, still valued at 2022 billing rates — are a quiet audit risk.

If the footnote has not been reviewed since adoption year, that is the place to start.

"Award period" and "period of performance" mean the same thing. What they authorize is narrower than most people assume.

Under 2 CFR 200.77, the period of performance is the time during which a non-federal entity may incur new obligations against the award. Costs incurred before the start date or after the end date are unallowable — regardless of when the invoice is paid.

Some federal awards include a liquidation period (commonly 90 days after the end date) during which costs incurred before the end date may still be paid. That is not the same as an extension of the project period.

A supply invoice received 10 days after the end date for goods delivered during the grant period may be allowable during the liquidation window. A purchase order issued after the end date is not, regardless of when payment clears.

The start date is also often misread. Some awards specify a project start date weeks before the award letter arrives. Costs incurred from the project start date — not the date the letter was received — are allowable.

Enter the exact dates from the Notice of Award. Not from the application. Not from an email confirmation. From the Notice of Award.

# Grant Compliance 101: What Actually Happens After You Win the Grant

The award letter arrives. The organization celebrates. Then, within a week, someone asks: "So what do we need to do now?"

That question marks the beginning of a multi-year operational obligation that most organizations are less prepared for than they were for the application itself. Grant compliance — what funders actually require after an award, and what happens when those requirements are not met — gets a fraction of the attention that proposal writing receives. The result is that compliance failures are more common than application rejections at many mid-sized nonprofits.

This article covers what post-award compliance actually requires, why restricted funds are the centerpiece of the compliance obligation, where the most expensive failures occur, and how to build a compliance posture that holds up through the entire grant period.

## The Reverse Pipeline

The application process has a clear goal: win the award. The post-award process has a different kind of goal: satisfy ongoing legal and financial obligations for a period that may last two to four years, plus additional time if the organization is selected for audit.

A federal grant with a 24-month performance period will typically generate: a grant agreement execution, an initial budget submission, quarterly SF-425 Federal Financial Reports, semi-annual or annual programmatic reports, budget modification requests, and a final report with supporting documentation. Each step has deadlines. Missing a reporting deadline can trigger a significant deficiency finding. Significant deficiency findings affect future eligibility.

Foundation grants vary more. Some require only an annual narrative report. Others require quarterly updates, site visits, and detailed financial reconciliations. The grant agreement specifies what is required. Reading it before the funds arrive — not when the first report is due — is the first compliance decision an organization makes.

## Restricted Funds: The Core Obligation

When a funder awards a $75,000 grant for a workforce development program, that money carries a restriction. It can only be spent on workforce development program expenses as defined in the approved budget and grant terms. Spending it on general operating costs — even temporarily, with every intention of repaying it — is a compliance violation.

Restricted fund accounting requires tracking grant dollars separately from unrestricted revenue. Every expenditure charged to the grant must meet three tests:

Allowable — the cost type is permitted under the grant terms and applicable cost principles. Federal grants use 2 CFR 200 (the Uniform Guidance) as the cost principles framework. Foundation grants specify their own allowable costs.

Allocable — the expense is directly attributable to the approved program activities. A salary charged to a workforce development grant should represent time actually spent on workforce development program work, documented accordingly.

Documented — the organization can produce records that support the expenditure. For personnel costs under federal grants, that means time records identifying the grant or cost objective for each hour worked — not a general timesheet that reads "40 hours, program work."

The most common compliance failure is fund commingling: grant dollars deposited into the general operating account and tracked only by a spreadsheet that someone updates irregularly. When an auditor asks for documentation of how $75,000 was spent, the answer cannot be "we believe it went to these things." The auditor needs to trace each dollar from the grant account to a specific, allowable, documented expenditure.

## The Three Most Expensive Compliance Failures

Audit findings in federal grant programs cluster in predictable categories. Understanding where failures happen is more useful than a general instruction to "maintain good records."

**Personnel cost documentation.** Salaries charged to grants must be supported by time records that identify the grant or cost objective for each hour. Under 2 CFR 200.430, federal grants require that payroll charges reflect an after-the-fact determination of actual activity. A time sheet completed weeks after the pay period — particularly one that shows the same allocation pattern every period — raises audit questions. Organizations with multiple grants and staff who split time across programs need a time-tracking discipline that captures actual activity, not estimated allocations.

**Budget modification violations.** Most grants allow reallocation of funds between budget categories up to a threshold, with anything above that threshold requiring advance funder approval. Federal awards under the Uniform Guidance permit up to 10% rebudgeting without prior approval in most cases, though some programs and DOJ awards may have stricter thresholds that are specified in the Notice of Award. Organizations that spend down one budget line and begin charging costs to another — without confirming the threshold or requesting approval — create findings that can result in cost disallowances.

**Subrecipient monitoring gaps.** When a nonprofit passes federal funds through to a subgrantee or contractor, the primary grantee retains compliance responsibility for how those funds are used. This means conducting risk assessments, reviewing subrecipient expenditure reports, and monitoring subgrantee compliance with award conditions including confidentiality requirements. Pass-through entity liability is real: findings at the subrecipient level become findings at the primary grantee level.

## The Compliance Calendar as Operating Infrastructure

Federal grants require two parallel reporting tracks. Financial reports — the SF-425 Federal Financial Report — go to the grant's financial management system on a quarterly or semi-annual schedule. Programmatic reports go to the program officer on a separate schedule with different deadlines.

For an organization managing five active federal grants, that can mean 20 or more distinct reporting deadlines per year, not including foundation reports. Each deadline has a different submission method, a different contact, and a different format.

Organizations that manage this with Outlook reminders and shared spreadsheets function until staff turnover or workload concentration creates a miss. A single missed SF-425 deadline can generate a significant deficiency finding. Two missed deadlines in the same grant period can trigger enhanced monitoring.

The compliance calendar is not an administrative convenience. It is operating infrastructure. It should be populated at grant setup — before the first expenditure — with every deadline for the full period of performance. Not just the final report deadline.

## The Reporting Threshold That Changes Everything

Organizations that expend $1,000,000 or more in federal awards in a fiscal year must undergo a Single Audit under the Uniform Guidance (2 CFR 200 Subpart F). The Single Audit examines both financial statements and compliance with specific federal program requirements.

Crossing the $1,000,000 threshold for the first time is a significant compliance event. The audit scope changes, the documentation requirements become more formal, and findings carry consequences that ripple beyond the affected grant. A GAO analysis from April 2024 (GAO-24-106173) found that roughly 17% of all federal award spending from 2017 to 2021 was linked to single audit findings that were both severe and persistent.

Organizations approaching this threshold for the first time should treat it as a readiness milestone, not a surprise. The audit preparation that a Single Audit requires — organized grant files, complete time records, documented expenditure methodology, reconciled restricted-fund balances — is the same preparation that good compliance management produces as a natural output.

## The Framework: Four Pillars of Compliance Readiness

Mid-sized organizations managing multiple grants across different funders need a compliance framework they can actually operate without a dedicated compliance staff. The four-pillar structure that works at this scale:

**Fund separation.** Every grant has its own accounting code or project code. Expenditures are coded to grants in real time, not at month-end. Restricted balances are visible from the accounting system without manual compilation.

**Documentation discipline.** Personnel costs have contemporaneous time records. Direct costs have invoices, receipts, or purchase orders filed in the grant record. Budget modifications are documented and approved before costs shift between categories.

**Reporting calendar management.** Every reporting deadline for every active grant is in one place, assigned to a named owner, with a preparation window scheduled in advance. The calendar includes both financial and programmatic reporting tracks.

**Audit-ready grant files.** Each active grant has a complete file: award letter and all amendments, all submitted reports with submission confirmation, all expenditure documentation, time records, and the current compliance calendar. The test: could a new grants manager pick up any active grant file and understand the compliance status within an hour?

## The Most Common Mistake: Treating Setup as an Afterthought

The setup work done when a grant is received determines how easy or difficult compliance management will be for the entire period. Organizations that enter a grant name, a total award amount, and a final report deadline have created a record, not a compliance tool.

A compliance-ready setup includes: the exact project period start and end dates from the Notice of Award; the approved budget broken down by category; the restriction type; the complete reporting schedule with every deadline for the full period; funder contact information; prior approval requirements from the award terms; and the accounting system grant code, confirmed with finance before any invoices are approved.

The hour spent on a complete setup at award receipt pays for itself many times over. An incomplete setup is corrected under time pressure, usually when the first report is due and someone realizes the compliance record does not reflect what actually happened.

## What to Do This Week

If your organization has any active grants, run the four-pillar check on each one. For each active award: confirm that expenditures are coded against the correct grant in the accounting system; confirm that time records are current for any staff charging time to the award; pull the compliance calendar and confirm that every upcoming deadline has a named owner and a preparation date scheduled; and open the grant file to verify that submitted reports have saved confirmation documentation.

The gaps this exercise surfaces are the gaps an auditor would find. Finding them now is better than finding them when a program officer asks an unexpected question or a funder schedules a site visit.

GrantPipe is built for the mid-sized organization managing this across multiple grants, funders, and fiscal years — with donor records and grant compliance in the same system, restricted-fund visibility that does not require a manual compilation, and a compliance calendar that surfaces every deadline alongside the full context of each award.

Six fund accounting platforms, one distinction that matters before evaluating any of them.

Sage Intacct ($10,000–$30,000+/yr): The strongest option for organizations above $5M that need FASB ASC 958 compliance built into the data model and AICPA-recognized reporting. Implementation runs $15,000–$50,000 additional through a certified partner.

MIP Fund Accounting ($5,000–$20,000+/yr): Purpose-built for nonprofits, strong federal compliance and SEFA capability, integrated payroll for personnel cost allocation. Interface is dated but the fund accounting depth is genuine. Best fit $2M–$10M.

NetSuite ($20,000–$60,000+/yr): Full ERP for multi-entity structures. Cost-complexity ratio is unfavorable for most mid-sized nonprofits.

QuickBooks Online ($360–$2,400/yr): Class tracking is not fund accounting. It approximates it. Auditors increasingly flag it for organizations above $1M in grant revenue.

Xero ($180–$936/yr): Same limitation as QuickBooks for fund accounting purposes. Adequate for small nonprofits where the board accepts non-fund-accounting software.

Aplos ($708–$2,388/yr): True fund accounting at an accessible price. Federal compliance capabilities are basic — not appropriate for heavy federal award portfolios.

The distinction that matters: fund accounting handles the financial record. Grant management handles the operational record — award terms, reporting deadlines, funder relationships. Most organizations need both. They are usually different systems.

Virginia gives nonprofits 90 days to file their charitable registration renewal after fiscal year end.

Most states allow 4.5 to 10 months. New York's CHAR500 deadline is 4.5 months out. California's RRF-1 gives 4 months 15 days. Connecticut allows 10 months.

A Single Audit finding requires a written Corrective Action Plan under 2 CFR 200.511(c). The plan must include five elements: finding reference, the auditee's position (agree or disagree), the specific corrective action, a named responsible party, and a target completion date.

Missing any one of those five elements invites awarding-agency follow-up — and often leads to enhanced reporting requirements or specific conditions on future draws.

The most common weakness is vague language. "We will improve our procurement controls" is not a CAP. "The CFO will update the procurement policy by May 31, distribute it to all staff with signed attestations, and present completed attestations to the audit committee at the June meeting" is a CAP.

The second most common weakness is addressing the effect rather than the cause. A finding that expenditures were unallowable because procurement policy was not followed requires a procurement policy fix — not just refunding the questioned costs.

Questioned costs do not automatically require repayment. The awarding agency reviews and determines whether costs are allowable, unallowable, or resolvable through additional documentation. Include the repay/dispute/allow decision in the CAP rather than waiting for the agency to ask.

The submission deadline is tight: the CAP goes to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse with the full Single Audit report, due the earlier of 30 days after the auditor's report or nine months after fiscal year-end under 2 CFR 200.512(a)(1).

Repeat findings in two or more consecutive audits trigger specific conditions under 2 CFR 200.208 — including prior approval requirements and high-risk designation.

Donor-restricted funds and board-designated funds are not the same category. Treating them as equivalent creates fiduciary exposure that can reach board level.

Donor restrictions are external legal obligations. When a donor or grantor attaches conditions to a contribution, those conditions are contractually binding under the gift agreement. The state attorney general has enforcement jurisdiction over charitable assets. A board vote cannot override a donor restriction — only the donor can release it, or the restriction terms must be satisfied.

Board designations are internal governance decisions. A board can resolve to set aside funds for a capital project, a reserve, or a strategic initiative — and the same board can reverse that decision at a later meeting. The designation is organizational policy, not a legal obligation to an outside party.

Under ASU 2016-14, donor-restricted funds appear in the with-donor-restrictions net asset class on the Statement of Financial Position. Board-designated funds appear within without-donor-restrictions — disclosed in notes, but not classified as restricted.

Commingling is where things break. If restricted and unrestricted funds share a bank account without project-level sub-account tracking, it becomes impossible to demonstrate that restricted dollars were spent on authorized purposes. That appearance of misuse is the problem — even if actual spending was correct.

Practical controls: assign a unique GL code to each restricted grant, code expenditures to the grant at transaction time (not in batch), and run a restricted fund balance report monthly showing opening balance, receipts, expenditures, and closing balance by grant.

A negative balance on a restricted fund means you spent more than was in it. That is a misappropriation signal, not an accounting rounding issue.

2 CFR 200.430 requires that salary charges to federal awards be based on records reflecting actual work performed — maintained contemporaneously.

Employees working 100% on one federal program may use semi-annual certifications — signed attestations that all compensated time went to that program. Employees working across multiple grants or activities must maintain personnel activity reports (PARs) that account for 100% of compensated hours, prepared at least monthly, and signed by the employee.

The second most common mistake: completing all time logs at year-end or before the auditor arrives. When records for 12 months are all dated within a two-week window in December, the records are not contemporaneous.

# How Nonprofits Are Leaving Real Money on the Table: The Indirect Cost Rate Problem

A finance director at a $2M nonprofit once described the grant budgeting process at her organization as "writing checks to the government." Every federal grant her team received was partially subsidized by unrestricted operating funds. The grants showed up in reports as revenue, but the organizational overhead those programs consumed was never recovered. After three years, the operating reserve was gone.

The problem was not bad programming or weak fundraising. It was indirect cost underrecovery — a structural financial issue that is common, measurable, and largely avoidable.

## What Indirect Costs Actually Are

Indirect costs — also called facilities and administrative costs, or F&A costs — are real organizational expenses that support program delivery without being directly traceable to any single grant. Rent, utilities, executive director time spent on management rather than specific programs, central bookkeeping, IT infrastructure, general supplies: every dollar spent running the organization as a functioning entity is an indirect cost.

These costs are not overhead in the pejorative sense. Every dollar your organization spends on administration is a dollar that enables your programs to operate. Indirect cost recovery through grants is the mechanism by which grant-funded programs pay their proportional share of those enabling expenses, rather than drawing down organizational reserves.

Organizations that do not claim indirect costs are effectively asking unrestricted donors to subsidize federally funded programs. That is a defensible choice in some situations. In most, it is an unexamined habit.

## The De Minimis Path Most Organizations Miss

Under 2 CFR 200.414(f), any nonprofit that has never had a federally negotiated indirect cost rate may use 15% of Modified Total Direct Costs as an indirect cost charge on any federal grant — without submitting a rate proposal or negotiating with any federal agency.

This is the 15% de minimis rate. It is available to organizations that have never negotiated a NICRA. It requires no paperwork beyond consistent application and disclosure in the grant budget.

MTDC is direct costs minus specific exclusions: equipment above the capitalization threshold (typically $5,000), capital expenditures, subcontract costs above $25,000 per subcontract, patient care costs, tuition remission, and participant support costs.

A practical example: a grant with $200,000 in direct costs — $120,000 personnel, $30,000 supplies, $20,000 in a single equipment item, $30,000 in a subcontract — has an MTDC of $175,000 ($200,000 minus $20,000 equipment minus $5,000 of the subcontract above the $50,000 threshold). At 15% de minimis: $17,500 in recoverable indirect costs. Per year, across a portfolio of five active federal grants, that math compounds significantly.

The consistency requirement matters: once an organization elects the de minimis rate, it applies to all federal awards until the organization formally negotiates a NICRA. The rate cannot be applied selectively.

## The Three-Step Rate Calculation

The Uniform Guidance Mechanism for Indirect Cost Recovery

Even organizations using the de minimis rate benefit from knowing their actual indirect cost rate — if only to understand how much they are underrecovering.

**Step 1: Define the indirect cost pool.** List every organizational cost that is not directly attributable to a specific program: executive and administrative salaries (the portion not directly charged to grants), rent and utilities for shared space, general accounting, HR, IT support, software licenses used across the organization, and general office supplies.

**Step 2: Sum the pool and identify the allocation base.** Calculate total indirect costs for a full fiscal year. The most common allocation base is MTDC — consistent with the Uniform Guidance calculation.

**Step 3: Divide.** Total indirect costs ÷ MTDC allocation base = actual indirect cost rate. For example: $180,000 in indirect costs ÷ $600,000 MTDC = 30% actual indirect cost rate.

If the organization is using the 15% de minimis rate on a $600,000 MTDC base, it is recovering $60,000 of its $180,000 in actual overhead. The remaining $120,000 is absorbed by unrestricted funds or operating reserves. That is not a sustainable structural position for a grant-dependent organization.

## When to Negotiate a NICRA

The Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement

A NICRA is appropriate when the 15% de minimis rate materially underrecoves actual overhead, when the organization receives federal funding from multiple agencies (the NICRA applies to all of them), or when a specific federal program requires a negotiated rate.

The process starts with identifying the cognizant federal agency — typically the agency that provides the most federal funding to the organization. For community health and social service nonprofits, this is often HHS. For workforce development organizations, it is often DOL.

The rate proposal submitted to the cognizant agency includes audited financial statements, a cost allocation plan describing how the organization classifies costs as direct versus indirect, a breakdown of the indirect cost pool, and the proposed allocation base with the calculated rate. The negotiation typically takes several months; a provisional rate can be used in the interim.

NICRA rate types offer different levels of certainty:

A **predetermined rate** is fixed for the agreement period regardless of actual costs. It provides budget certainty at the cost of potential over- or underrecovery.

A **fixed rate with carryforward** is fixed for the period, but over- or underrecoveries carry into the next negotiation. It tracks actual costs more closely over time.

A **provisional/final rate** uses an estimated rate during the year, settled to a final rate after year-end cost analysis. It is the most accurate but requires adjustment billing after close.

Organizations with actual indirect rates above 20% should seriously evaluate whether negotiating a NICRA is worth the administrative investment. On a portfolio of active federal grants, the additional recovery can be substantial.

## The Foundation Indirect Cost Gap

Private foundations operate outside the Uniform Guidance. Many impose their own indirect cost limits: no indirect allowed, a fixed cap of 10–15% regardless of NICRA rate, or — at the larger end — acceptance of the federally approved rate.

When a foundation's allowable rate is below the organization's actual overhead rate, the grant is partially subsidized by operating funds. The net revenue on that grant is less than the face value of the award.

The calculation every grants manager should run before accepting a foundation award: (grant amount) minus (unrecovered overhead). A $100,000 grant with 10% indirect allowed but an actual 25% overhead rate generates $100,000 in revenue against $125,000 in total program cost. After the indirect recovery, the net contribution to operations is $85,000, not $100,000. Across a portfolio of ten foundation grants under-recovering at 15 points, the annual structural deficit compounds into a real operating exposure.

This is not a reason to decline foundation grants. It is a reason to include the underrecovery calculation in financial planning and to build unrestricted fundraising goals that account for the gap.

## The Common Mistake That Costs the Most

The single most common failure in indirect cost management is not calculating the rate at all.

Organizations that have never run the calculation do not know whether they are recovering 10%, 30%, or 5% of their actual overhead through grants. The de minimis rate feels adequate because there is no comparison number. The NICRA process feels bureaucratic because the recovery gap has never been quantified.

The consequence is not a finding — no auditor will cite you for leaving indirect cost money on the table. The consequence is a structural deficit that compounds quietly over years until the operating reserve runs low and the organization faces a financial crisis that looks, from the outside, like a sudden problem.

Running the indirect cost rate calculation once — a half-day exercise using audited financial statements — produces the comparison number that drives the decision. If the actual rate is close to 10%, the de minimis rate is adequate. If the actual rate is 25% or 30%, the case for NICRA negotiation is significant.

## What to Do This Week

Pull your most recent audited financial statements. Identify your indirect cost pool: every organizational expense not directly charged to a specific program or grant. Sum it. Divide by your estimated MTDC base (total direct costs, minus equipment and subcontracts above $50,000). That is your actual indirect cost rate.

Compare it to what your current grants are recovering. If the gap is more than 10 points, the NICRA conversation with your cognizant agency is worth having.

The SEFA cluster-identification error appears in approximately 30% of audited entities with multiple federal programs, according to OMB's Single Audit Quality Study.

The Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards is the foundation of every single audit. Auditors use it to determine which programs are "major programs" requiring audit opinions. A misclassified program means the major-program selection is wrong — and audit scope expands.

The cluster problem: OMB defines program clusters in Appendix VI to 2 CFR Part 200, updated annually in the Compliance Supplement. When an organization receives funding under two ALNs that belong to the same cluster, those ALNs must be grouped together and labeled with the cluster name. Listing them separately understates cluster expenditures and can cause the auditor to undercount which programs cross the major-program threshold.

The pass-through problem: for every program where the organization passes federal funds to a subrecipient, the SEFA must identify the subrecipient name and total amount passed through, per 2 CFR 200.510(b). A $5,000 subaward from a $500,000 federal grant must still be disclosed. This is one of the most common HHS-funded audit findings.

Indirect costs belong on the SEFA too. Organizations that omit indirect cost recovery from SEFA expenditures understate their federal program activity and may misidentify which programs cross the major-program threshold.

Each year's cluster definitions must be verified against the current OMB Compliance Supplement — cluster membership changes annually.

Releasing restricted net assets at year-end is not an accounting choice — it is an accounting event that requires specific evidence.

Under FASB ASC 958-205, a release from restriction is a reclassification on the Statement of Activities, not new revenue.

The restriction releases when the donor-imposed stipulation expires or is fulfilled. Not when the board approves the journal entry. Not when year-end close arrives.

For purpose-restricted funds, the release amount equals qualified expenditures incurred — not the total grant balance available.

If $80,000 was received and $65,000 was spent, $65,000 releases. The remaining $15,000 carries forward as restricted.

The release journal entry should be dated at the date the restriction was satisfied — not at the close date unless year-end is when the restriction was actually fulfilled.

One of the most common audit adjustments in this area: a release that exceeds the documented qualifying expenditures. Auditors trace the release amount back to expenditure records. If the backup is not there, it is an adjustment.

FASB ASU 2016-14 also requires footnote disclosure of the nature and amounts of donor-imposed restrictions and expected timing of their release.

Run the full restricted fund roll-forward monthly on active grants — year-end should be a calculation, not a three-day reconciliation.
