# Grant Compliance for Environmental Nonprofits: What the Uniform Guidance Doesn't Cover

A Clean Water Act Section 319 grant closes in 90 days. The project logged 480 acres of stream buffer restored across 14 sites over three years. Field monitoring records exist — but they are in three different staff members' hard drives, two of whom no longer work at the organization.

That is an EPA compliance failure waiting to materialize. Not a bookkeeping error. Not a missed deadline. A documentation gap that will surface the moment a program officer asks to see the underlying data for the outcome numbers in the final report.

Environmental nonprofit grant compliance sits at a harder intersection than most federal grantees face. The financial side follows standard Uniform Guidance rules — allowable costs, restricted fund tracking, SF-425 submissions, single audit obligations. The programmatic side requires technically defensible environmental outcome documentation, and that documentation must be organized in a way that survives staff turnover, multi-year project timelines, and monitoring visits.

Most organizations manage the financial compliance reasonably well. The programmatic documentation side is where findings actually happen.

## The Two-Layer Compliance Framework

EPA grants operate under two layers of requirements that are easy to conflate.

The first layer is the Uniform Guidance (2 CFR Part 200), which applies to all federal awards. It governs cost principles — the three-part test of allowable, allocable, and reasonable under 2 CFR 200.405 — procurement standards, equipment management, subrecipient monitoring under 2 CFR 200.332, and single audit obligations when federal expenditures reach $1,000,000 in a fiscal year (updated in the 2024 revisions, effective for fiscal years ending September 30, 2025 or later).

The second layer is EPA-specific: 2 CFR Part 1500 (EPA's implementation of Uniform Guidance), program-specific requirements in the notice of award, and for cooperative agreements, the substantial involvement requirements that give EPA active oversight of project decisions.

The distinction between a grant and a cooperative agreement matters operationally. Under a cooperative agreement, EPA has an active role — approving significant project decisions, participating in activities, or redirecting work. Grant recipients expect less program officer involvement. Cooperative agreement recipients should build EPA check-in requirements into their project management workflow from day one, not treat program officer contact as an exception.

## Grant Prospecting and Restricted Fund Complexity

Environmental nonprofits commonly receive funding through several EPA mechanisms: Environmental Justice Collaborative Problem-Solving (EJCPS) cooperative agreements, Clean Water Act Section 319 nonpoint source grants distributed by states, State and Tribal Assistance Grants (STAG), and — increasingly — Inflation Reduction Act-funded environmental justice and climate resilience programs.

IRA-funded programs deserve special attention. These are relatively new funding streams, and program officer interpretations of allowable activities are still developing. Organizations receiving IRA funds should maintain close communication with their program officers about allowable use questions, document those conversations, and not rely on informal guidance that was not put in writing.

For state pass-through grants, the compliance obligations flow through regardless of the intermediary. A nonprofit receiving Clean Water Act 319 funds from a state environmental agency is a subgrantee of the state — but 2 CFR Part 200 applies end-to-end. The state is the pass-through entity responsible for communicating applicable requirements, but that does not transfer the compliance obligation away from the nonprofit.

## The Restricted Fund Accounting Problem in Multi-Year Projects

A three-year watershed restoration grant of $600,000 creates a specific accounting challenge that does not exist for a single-year award: the restricted balance must carry forward correctly across fiscal years.

If year one expenditures total $185,000, the remaining $415,000 is still restricted and must be tracked as net assets with donor restrictions (or in the case of conditional government grants, as refundable advances until conditions are met). A year-end accountant who fails to carry forward the restricted balance accurately, or who releases the restriction before qualifying expenditures are documented, produces financial statements that misrepresent the organization's financial position.

Match tracking over multiple years creates a parallel problem. Clean Water Act 319 and Brownfields grants typically carry matching requirements. Match contributions must be documented as they are contributed — not front-loaded in year one to meet the requirement early, and not deferred to year three. A running match ledger maintained across the full project period is the only documentation approach that survives a closeout review.

Under FASB ASC 958-205, a purpose restriction releases when qualifying expenditures have been incurred and documented — not when the project period ends, and not when the board approves a journal entry. For environmental grants, that means the restricted fund balance should decrease as program costs are coded to the grant throughout the project period, not in a single year-end entry.

## The Four-Part Environmental Outcome Documentation Framework

Environmental outcome claims are what differentiate an EPA grant monitoring visit from a standard federal grant review. The financial compliance is reviewable from standard accounting documentation. The outcome compliance requires project-specific evidence.

**Field monitoring records.** Water quality improvements reported in a Clean Water Act 319 final report must be backed by water quality sampling records: date, location, sampling methodology, laboratory results. Stream miles addressed must be traceable to field activity logs showing which sites were visited, by whom, on what dates, and what practices were implemented. Outcome numbers that cannot be traced to contemporaneous field documentation are not accepted.

**Approved methodologies.** EPA programs specify which estimation tools or measurement methods are acceptable for each outcome measure. Pounds of pollutant reduced must be calculated using an EPA-approved estimation methodology. Using an unapproved methodology produces outcome numbers that may not be accepted even if the field data is complete. Before the first reporting period, identify and document the approved methodology for each outcome measure specified in the notice of award.

**Scope alignment documentation.** Every project activity should be traceable to a specific task in the approved work plan. A project log connecting each activity to the work plan task it supports is not bureaucratic overhead — it is the primary evidence that the organization did what it was funded to do. When project conditions require adapting from the approved approach, written approval from the program officer must be obtained before proceeding, not after.

**Subrecipient monitoring records.** Environmental organizations that fund community groups, local governments, or research partners for project activities are pass-through entities for those dollars. Subrecipient monitoring under 2 CFR 200.332 requires documenting the subrecipient's compliance, reviewing their financial reports, and maintaining records of monitoring activities. Subrecipient monitoring failures are among the most frequent EPA grant findings — and they receive heightened scrutiny from EPA's Office of Inspector General.

## The Most Common EPA Compliance Failure

The single most serious EPA grant compliance failure is reporting environmental outcomes that are not supported by field monitoring data.

A project that claims 500 acres of stream buffer restored must produce documentation showing that specific sites were treated, by whom, on what dates, using what conservation practices. The documentation must exist before the claim appears in a report — not as a reconstruction assembled during a monitoring visit.

This failure pattern follows a predictable sequence: project staff track outcomes informally throughout the project, annual reports are compiled from staff memory and rough estimates, final reports aggregate those estimates without connecting them to site-level documentation, and then a program officer or auditor asks for the underlying data.

The gap between the reported number and the documentable number is the compliance finding. The consequence ranges from requiring a corrected report to repayment of disallowed costs if the project outcomes do not justify the expenditures charged to the grant.

The preventive approach is not complicated: require site visit logs at the activity level, store them in a shared project file accessible to all project staff, and conduct a documentation review before each reporting period — not only at year-end.

## Staff Turnover and Project File Continuity

A three-year environmental project will almost certainly see staff turnover. The development director who wrote the grant may not still be at the organization when the final report is due. The field coordinator who ran year-one site visits may have left by year three.

The project file must be structured so that a new staff member can understand the project history, outstanding obligations, and compliance status from the documentation alone — without institutional memory from staff who are no longer there.

That means the project file must contain: the notice of award and all amendments, the approved work plan and any approved modifications, a running match ledger, site visit logs organized by activity, outcome calculation documentation with the approved methodology, all correspondence with the program officer (particularly any informal guidance on allowable activities), and all submitted reports.

Organizations with cloud-based project file management — not shared drives or individual desktops — maintain this continuity more reliably. When a staff member departs, the documentation should not depart with them.

## Indirect Cost Rate Consistency

Environmental organizations frequently have above-average indirect cost rates. Facility costs for labs, field equipment, and monitoring infrastructure are high. Indirect cost recovery under EPA grants follows the rules in 2 CFR 200.414: organizations with a negotiated indirect cost rate agreement (NICRA) should use that rate; organizations without a NICRA may use the 15% de minimis rate.

The compliance issue is inconsistency. Using the de minimis rate on some awards and the NICRA on others — or changing the allocation base mid-project — is a finding. The approved rate must be applied consistently across reporting periods for a given award, and the base to which it is applied must be the base defined in the award terms, not the organization's standard calculation.

If your actual indirect cost rate is materially higher than what your awards permit you to recover, that gap is not a compliance problem — but it is an organizational sustainability problem worth addressing through the NICRA negotiation process.

## What to Do This Week

Audit the project documentation for every active environmental grant. For each grant, answer three questions: Can you trace every outcome claimed in the most recent report to field documentation? Is the match ledger current? Are all project files accessible by someone other than the primary staff member?

If the answer to any of these is uncertain, address it now — not at the next reporting deadline. Gaps that are discoverable during a proactive review are manageable. Gaps discovered during a monitoring visit are findings.

Under 2 CFR 200.430, payroll charges to federal grants must reflect actual hours worked — not the budgeted percentage. Here is how to run the monthly allocation correctly.

Step 1: Pull the payroll register for every pay period in the month. Allocation requires employee-level data, not department totals.

Step 2: Determine the allocation basis from actual time records, not the grant budget. The budget is a ceiling, not a basis.

Step 3: Allocate base salary. Each employee's gross wages split by certified time percentages. The sum across all grants must equal total gross wages — no rounding errors.

Step 4: Allocate fringe benefits using the same percentages as salary. If the organization uses a pooled fringe rate, apply it consistently to all grants and document the rate calculation.

Step 5: Calculate indirect cost allocation separately. Apply the negotiated rate (or 15% de minimis under the 2024 Uniform Guidance revision) to the MTDC base for each grant. Do not blend indirect into the direct salary line.

Step 6: Post the journal entry. Each line specifies employee, grant, account, and amount. Attach the payroll register and allocation worksheet.

Step 7: Reconcile to time records. If an employee's timesheet shows 55% on Grant A but payroll posted at 60%, a correcting entry is required before month-end close.

The most common and most expensive error is skipping step 7.

"Net assets with donor restrictions" replaced two categories in 2017. Many nonprofits still report it wrong.

FASB ASU 2016-14, effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2017, eliminated "temporarily restricted" and "permanently restricted" as separate balance sheet line items and combined them into a single class: net assets with donor restrictions.

Three types of restrictions create this classification: purpose (spend only on a specific program), time (unavailable until a future date), and perpetual (principal must be held in perpetuity).

The release mechanism: when the donor condition is satisfied — qualifying expenditure made, time elapsed, or event occurred — the organization records "net assets released from restrictions" on the statement of activities.

The most common misconceptions: board-designated funds are not donor-restricted, even if the board labeled them "restricted." Reporting requirements in a grant agreement do not automatically create donor restrictions. Reporting conditions differ from use conditions.

Underwater endowments — where fair value has dropped below the original gift amount — remain in the donor-restricted class under ASU 2016-14, not reclassified elsewhere.

If your audited financial statements still show "temporarily restricted" or "permanently restricted" as line items, that is an error. The transition was required eight fiscal years ago.

Grant closeout is not a single event. Federal grants require submission within 120 days of the period-of-performance end date. Here is the sequence that avoids findings.

Step 1: Reconcile every expenditure against the approved grant budget. Pull all transactions charged to the grant — personnel, direct expenses, indirect costs — and verify each has adequate documentation: invoice, receipt, payroll record, or time sheet.

Step 3: Calculate and report program income if applicable. Revenue generated by program activities during the grant period must be reported and applied per the grant agreement. Failure to report program income is a recurring closeout finding on federal grants.

Step 5: Submit the final programmatic report using data collected during the grant period — not reconstructed from memory. Funders compare final numbers against interim reports already on file.

Step 6: Resolve unspent funds according to the grant agreement. Do not assume unspent restricted funds are available for operations. Restricted funds remain restricted until the funder releases them.

Step 7: Archive the complete grant file for a minimum of three years from the date the final expenditure report is submitted. Some federal programs require five to seven years.

A written cost transfer policy is required under 2 CFR 200.302(b)(7). Here is what it must cover and how to build one that survives audit.

Step 1: Write the policy document. Define what constitutes a cost transfer (any journal entry moving a cost between grants or cost centers after original posting), the 90-day timeliness standard, required documentation for each transfer, and the approval hierarchy.

Step 2: Build a standard cost transfer request form. Capture: transfer date, original posting date, amount, original award and account, receiving award and account, reason for original posting, description of benefit to receiving award, and approval signatures. Consistency creates the audit trail.

Step 3: Maintain a central cost transfer log. Every transfer by date, amount, awards affected, and approval status. The log lets auditors test the population without reconstructing individual GL entries — and lets finance staff spot patterns that indicate a systemic cost allocation problem.

Step 4: Apply the 90-day review at each submission. Transfers within 90 days use standard documentation. Transfers over 90 days require expanded justification explaining why the error was not caught sooner. Transfers after period end require prior written federal agency approval before posting.

Step 5: For personnel transfers, attach time records before initiating the transfer. Under 2 CFR 200.430, the receiving award can bear the salary cost only if the employee actually worked on that award during the period being adjusted. Discovering mid-transfer that the time records do not support the reallocation wastes time and creates a problematic paper trail.

Late cost transfers with generic justifications are consistently in the top ten single audit findings for HHS and DOJ grants. The documentation is the compliance — not the transfer itself.

# 21st CCLC Compliance: What After-School Program Leaders Actually Owe the Federal Government

An after-school program in Ohio received a 21st Century Community Learning Centers subaward last fall. The program director had run enrichment programs for years. She understood the academic work. What she did not understand — until the first monitoring visit — was that the federal compliance obligations attached to the subaward were nearly as demanding as the program obligations.

That gap between program competence and compliance knowledge is common in 21st CCLC. The program model is familiar. The federal paperwork behind it is not.

This article is a practical map of what 21st CCLC grantees are actually required to do: the legal authority, the funding structure, the performance reporting system, and the Uniform Guidance overlay that applies to every dollar of federal money in the award.

## Authority and Money Flow

21st Century Community Learning Centers is authorized under Title IV Part B of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (20 USC 7171 et seq.). That statutory basis matters because it means 21st CCLC is a federal formula grant — not a discretionary program — with a specific allocation methodology and a defined set of permissible activities.

The US Department of Education allocates funds to state educational agencies based on each state's Title I Part A share. The SEA — typically the state department of education — does not run the programs directly. It runs a competitive Request for Application process and subawards to eligible organizations: local educational agencies, community-based organizations, Indian tribes, faith-based organizations, and other public or private entities.

The subawardee operates the program, administers the funds, and reports through the state. The state aggregates and submits to USED. This pass-through structure has compliance implications at every level.

## What Subawardees Are Required to Deliver

21st CCLC programs must provide academic enrichment activities during non-school hours — after school, before school, weekends, and summer. The statute specifies that activities must align to state and local academic standards and serve students attending schools with high concentrations of students from low-income families or schools identified for comprehensive support and improvement.

Permissible activities include tutoring, homework help, STEM enrichment, arts programming, literacy instruction, physical activity, college and career readiness, and family engagement services. Activities are broad — the compliance discipline is in documenting that what the program actually did falls within the approved scope.

Family engagement is required, not optional. Programs must offer services that help families support student learning — literacy programs, parent involvement in academic events, activities that connect the school day to the home. This requirement appears in monitoring checklists and should appear in the program's service documentation.

An independent program evaluation is also required. The SEA sets the evaluation framework and schedule. Most SEAs require external evaluators. Evaluation findings feed program improvement cycles and are referenced in monitoring visits.

## GPRA Performance Measures

The federal Government Performance and Results Act requires 21st CCLC to demonstrate performance against specific measures. For after-school programs, those measures cover three domains:

**Academic achievement:** Increases in the share of regular participants reaching proficiency on state reading and math assessments. "Regular participants" is typically defined by the SEA as students attending the program a specified minimum number of hours. Programs must track participant attendance carefully to accurately identify who qualifies as a regular participant for reporting purposes.

**School behavior:** Improvement in indicators such as classroom behavior and school-day attendance. Programs collect teacher-reported data or use school records. The data collection methodology must be established early in the program year — retrofitting it at reporting time creates inconsistencies that monitoring visits flag.

**School engagement:** Improvement in indicators such as homework completion and classroom participation. Like behavior data, this requires a defined collection process tied to specific data sources that exist independently of the program's own records.

These three domains sound straightforward. The compliance work is in collecting the underlying data systematically throughout the program year, not reconstructing it when the Annual Performance Report window opens.

## The Annual Performance Report and 21APR System

The APR captures program operations data, participant demographics, attendance, and performance against GPRA measures. It is submitted through the 21APR reporting system — the federal data collection tool through which states collect grantee submissions and submit aggregated data to USED.

The SEA sets the submission timeline and requirements. Grantees submit to the SEA; the SEA reviews, aggregates, and submits to USED. The practical implication: the grantee's data must be complete and accurate before the SEA's internal deadline, which is earlier than the federal submission window.

Programs that treat APR completion as a once-a-year documentation event — rather than an ongoing data collection practice — consistently find themselves reconstructing attendance records and outcome data under time pressure. The APR is only as accurate as the program-year records that feed it.

## Program Quality Assessment

21st CCLC requires grantees to use a validated program quality assessment to evaluate point-of-service quality. The Youth Program Quality Assessment from the Weikart Center is the most commonly used tool. States may approve equivalent assessments.

The YPQA is an observational instrument — trained assessors observe program activities and score quality across multiple domains: safe environment, supportive environment, interaction, and engagement. The assessment produces a quality profile that programs use for continuous improvement planning.

Results from the program quality assessment feed into program evaluation and state monitoring. Programs that conduct the assessment perfunctorily — without using the results for actual improvement cycles — will find that monitoring visits ask about the improvement actions that should have followed assessment findings.

## The Uniform Guidance Overlay

Because 21st CCLC funds are federal, 2 CFR Part 200 (Uniform Guidance) applies end-to-end. This is the layer of compliance that surprises most program-side staff who have not worked with federal grants before.

The Uniform Guidance governs allowable costs, procurement standards, equipment management, record retention, and financial reporting. For subawardees, the specific obligations include:

**Allowable costs:** Expenditures charged to the 21st CCLC award must be allowable (permitted under 2 CFR Part 200 Subpart E and the grant agreement), allocable (benefiting the program being funded), and reasonable (consistent with market prices for equivalent goods or services). A program that charges an expense to the grant without confirming all three conditions is creating a potential questioned cost.

**Personnel costs:** Under 2 CFR 200.430, salary charges to federal awards must reflect actual time worked on the program, not budgeted percentages. After-school programs that split staff time between 21st CCLC and other programs need documented time allocation records. Staff who work 100% on 21st CCLC may use semi-annual certification; staff on multiple programs need monthly documentation.

**Procurement:** Goods and services above the micro-purchase threshold ($10,000 as a general rule) require documented competitive procurement. Many after-school programs use vendors for snacks, enrichment activities, or transportation. Procurement documentation must exist and must demonstrate that costs are reasonable.

**Single audit:** The October 2024 Uniform Guidance revision raised the single audit threshold to $1,000,000 in total federal expenditures in a fiscal year. Organizations crossing that threshold across all their federal awards — not just 21st CCLC — owe a single audit under 2 CFR Part 200 Subpart F. The audit covers all major federal programs, not just the one that pushed the organization over the threshold.

**Subrecipient monitoring:** If a 21st CCLC subawardee further subawards to partner organizations (a school operating out of a community-based organization's space, for example), 2 CFR 200.331 and 200.332 subrecipient monitoring requirements apply to the relationship.

## The Three Compliance Failures That Monitoring Visits Find

**Participation data not collected in real time.** GPRA reporting requires attendance and outcome data that must be collected through defined processes tied to school records, teacher reports, or program databases. Programs that intend to collect this data but have not established the collection process early in the program year find themselves unable to accurately populate the APR.

**Personnel cost documentation gaps.** Staff split across 21st CCLC and other activities without documented time allocation records. When monitoring visits request payroll and time records, the absence of contemporaneous time documentation creates a questioned cost — even if staff actually worked the hours they are claiming.

**Family engagement treated as optional.** The statute requires family engagement activities. When monitoring asks for documentation of family engagement programming, programs that treated this requirement informally have documentation gaps. Document every family engagement activity with attendance records, dates, and a brief description of the activity.

## What to Do This Month

If your organization is a 21st CCLC subawardee and has not reviewed compliance posture recently, three immediate actions reduce risk:

Review the APR data collection process for the current program year. Confirm that participation data — attendance, academic assessment data, behavior and engagement indicators — is being collected through a documented process, not informally.

Pull payroll records for any staff splitting time between 21st CCLC and other programs. Confirm that time allocation documentation exists for each pay period since the award year began. If gaps exist, address them before the monitoring visit calendar, not after.

Locate the program quality assessment schedule in the award agreement and confirm the assessment has been conducted or scheduled as required. Confirm that improvement action planning has followed the assessment results.

21st CCLC compliance is manageable when the documentation infrastructure is built into the program year from the start. FASB ASC 958 governs how every grant-funded U.S. nonprofit presents its financial statements. Here is what ASU 2016-14 requires and where finance teams most often get it wrong.

Step 1: Classify net assets into exactly two classes. With-donor-restrictions (purpose, time, or perpetual) and without-donor-restrictions (everything the board controls, including board designations). Using the old three-class language — unrestricted, temporarily restricted, permanently restricted — in audited statements is an error.

Step 2: Present four financial statements. Statement of Financial Position, Statement of Activities, Statement of Cash Flows, and Statement of Functional Expenses. The functional expense statement allocates costs across program services, management and general, and fundraising — required by ASU 2016-14 for all nonprofits.

Step 3: Record net assets released from restrictions correctly. When a donor condition is satisfied, record "net assets released from restrictions" — a reclassification, not new revenue. Equal decrease in the restricted class and increase in the unrestricted class on the Statement of Activities.

Step 4: Prepare the liquidity disclosure. Quantitative: financial assets available to meet general expenditures within one year, net of donor-restricted and unavailable amounts. Qualitative: how the organization manages liquidity, including credit lines, reserves, and seasonal variations.

Step 5: Allocate functional expenses using actual time and space data, not arbitrary estimates. Auditors test functional allocation methodology. Grants that restrict funds to direct program costs require separating shared overhead accurately.

The most common error: board-designated funds classified as donor-restricted. Boards can set aside reserves by resolution, but those designations live inside without-donor-restrictions — not in the restricted class.

Under 2 CFR 200.308(e)(4), nonprofits can transfer funds among direct cost categories up to 10% of the total federal award budget without federal prior approval — as long as the change doesn't alter project scope.

That 10% is calculated against the total award, not the category being changed. On a $500,000 award, that's $50,000 in flexibility. On a $200,000 award, it's $20,000.

Misapplying this rule is one of the most common subaward compliance errors. Pass-through entities that approve subrecipient modifications without checking whether the change requires federal prior approval create compliance findings — approving a change your prime award prohibits is a finding. Requiring your subrecipient to seek approval you already hold authority to grant is a different finding.

The sequence that avoids both: receive the modification request in writing, check the prime award terms, apply the 10% calculation with scope assessment, determine whether the change requires federal sign-off before you sign anything.

Federal prior approval for modifications that exceed the threshold can take four to twelve weeks depending on the agency. A no-cost extension gives you time. That's all it does.

The award amount stays the same. The compliance obligations stay the same. The work still has to get done. What changes is when the authorized period ends — and that change propagates to every deadline keyed to the end date: the final SF-425 due date, the final programmatic report, and any subrecipient obligations tied to the prime award.

Under 2 CFR 200.308, most federal agencies require NCE requests at least 30 calendar days before the period of performance end date. Many prefer 60 days. Submitting 10 days before the end date risks the review timeline exceeding the remaining grant period.

The critical misunderstanding: costs incurred after the authorized end date — even after an NCE request has been submitted and is under review — are unallowable. The extension does not retroactively authorize spending in the gap. Approval must precede expenditure.

One other distinction worth knowing: NIH and NSF grantees with expanded authorities can request NCEs without program officer approval in many cases. The request goes through the agency's electronic system and is administrative rather than discretionary — but it must still be submitted before the end date.

The best time to recognize an extension will be needed is 60–90 days before the end date, not 10.

QuickBooks Classes are a cost-tracking feature, not fund accounting.

A Class in QuickBooks is a tag on a transaction. It lets you filter and subtotal expenses by program, department, or grant. What it cannot do is maintain a fund balance — the live number showing how much of a specific restricted award remains unspent.

Fund accounting requires each restricted fund to carry its own ledger: what came in under the restriction, what was spent against it, and what remains. When a restricted grant arrives, a fund accounting system creates a liability. As qualifying expenses are incurred, the restricted balance decreases. At closeout, it should be zero or returned.

The practical consequence: when a funder asks for a current restricted balance by grant, the QuickBooks answer is a manual calculation from a Class report — starting balance, plus additions, minus posted expenses. That calculation is a spreadsheet exercise, not a system output.

AmeriCorps grantees file two fiscal reports each quarter: the Program Expense Report through eGrants and the SF-425 Federal Financial Report. Both are due 30 days after each quarter closes. Missing either generates delinquency flags that affect future funding decisions.

The classification error that appears in most AmeriCorps OIG audit findings: member living allowances coded as staff salaries.

Living allowances are member support costs — stipends, not wages. They go in a separate general ledger account from payroll. Merging them with staff salaries inflates the apparent payroll base, distorts fringe benefit calculations, and inflates the administrative cost ratio against the 10% cap.

The 10% administrative cost cap applies to the federal share only. Administrative costs include indirect costs, general management, accounting, and HR overhead. Program staff, member support costs, and training directly tied to program delivery are not administrative costs. Exceeding 10% produces disallowed costs that must be repaid.

Match requirements for most AmeriCorps State and National grants are 24% non-federal of total program costs. Volunteer time counts as in-kind match when documented contemporaneously with date, activity, hours, and fair-market rate. Reconstructed match logs at year-end are a common audit finding.

Personnel costs are typically the largest expenditure on a federal grant. They're also the most commonly questioned in audits.

The risk isn't that employees worked on the wrong things. The risk is that the documentation to support what they worked on doesn't exist in the right form.

Under 2 CFR 200.430, compensation for personal services charged to federal awards must be based on records that reflect actual activity, account for total compensated effort, and are certified by the employee or a supervisory official with first-hand knowledge.

Key distinction: effort reporting documents the percentage of time devoted to an award relative to total compensated effort — not clock hours. An employee working 50 hours per week with 20 hours on a grant project certifies 40% effort to the grant, regardless of total hours logged.

# What to Do When You Find a Misposting on a Closed Federal Grant

A grants manager at a mid-sized workforce development nonprofit discovers in October, during annual audit prep, that a $14,000 personnel cost was charged to a federal DOL grant that closed in June. The expense was incurred in March — inside the period of performance — but was posted to the wrong award. The correct award is still open. The problem is the closed one.

This is a post-closeout cost transfer situation. It is also one of the most procedurally demanding compliance scenarios a grantee organization can face — and one of the most preventable.

## Why Post-Closeout Transfers Are Different

A standard cost transfer happens while an award is open. The grantee identifies a misposting, prepares a journal entry with supporting documentation, and corrects the record — typically within 90 days of the original transaction, which is the timeliness standard cited in NIH Grants Policy and most federal agency cost transfer policies.

A post-closeout transfer involves a closed award, which means the financial records have already been finalized and submitted. When a grantee submitted the final SF-425 Federal Financial Report, it certified those figures. Adjusting them after the fact requires admitting an error in a certified submission — and it requires written federal prior approval before a single correcting journal entry can be booked.

Under 2 CFR 200.344, grantees have 120 calendar days after the period of performance ends to submit final reports and liquidate obligations. An award that cleared that window without the error being caught is, for practical purposes, administratively closed. A post-closeout transfer then requires explicit federal agency authorization — and that authorization is not guaranteed.

The difference in consequence: a timely cost transfer correction is a documentation exercise. A post-closeout transfer is a compliance event.

## The 120-Day Window Is the Central Variable

The first thing to determine when a potential misposting surfaces on a closed award is where that award stands in the closeout calendar.

An award whose final reports have been submitted but not yet accepted by the federal agency is still in an open administrative state. A correction at this stage — with agency notification — is far less fraught than one attempted after full administrative closure.

An award inside the 120-day window but with final reports not yet submitted is in the most favorable position. There is still time to correct the books, update the financial report before it goes out, and avoid a post-closeout situation entirely.

An award that has been fully closed — final reports accepted, drawdowns reconciled — requires the full prior approval process. This is the scenario most organizations face when the error surfaces during audit preparation six to eight months after fiscal year end.

The lesson: monthly reconciliation that checks expenditures against period-of-performance dates catches these errors while the award is still open and correctable through normal procedures.

## The Prior Approval Process

### The Four-Phase Approach to Post-Closeout Corrections

**Phase 1: Document the error completely before contacting anyone.**

Identify exactly which cost needs to transfer: the original posting date, the dollar amount, the account it currently sits in, the grant it was incorrectly charged to, and the grant it should have been charged to. Confirm that the receiving grant's period of performance included the date the expense was incurred. A cost incurred outside that window cannot be transferred in — no authorization will change that.

**Phase 2: Contact the federal program officer and grants management specialist immediately, in writing.**

Early, transparent notification is treated more favorably than a correction request that arrives after auditors find the problem. An email that describes the situation clearly — the amount, the affected awards, what happened, and what correction you're requesting — starts the clock on a documented, proactive response.

Do not attempt to book a correcting entry before this contact. An unauthorized journal entry on a closed federal award creates a second compliance problem on top of the original misposting.

**Phase 3: Prepare a complete prior approval request package.**

The package should include: a written narrative explaining the error and proposed correction, copies of the original expenditure documentation (invoice, payroll register, or both), copies of the general ledger entries showing where the cost is currently coded, a statement that the expenditure was incurred during the period of performance of the receiving grant, and confirmation that the cost is allowable, allocable, and reasonable under both awards' terms.

A request that arrives without supporting documentation generates follow-up questions that add weeks to the review timeline. Include everything in the initial submission.

**Phase 4: Wait for written authorization from an official with grants management authority.**

A program officer's verbal agreement or a helpful email saying "sounds fine" is not sufficient. The authorization must come from the grants management specialist, contracting officer, or an equivalent official with financial authority — on agency letterhead or official agency email. Average response times range from 30 to 90 days, with HHS and NSF generally faster and DOJ or HUD taking longer for complex requests.

## The Most Common Mistakes

**Booking the entry without written approval.** This is the most consequential error. The correcting journal entry creates a second unauthorized transaction. Always wait.

**Assuming the program officer can authorize the correction.** Program officers are typically knowledgeable about the programmatic substance of awards, but they do not hold independent financial authority to approve post-closeout adjustments. The grants management specialist or contracting officer must be involved.

**Missing the FFR amendment.** If the transfer changes the figures reported on the final SF-425, the final FFR is misstated and must be amended. Leaving the original FFR in place while correcting the general ledger creates a permanent inconsistency between the organization's books and the federal record. The amended FFR submission should be coordinated with the grants management specialist before the corrected financial records are finalized.

**Inadequate documentation of root cause.** Federal auditors reviewing a post-closeout transfer will look for evidence that the organization identified what went wrong and changed the process. A file that contains only the approval letter and the correcting entry, without any analysis of how the error occurred, signals that the failure mode is still present.

## After Authorization Arrives

Once written authorization is in hand, book the transfer entry. Credit the grant that currently holds the cost — returning the expenditure — and debit the correct grant. Attach the federal authorization letter, the original expenditure documentation, and the prior approval request to the journal entry record. Date the entry accurately; do not backdate to the original expenditure date.

File the complete documentation package in both the closed award's file and the receiving award's file. Auditors will look for it in both places.

Then document the root cause. What reconciliation process should have caught this error before closeout? At what point in the award's lifecycle would the misposting have been visible if someone had been looking? What changes to the monthly close or the grant expenditure review will prevent recurrence?

This memo does not need to be long. It needs to be honest and specific. An auditor reviewing a post-closeout transfer wants to see that the organization understands what failed and has addressed it — not a general statement about improving internal controls.

## The Single Audit Disclosure Question

If the transfer involved a material amount, or if the error reflects a systemic weakness in cost allocation controls, the auditor may include it as a finding in the Single Audit. Proactive disclosure to the auditor before fieldwork begins — rather than waiting for them to discover it — changes how the finding is characterized.

Auditors treat self-disclosed corrected errors differently from errors they identify first. An organization that found the problem, got federal authorization, corrected the books, amended the FFR, and documented root cause has demonstrated functional controls even in the presence of an error. An organization where the auditor found it first has demonstrated the opposite.

## What This Event Signals About the Monthly Close

Post-closeout cost transfers are the visible symptom of a reconciliation process that did not catch the error in time. Organizations with strong monthly practices — reconciling grant expenditures against period-of-performance dates before each close, running budget-vs-actual by award every month, reviewing any cost that posts to a grant in its final quarter — rarely encounter this situation.

The 120-day closeout window exists precisely to provide time for final reconciliation. Organizations that use that window for administration only — submitting final reports and drawing down remaining funds — rather than for a final budget and expenditure review are most vulnerable to discovering errors in audit prep six months later.

Building a grant-by-grant expenditure review into the monthly close is not an onerous process for most mid-sized organizations. It takes a few hours per close and eliminates the category of problem entirely.

## This Week

Pull the period-of-performance end dates for any federal awards that closed in the last twelve months. Confirm whether the 120-day closeout window is still open for any of them. If a cost review hasn't happened since closeout, run one now. Any mispostings discovered in the next few weeks can still be corrected with standard procedures. Discovered during audit prep, they become post-closeout transfer events.

For ongoing awards, set a reminder to run an expenditure-against-period-of-performance review in the final 60 days before each grant's end date. Catching a misposting with 45 days left in the period is a 30-minute correction. Catching it after closeout is a 90-day approval process.

The SEFA (Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards) determines how much of your Single Audit is testing versus procedural.

# What a Grant Report Actually Needs to Say

A program officer at a mid-sized community foundation reviews 40 to 60 grant reports per quarter. She is not reading for narrative quality. She is scanning for three data points: are you on track to meet your performance targets, is the money being spent as planned, and are there any signals that warrant a follow-up conversation?

Most reports she reads fail that scan — not because the programs are off track, but because the reports cannot be read quickly. They describe activity without outcome data. They show total expenditures without line-item breakdowns. They include no variance explanations. The program officer marks them for follow-up, which costs her time and signals organizational weakness to the funder.

This is a correctable problem. Understanding what funders actually need in a grant report — and what the two most common report types require — eliminates most of the compliance risk that reporting creates.

## Why Grant Reporting Is a Compliance Function

Grant reporting is commonly treated as a development task: write something compelling, submit it on time, move on. That framing misses the compliance dimension.

For federal grants, the SF-425 Federal Financial Report is a legal document. Missing the submission deadline is a compliance finding under 2 CFR Part 200, independent of whether the underlying spending was compliant. A late report can trigger a hold on future drawdowns from the Payment Management System, creating an organizational cash flow problem. Federal audit findings are public record — they appear on the Federal Audit Clearinghouse and affect future funding eligibility.

For foundation grants, the stakes are relational rather than regulatory, but the consequences are similarly serious. Foundations share information about grantees within their networks. A program officer who needed to send three follow-up emails to get a clear answer from a prior grantee will note that when the organization applies to a different program at the same foundation.

The median nonprofit spends 6 to 8 hours per grant per year on reporting, with cumulative lifetime compliance effort reaching 30 or more hours per grant (Center for Effective Philanthropy Grantee Perception Reports, 2021–2023). That time investment only pays off if the report actually closes the funder's information loop.

## The Two Sections Every Report Must Have

Funder reporting formats vary widely, but the underlying content requirements are consistent across federal agencies, community foundations, and private funders. Every report needs a financial section and a narrative section.

**The financial section** answers the question: was the money spent as planned? The minimum content is a budget-vs-actual table showing the approved budget and actual expenditures for each line item, year-to-date totals, remaining balances, and variance explanations for any category that is more than 10 to 15 percent over or under budget. Funders do not expect perfect alignment to the budget — they expect that variances are visible and explainable.

**The narrative section** answers the question: is the program delivering what was committed? The minimum content is actual outcome data matched against the targets from the original grant application, a description of the activities implemented, the population served, and an explanation of any significant gaps between planned and actual performance.

Neither section is optional. A report with strong narrative but no financial detail leaves the funder unable to verify restricted fund compliance. A report with a clean budget-vs-actual table and no outcome data leaves the funder unable to evaluate programmatic progress.

## The Financial Reconciliation: A Concrete Example

Consider a $50,000 workforce training grant from a state workforce agency, six months into a 12-month performance period.

At the midpoint, a well-formatted report shows each budget category with the approved amount, period expenditures, year-to-date total, remaining balance, and percentage of budget used. If total year-to-date expenditures are approximately $25,000 — 50% of budget at the midpoint — the table communicates alignment without requiring narrative explanation.

Variances that require explanation: a participant stipends line that is 48% of budget at mid-year rather than 50% because a January enrollment delay pushed two cohorts to early February. The variance is minor and explainable. The report notes it and states that the program is on track to meet enrollment targets by Q3.

What is not acceptable: reporting a $25,035 total expenditure figure without the line-item breakdown. The funder cannot determine from the total whether restricted funds were spent in approved categories. Personnel costs at 50% of budget tell a different story than participant stipends at 48% and training materials at 58%. The line-item detail is not optional for any federal report and is standard practice for foundation reports.

## The Narrative Report: Outcomes, Not Activities

This is the section where most reports fail. The pattern is predictable: the report describes what the organization did rather than what the program produced.

Activities are inputs. "The program conducted 14 community health screenings at 8 partner sites" is an activity description. It tells the funder the organization was operating, but not whether the program is succeeding.

Outcomes are what changed because of those activities. "Of 342 unduplicated participants screened, 67 — 20% — received referrals for follow-up care. The program has served 58% of the annual target of 590 participants through the first six months" is an outcome report. It answers the funder's questions directly: are you reaching the people you committed to reach, and is the program having the effect you said it would?

The practical rule: report against the performance targets from the original grant application. If the application committed to serving 200 participants with a 75% employment placement rate, the interim report should show actual enrollment against the 200 target and actual placement rates as they develop. Funders evaluate reports against commitments, not against retrospective assessments of what you should have committed to.

When the program is behind on a target, the report should say so explicitly and explain what corrective action is underway. Funders can work with problems they know about. A program officer who learns about a significant performance gap at the final report — rather than at the midpoint — loses confidence in the organization's monitoring capacity.

## The Three-Part Framework for Any Grant Report

Regardless of funder type, a report that answers these three questions clearly will pass review with minimal follow-up:

**Financial alignment.** Is spending proportional to the grant period elapsed? Are any categories significantly over or under, and if so, why?

**Program progress.** Are activities being implemented as planned? Are the people being served? Are the early outcome indicators moving in the right direction?

**Risk flags.** Is there anything that warrants a conversation with the program officer — a staffing change, an external disruption, a shift in program design, or an anticipated deadline challenge?

The third point is where organizations create unnecessary risk. Withholding information about a program challenge until it becomes a crisis is the most reliable way to damage a funder relationship. Program officers generally respond well to early, honest disclosure of challenges paired with a mitigation plan. They respond poorly to surprises in final reports.

## The Most Common Reporting Mistake

The single most common compliance failure in grant reporting is missing expenditure detail in the financial section. Organizations submit total expenditure figures or cash drawdown amounts without the line-item breakdown that demonstrates restricted fund compliance. This is especially common in reports generated from accounting software that was not set up for grant-level reporting.

The consequence is not always visible immediately. A program officer may accept an incomplete report the first time. An auditor reviewing the same grant months later will not. Under 2 CFR Part 200, expenditure documentation must be contemporaneous — assembled at the time of the transaction, not reconstructed at audit request. A report that does not include line-item expenditure detail signals that the underlying documentation may not exist in audit-ready form.

The fix is structural: a reporting workflow that generates line-item expenditure data from the same system used to track grant transactions, rather than assembling the financial section separately from the accounting data. When the report is produced by manually reconciling two or more systems, each reconciliation introduces error potential and creates the documentation gap that auditors find.

## What to Do This Week

Review the last report you submitted for any active grant. Does the financial section show line-item budget vs. actual? Does the narrative section cite specific outcome data against the targets from the grant application? Does the report explain any variances above 10 to 15 percent?

If the answer to any of those questions is no, the report did not fully close the compliance loop — even if the funder accepted it without follow-up.

Set up a reporting template for each active grant that captures the three required elements before each submission deadline: the budget-vs-actual table pulled from grant-level expenditure data, the outcome data against application targets, and any risk flags worth disclosing. Build the template now, not the week a report is due.

If your current workflow requires reconciling multiple systems to produce a single funder report, it is worth evaluating whether a unified platform changes the effort.

UBTI — Unrelated Business Taxable Income — applies when a tax-exempt organization earns money from a commercial activity that fails all three of these tests: it is a trade or business, it is regularly carried on, and it is not substantially related to the exempt purpose.

The word "substantially" in the third test is where most analysis concentrates. The question is not whether the profits fund the mission. The question is whether the activity itself contributes importantly to accomplishing the exempt purpose.

A nonprofit hospital's parking garage open to the general public: UBTI. A university bookstore selling required textbooks to enrolled students: program service revenue. The same bookstore selling branded merchandise to the general public: potentially UBTI on that portion.

Since the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, each unrelated business activity is treated as a separate silo under IRC Section 512(a)(6). Losses from one activity cannot offset income from another. The strategy of using a rental property loss to shelter a profitable parking lot is no longer available.

The Form 990-T filing threshold is $1,000 in gross UBTI income. The tax rate is 21%, regardless of the organization's exempt status.

More than 30,000 tax-exempt organizations file Form 990-T annually. The distinction between program service revenue and UBTI is one of the most consequential — and most frequently miscategorized — lines in nonprofit tax compliance.

# Time-and-Effort Certification: The Monthly Control That Makes Payroll Auditable

A grants manager at a $3M workforce development nonprofit discovers during Single Audit fieldwork that three employees certified their time semi-annually — but two of them split time between a federal workforce grant and the organization's general fund. The auditor flags it as a compliance error under 2 CFR 200.430(i). Questioned costs on both employees' salaries for the full year are now on the table.

This is not an unusual scenario. It is one of the most consistent findings in federal single audits, and it stems from a rule that most finance staff understand in outline but misapply in practice: the semi-annual certification exception is narrower than organizations assume.

## What the Regulation Actually Requires

Under 2 CFR 200.430, payroll charges to federal awards must reflect actual time worked. The mechanism for demonstrating that is the time-and-effort certification — a signed document confirming how an employee's time was distributed across grants and other activities for a specific period.

The after-the-fact confirmation principle is the core requirement: charges must be based on records that reflect actual work, confirmed after the period ends. Budget-based allocations that are never reconciled to actual time violate this principle regardless of how carefully the budget was constructed.

The semi-annual option is real, but it is constrained. Employees working solely on a single federal award or cost objective may certify every six months. All other employees — those split across multiple awards, or whose time is divided between federal and non-federal activities — must certify more frequently. The regulation does not specify "monthly" for the latter group, but the after-the-fact principle is most reliably satisfied with monthly certification. Quarterly creates too much opportunity for recall that drifts from what actually happened.

The practical implication: an employee working 80% on one federal grant and 20% on administrative duties is not a single-award employee. The 20% is a separate cost objective. Monthly certification is required. This misclassification is exactly what auditors test for.

## The Three-Step Monthly Certification Cycle

Reliable time-and-effort compliance runs on a defined monthly cycle. The steps are straightforward; the discipline of executing them without exception is where organizations fail.

**Step 1: Identify and classify every employee with federal grant charges.** Pull a list of every employee whose salary or wages were charged to a federal award during the period. Include employees fully funded by a single award and employees splitting time across awards or between federal and non-federal activities. For each employee, confirm the correct certification frequency: semi-annual only if the employee works 100% on a single federal cost objective, monthly for everyone else.

**Step 2: Distribute certification forms within two weeks of period end.** The longer the gap between the period and the certification request, the less reliable the employee's recollection of time distribution. Distribute within two weeks; set a one-week return deadline. Certifications requested 90 days after the period are not credible after-the-fact records. They are reconstructions from memory, payroll reports, and email review. Auditors can identify the difference in the specificity of the responses and the consistency across employees.

**Step 3: Reconcile certification percentages to posted payroll before filing.** This is the step most organizations skip entirely. Collecting and filing certifications without comparing the stated percentages to what was posted to the general ledger provides no assurance — it is documentation theater. The comparison is the control. If an employee certified 50% on Grant A and payroll was posted at 55%, the posting is incorrect by 5%. A correcting journal entry is required, and the grants manager should be notified because the correction affects budget-versus-actual comparisons.

## What a Compliant Certification Must Contain

The format is flexible. A time sheet, a signed activity report, or a dedicated certification form are all acceptable under 2 CFR 200.430. The content requirements are not flexible.

A compliant certification must: reflect an after-the-fact distribution of the employee's actual activities across cost objectives, expressed as percentages that add to 100%. It must cover a specific period, identified by date. It must be signed by the employee or a supervisory official with direct, firsthand knowledge of the work performed. An unsigned certification is not compliant. A certification without a date is not compliant. A certification that lists only the employee name and grant number without any time distribution is not compliant.

Supervisor sign-off is permitted under 2 CFR 200.430(i), but the supervisor must have direct knowledge of the work — not just awareness of the assignment. A supervisor who managed the work and observed the time allocation can certify. A supervisor who approved the budget but was not present is not in a position to provide firsthand confirmation. Employee self-certification is more defensible and easier to explain to auditors.

## The Most Common Failure and Its Consequences

The single most common time-and-effort failure is applying semi-annual certification to employees who do not qualify. Organizations establish a certification schedule early in the grant period, assign employees to semi-annual or monthly cycles based on initial assessments, and then do not revisit the classification when circumstances change.

An employee who picks up a small assignment on a second federal award midway through the grant year is no longer a single-award employee. The classification must change. The organization should conduct an annual review of semi-annual certifiers — typically at fiscal year-end — to confirm that each person still meets the single-cost-objective criterion.

The consequence of misclassification is not administrative. Personnel costs are consistently among the largest findings categories in federal single audits. GAO's April 2024 analysis (GAO-24-106173) confirmed that time-and-effort documentation deficiencies — inadequate records, missing certifications, misallocated charges — appear across federal programs with regularity.

When an auditor identifies a missing or non-compliant certification for an employee with federal grant charges, the payroll charges for that employee for that period become questioned costs. The organization must demonstrate that the charges were reasonable and allocable to the specific award. If the certification cannot be produced and the allocability cannot be established from other records, the charges may need to be returned to the awarding agency.

## Audit-Ready Filing Structure

For each pay period or month, maintain a complete set of documentation: the list of employees with federal grant charges for the period, completed and signed certifications for each employee covering the correct period, the reconciliation worksheet comparing certification percentages to posted payroll, any correcting journal entries with the supporting certification basis, and notation if any certification was received late.

File by employee and by period. Auditors test time-and-effort compliance in two dimensions: they select a sample of employees and request all certifications for those employees across the audit year, and they select a sample of periods and request all certifications across all employees for those periods. Your filing structure must support both sampling approaches without requiring a search.

An auditor who cannot locate the certification for a sampled employee expands the sample. A larger sample means more potential findings. Organized filing prevents that cascading outcome.

## What to Do This Week

Review the list of employees currently assigned to semi-annual certification. For each one, confirm they work 100% on a single federal award or cost objective with no split to other programs or administrative duties. If any semi-annual certifiers are actually split, reclassify them to monthly certification effective immediately and note the correction in the compliance file.

If the organization is currently filing certifications without reconciling percentages to posted payroll, add the reconciliation as a mandatory step in the month-end close checklist. The comparison takes 15-30 minutes for a typical grant portfolio. The audit risk it eliminates is significant.

A Single Audit finding is not a disaster. Responding to one without a Corrective Action Plan is.

Under 2 CFR 200.511(c), every finding requires a written CAP that identifies five things: auditee position (agree or disagree), specific corrective action, responsible party, completion date, and the finding reference number.

"We will strengthen our controls" does not satisfy any of those five requirements.

The CAP goes to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse with the Single Audit package — due the earlier of 30 days after the auditor's report or nine months after fiscal year end, per 2 CFR 200.512(a)(1).

A finding in two consecutive audits is a repeat finding. That triggers specific conditions under 2 CFR 200.208: prior approval for draws, enhanced monitoring, possible high-risk designation.

Break the repeat pattern before the second audit, not after.

Every questioned cost decision — repay, dispute, or request allowance — should be communicated to the awarding agency alongside the CAP, not months later.

Every nonprofit expense has two labels. Most finance teams only track one.

The natural label says what you bought: salaries, rent, supplies, depreciation.

The functional label says why you spent it: program services, management and general, or fundraising.

FASB ASC 958-205 requires nonprofits to present expenses by both classifications. Acceptable methods under ASC 958-720 include time studies, FTE allocations, square footage, and direct charging.

The most common error: treating the Executive Director as 100% program. Most EDs perform a mix of program oversight, management, and fundraising. Allocating the full salary to programs inflates the program ratio and is a routine audit finding.

Stale percentages are the second most common error — applying the same 70/20/10 split for five years without a review. ASC 958-720 requires methods that reflect current resource consumption.

Roughly 20% of Form 990 amendments filed by public charities relate to reclassification between functional expense categories, per Urban Institute analysis.

The methodology must be documented, consistently applied, and defensible under audit.

The evidence that survives a Single Audit is not created in the weeks before the auditor arrives. It is created throughout the year.

Time records completed every pay period rather than reconstructed quarterly. Invoices attached to expenditure entries at payment rather than filed separately. Subrecipient monitoring completed on schedule rather than assembled retroactively.

For a financial statement audit, the request list includes: general ledger, bank reconciliations for each month, board minutes, major contracts and grant agreements, fixed asset schedules, and functional expense allocation methodology.

A Single Audit adds: the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (SEFA), all federal award agreements, personnel time records by grant, procurement records for federally funded purchases, and subrecipient monitoring documentation.

The SEFA preparation should start 60-90 days before fiscal year end — not at year end. Missing federal programs (often passthrough awards from state agencies) result in audit adjustments.

The formal evidence binder organized by auditor request categories reduces fieldwork duration and demonstrates that records were maintained contemporaneously.

Organizations that close audits quickly are not doing more work at audit time. They are doing less — because the work was already done.

Pennsylvania's BCO-10 charitable registration has a deadline that most nonprofits get wrong: 315 days after fiscal year end, not the end of the calendar year.

For a December 31 fiscal year end, that puts the renewal due date around November 11.

Fees scale with gross annual contributions: $15 at the bottom tier (under $25,000), $250 at the top tier (above $1,000,000). Using the wrong tier is one of the five most common rejection reasons.

The audit attachment threshold matches the top fee tier: audited financial statements are required above $1,000,000 in gross contributions. Reviewed statements apply at mid-tiers; compiled statements at lower tiers.

A nonprofit that crosses $1,000,000 for the first time needs to engage a CPA early — an audit started the month before the 315-day deadline rarely finishes without rush billing.

Pennsylvania accepts the Uniform Registration Statement (URS) in place of BCO-10, with a PA-specific supplement and fee. Organizations filing in multiple URS states use this to reduce duplicate data entry.

The BCO-10 fee and audit thresholds can shift when the Department of State updates the schedule — verify against the current schedule before each filing, not the prior year.
